abstract: This paper proposes a means of using the knowledge in a network to determine the functionality or relevance of individual units, both for the purpose of understanding the network's behavior and improving its performance. The basic idea is to iteratively train the network to a cer(cid:173) tain performance criterion, compute a measure of relevance that identi(cid:173) fies which input or hidden units are most critical to performance, and automatically trim the least relevant units. This skeletonization tech(cid:173) nique can be used to simplify networks by eliminating units that con(cid:173) vey redundant information; to improve learning performance by first learning with spare hidden units and then trimming the unnecessary ones away, thereby constraining generalization; and to understand the behavior of networks in terms of minimal "rules."

paragraphs: This paper proposes skeletonization, a method for simplifying a neural network by assessing how much its individual units matter. The guiding idea is to use what the trained network has learned to identify which inputs and hidden units are critical to its performance and which contribute redundant information.

The procedure repeats a sequence: train to a specified performance level, calculate a relevance measure, and remove the least relevant units. This makes simplification depend on the network’s learned function. Both input units and hidden units can be considered, so the process can reduce the information supplied to the network as well as its internal machinery.

The authors describe three uses for this approach: eliminating redundancy, improving learning by starting with spare hidden units and later removing unnecessary ones, and interpreting behavior through a smaller set of rules. Trimming also constrains generalization by reducing the retained representation. The contribution ties network size and interpretability to an explicit assessment of functional relevance after learning.
summary.tldr: Skeletonization repeatedly trains a network and removes its least relevant units to simplify representations and expose their essential structure.

title: Skeletonization: A Technique for Trimming the Fat from a Network via Relevance Assessment

paragraphs: This paper presents compact CMOS synapse circuits that operate directly on asynchronous pulse streams. The proposed circuits use only three or four MOS transistors per synapse. Neural activity is represented by how frequently pulses occur, while pulse magnitude remains constant. This takes inspiration from the pulse-based signaling of biological neurons.

Each synapse uses incoming pulses to increase or decrease the receiving neuron's activity. The sender's activity determines how often the changes occur, and the synaptic weight determines their size. The representation and arithmetic therefore work together: the timing of events carries the sender's state, while the connection controls their effect on the receiver.

The authors describe chips containing more than one hundred fully programmable synapses and project designs toward networks with hundreds of neurons. These are different scales of claim: the synapse chips are described implementations, while the larger neuron networks are projections. The significance lies in the compact synapse circuit and its direct processing of pulses, providing a hardware basis for the proposed expansion.
summary.tldr: Compact programmable synapse circuits compute directly on asynchronous pulses, with implemented chips supporting projections toward networks of hundreds of neurons.

title: Pulse-Firing Neural Chips for Hundreds of Neurons

abstract: In response to a puff of wind, the American cockroach turns away and runs. The circuit underlying the initial turn of this escape response consists of three populations of individually identifiable nerve cells and appears to em(cid:173) ploy distributed representations in its operation. We have reconstructed several neuronal and behavioral properties of this system using simplified neural network models and the backpropagation learning algorithm con(cid:173) strained by known structural characteristics of the circuitry. In order to test and refine the model, we have also compared the model's responses to various lesions with the insect's responses to similar lesions.

paragraphs: This paper models the initial turn a cockroach makes when escaping a puff of wind. The biological circuit contains three populations of individually identifiable nerve cells and appears to represent information across multiple cells. The study asks how this distributed activity can account for both neuronal responses and the animal's turning behavior.

The researchers build simplified neural networks and train them with backpropagation, while restricting their structure according to known features of the biological circuitry. Those constraints connect the learning problem to the actual nervous system. The resulting models reconstruct several properties of the neurons and behavior, showing how a simplified circuit can capture aspects of the transformation from sensory input to movement.

The researchers also compare the effects of lesions in the model with responses to similar lesions in the insect. These comparisons serve to test and refine the model beyond its ordinary responses. The approach matters because matching behavior after circuit damage provides another way to assess a proposed explanation of distributed sensorimotor control.
summary.tldr: An anatomically constrained neural model reconstructs aspects of the cockroach escape turn and is tested against biological lesion responses.

title: A Model of Distributed Sensorimotor Control in the Cockroach Escape Turn

abstract: Automatic determination of proper neural network topology by trimming over-sized networks is an important area of study, which has previously been addressed using a variety of techniques. In this paper, we present Information Measure Based Skeletonisation (IMBS), a new approach to this problem where superfluous hidden units are removed based on their information measure (1M). This measure, borrowed from decision tree in(cid:173) duction techniques, reflects the degree to which the hyperplane formed by a hidden unit discriminates between training data classes. We show the results of applying IMBS to three classification tasks and demonstrate that it removes a substantial number of hidden units without significantly affecting network performance.

In this paper, we present Information Measure Based Skeletonisation (IMBS), a new approach to this problem where superfluous hidden units are removed based on their information measure (1M). This measure, borrowed from decision tree in(cid:173) duction techniques, reflects the degree to which the hyperplane formed by a hidden unit discriminates between training data classes. We show the results of applying IMBS to three classification tasks and demonstrate that it removes a substantial number of hidden units without significantly affecting network performance.

paragraphs: Choosing a neural network's size can involve starting with more hidden units than necessary and removing those that contribute little. This paper introduces Information Measure Based Skeletonisation, or IMBS, as a way to perform that trimming automatically. Its goal is to simplify the network while retaining classification performance.

IMBS evaluates hidden units using an information measure adapted from decision-tree learning. The measure describes how well the hyperplane associated with a hidden unit separates training examples from different classes. It therefore connects the removal decision to the unit's ability to discriminate among the categories the network is learning.

The authors apply IMBS to three classification tasks and report removing a substantial number of hidden units without a significant effect on network performance. These findings support the use of class-discrimination information when deciding which units are superfluous. The contribution is a concrete criterion for reducing an oversized network, with demonstrations that considerable trimming can preserve its useful classification behavior.
summary.tldr: IMBS prunes hidden units using their class-discrimination information, substantially shrinking networks while largely preserving performance.

title: Information Measure Based Skeletonisation

abstract: Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) can be applied to several impor(cid:173) tant problems in molecular biology. We introduce a new convergent learning algorithm for HMMs that, unlike the classical Baum-Welch algorithm is smooth and can be applied on-line or in batch mode, with or without the usual Viterbi most likely path approximation. Left-right HMMs with insertion and deletion states are then trained to represent several protein families including immunoglobulins and kinases. In all cases, the models derived capture all the important statistical properties of the families and can be used efficiently in a number of important tasks such as multiple alignment, motif de(cid:173) tection, and classification. *and Division of Biology, California Institute of Technology. t and Department of Psychology, Stanford University.

paragraphs: The paper develops hidden Markov models for representing protein families and supporting molecular-biology tasks. It introduces a convergent learning algorithm described as smooth, in contrast to classical Baum-Welch learning. The algorithm can operate online or in batches, giving it alternative ways to incorporate training observations.

Learning can also proceed with or without the Viterbi approximation, which uses the most likely hidden-state path. The authors train left-to-right models containing insertion and deletion states on several protein families, including immunoglobulins and kinases. These states allow the family representation to accommodate sequence differences involving inserted or missing elements.

Across the families studied, the authors report that the models capture all important statistical properties. They describe efficient uses in multiple alignment, motif detection, and classification. The significance is that a learned statistical representation of a family can support several related sequence-analysis tasks. The paper thus combines a learning-method contribution with applications that demonstrate the usefulness of the resulting protein-family models.
summary.tldr: A convergent HMM learning algorithm builds protein-family models useful for sequence alignment, motif detection, and classification.

title: Hidden Markov Models in Molecular Biology: New Algorithms and Applications

paragraphs: This paper studies random k-SAT formulas, where each clause contains exactly k variables and the whole formula must be satisfied simultaneously. It considers M clauses built from N variables with random negations, keeping the clause-to-variable ratio fixed. This ratio expresses how densely the formula constrains the available variables.

For k equal to two, a sharp threshold at a ratio of one was already proven: as formula size grows, instances change from almost always satisfiable to almost never satisfiable across that boundary. The authors report computer experiments for k values from two through six showing similar threshold behavior for each value.

The paper uses finite-size scaling from statistical physics to characterize how behavior near the threshold depends on formula size. Annealed and replica-based mean-field theories also give a good account of the observations. The contribution is to describe satisfiability as a collective threshold phenomenon, connecting finite computational experiments with theories of how sharp transitions emerge as systems become larger.
summary.tldr: Experiments and statistical-physics methods characterize sharp satisfiability transitions in random k-SAT formulas.

title: The Statistical Mechanics of k-Satisfaction

abstract: Perceptual learning is defined as fast improvement in performance and retention of the learned ability over a period of time. In a set of psy(cid:173) chophysical experiments we demonstrated that perceptual learning oc(cid:173) curs for the discrimination of direction in stochastic motion stimuli. Here we model this learning using two approaches: a clustering model that learns to accommodate the motion noise, and an averaging model that learns to ignore the noise. Simulations of the models show performance similar to the psychophysical results.

In a set of psy(cid:173) chophysical experiments we demonstrated that perceptual learning oc(cid:173) curs for the discrimination of direction in stochastic motion stimuli. Here we model this learning using two approaches: a clustering model that learns to accommodate the motion noise, and an averaging model that learns to ignore the noise. Simulations of the models show performance similar to the psychophysical results.

paragraphs: The paper studies how people improve at judging motion direction when the visual stimulus contains randomness. The authors report psychophysical experiments demonstrating perceptual learning for this task. They describe perceptual learning as a rapid performance improvement whose benefit persists over time, making retained improvement the behavior that their models seek to explain.

They investigate two ways learning might handle the motion noise. A clustering model learns to accommodate it, whereas an averaging model learns to ignore it. This distinction concerns what changes during learning: the models take different approaches to the same noisy evidence while aiming to improve the direction judgment.

Simulations of both models produce performance similar to the psychophysical results. The reported agreement shows that the observed learning is compatible with two different computational treatments of noise. It therefore connects a behavioral finding to explicit candidate mechanisms without identifying a single mechanism as the sole explanation. The contribution is the joint experimental and modeling account of how motion discrimination can improve through learning.
summary.tldr: Clustering and averaging models both reproduce aspects of perceptual learning in noisy motion-direction judgments.

title: Learning direction in global motion: two classes of psychophysically-motivated models

abstract: Using a statistical mechanical formalism we calculate the evidence, generalisation error and consistency measure for a linear percep(cid:173) tron trained and tested on a set of examples generated by a non linear teacher. The teacher is said to be unrealisable because the student can never model it without error. Our model allows us to interpolate between the known case of a linear teacher, and an un(cid:173) realisable, nonlinear teacher. A comparison of the hyperparameters which maximise the evidence with those that optimise the perfor(cid:173) mance measures reveals that, in the non-linear case, the evidence procedure is a misleading guide to optimising performance. Finally, we explore the extent to which the evidence procedure is unreliable and find that, despite being sub-optimal, in some circumstances it might be a useful method for fixing the hyperparameters.

paragraphs: This paper studies hyperparameter selection when a learner cannot perfectly represent the rule generating its data. The learner is a linear perceptron, while the teacher can be nonlinear. In the nonlinear setting, the rule is called unrealisable because some error remains unavoidable for that student, regardless of how its parameters are chosen.

Using a statistical mechanical formulation, the authors calculate evidence, generalization error, and a consistency measure. Their model moves between a linear teacher and a nonlinear teacher, allowing them to examine how representational mismatch changes the relationship between these quantities. They compare hyperparameters selected by maximizing evidence with those that directly optimize the performance measures.

For the nonlinear case, evidence maximization can give misleading guidance about performance. The study nevertheless finds circumstances in which it remains useful despite being suboptimal. The result is a qualified assessment of evidence-based selection: its preferred hyperparameters need not produce the best predictions when the student's model class cannot express the teacher's rule.
summary.tldr: Evidence maximization can select suboptimal hyperparameters when a linear learner cannot represent a nonlinear teacher.

title: Hyperparameters Evidence and Generalisation for an Unrealisable Rule

abstract: We present a neural network-based face detection system. A retinally connected neural network examines small windows of an image, and decides whether each window contains a face. The system arbitrates between multiple networks to improve performance over a single network. We use a bootstrap algorithm for training, which adds false detections into the training set as training progresses. This eliminates the difficult task of manually selecting non-face training examples, which must be chosen to span the entire space of non-face images. Comparisons with another state-of-the-art face detection system are presented; our system has better performance in terms of detection and false-positive rates.

The system arbitrates between multiple networks to improve performance over a single network. We use a bootstrap algorithm for training, which adds false detections into the training set as training progresses. This eliminates the difficult task of manually selecting non-face training examples, which must be chosen to span the entire space of non-face images. Comparisons with another state-of-the-art face detection system are presented; our system has better performance in terms of detection and false-positive rates.

paragraphs: The paper presents a face detector that applies a neural network to small image windows. Each window receives a decision about whether it contains a face. The system also arbitrates among multiple networks, combining their decisions to improve performance beyond what a single network achieves.

A central training problem is choosing examples of images that are not faces. Such images cover an enormous variety of possible appearances, making manual selection difficult. The authors use a bootstrap process that adds false detections to the training set as learning proceeds. The detector's own mistakes therefore identify non-face examples that need further attention during training.

This creates a direct connection between observed errors and the construction of the training data. The paper reports comparisons with another leading face detection system and finds better performance in both detection and false-positive rates. Together, the results support a system combining local neural classification, decisions from multiple networks, and repeated training on the misleading image regions the detector actually encounters.
summary.tldr: A neural face detector combines multiple networks and learns from its false detections to improve detection and false-positive rates.

title: Human Face Detection in Visual Scenes

paragraphs: The paper studies overfitting in a deliberately simple setting: one perceptron learns outputs generated by another perceptron with the same architecture. The task is realizable, meaning that the learner's model class contains a solution capable of representing the generating rule. This makes it possible to study overfitting even when the architecture is adequate.

Both perceptrons use sigmoid output functions. Their gain controls the strength of the nonlinearity, providing a way to vary the learning problem while keeping the architectural match intact. The authors observe that strong nonlinearity produces overfitting. Having a correct solution available within the model class therefore does not ensure that learning from examples will generalize well.

The authors explain this behavior and develop a method to avoid it. They give two interpretations of the method: learning with noise and early stopping selected through cross-validation. The simple model provides a tractable setting for understanding behavior that also appears qualitatively in multilayer perceptrons, linking the shape of the learning problem to the need to control training.
summary.tldr: A perceptron can overfit data generated by an identical architecture when the output nonlinearity is strong.

title: A Realizable Learning Task which Exhibits Overfitting

abstract: Parti-game (Moore 1994a; Moore 1994b; Moore and Atkeson 1995) is a reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm that has a lot of promise in over(cid:173) coming the curse of dimensionality that can plague RL algorithms when applied to high-dimensional problems. In this paper we introduce mod(cid:173) ifications to the algorithm that further improve its performance and ro(cid:173) bustness. In addition, while parti-game solutions can be improved locally by standard local path-improvement techniques, we introduce an add-on algorithm in the same spirit as parti-game that instead tries to improve solutions in a non-local manner.
originalAbstract: Parti-game (Moore 1994a; Moore 1994b; Moore and Atkeson 1995) is a reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm that has a lot of promise in over(cid:173) coming the curse of dimensionality that can plague RL algorithms when applied to high-dimensional problems. In this paper we introduce mod(cid:173) ifications to the algorithm that further improve its performance and ro(cid:173) bustness. In addition, while parti-game solutions can be improved locally by standard local path-improvement techniques, we introduce an add-on algorithm in the same spirit as parti-game that instead tries to improve solutions in a non-local manner.

paragraphs: The paper develops improvements to parti-game, a reinforcement learning algorithm motivated by the difficulty of learning in high-dimensional problems. The authors describe the existing algorithm as promising for overcoming the curse of dimensionality. Their work builds on that promise by modifying the algorithm to improve its performance and robustness.

A second contribution concerns improving the solutions parti-game already finds. Standard path-improvement techniques can refine a solution locally, making changes in its immediate vicinity. The authors introduce an additional algorithm that instead attempts non-local improvements. This broadens the kind of revision considered, allowing the improvement process to look beyond nearby adjustments to the current solution.

The two contributions address different aspects of the method: the core modifications improve its operation, while the add-on targets further improvement of its solutions. The abstract describes the non-local procedure as an attempt to improve solutions, so its significance is the expanded search strategy rather than a stated guarantee of global optimality. Together, the changes extend parti-game's approach to difficult reinforcement learning problems.
summary.tldr: The paper improves parti-game's performance and robustness and adds a procedure that seeks non-local improvements to its solutions.

title: Robust, Efficient, Globally-Optimized Reinforcement Learning with the Parti-Game Algorithm

abstract: A challenging, unsolved problem in the speech recognition com(cid:173) munity is recognizing speech signals that are corrupted by loud, highly nonstationary noise. One approach to noisy speech recog(cid:173) nition is to automatically remove the noise from the cepstrum se(cid:173) quence before feeding it in to a clean speech recognizer. In previous work published in Eurospeech, we showed how a probability model trained on clean speech and a separate probability model trained on noise could be combined for the purpose of estimating the noise(cid:173) free speech from the noisy speech. We showed how an iterative 2nd order vector Taylor series approximation could be used for prob(cid:173) abilistic inference in this model. In many circumstances, it is not possible to obtain examples of noise without speech. Noise statis(cid:173) tics may change significantly during an utterance, so that speech(cid:173) free frames are not sufficient for estimating the noise model. In this paper, we show how the noise model can be learned even when the data contains speech. In particular, the noise model can be learned from the test utterance and then used to de noise the test utterance. The approximate inference technique is used as an approximate E step in a generalized EM algorithm that learns the parameters of the noise model from a test utterance. For both Wall Street J our(cid:173) nal data with added noise samples and the Aurora benchmark, we show that the new noise adaptive technique performs as well as or significantly better than the non-adaptive algorithm, without the need for a separate training set of noise examples.

paragraphs: Speech recognition becomes difficult when loud noise changes substantially during an utterance. One approach estimates clean speech features before passing them to a recognizer trained on clean speech. The authors’ earlier method combined separate probability models of speech and noise, using an iterative second-order Taylor approximation for inference.

The new contribution is learning the noise model directly from an utterance that also contains speech. This matters when isolated noise examples are unavailable, or when speech-free portions fail to capture noise changes throughout the utterance. The same test utterance supplies the information for adapting the noise model and is then denoised using that model.

The method uses approximate inference as the expectation step within a generalized EM procedure for learning noise parameters. On Wall Street Journal speech with added noise and on the Aurora benchmark, the adaptive method performs as well as or significantly better than the nonadaptive method. These results support adaptation without a separate noise-training collection, including settings where noise cannot be estimated adequately from silent intervals.
summary.tldr: ALGONQUIN learns a changing noise model from the test utterance itself, matching or improving nonadaptive performance without separate noise-training examples.

title: ALGONQUIN - Learning Dynamic Noise Models From Noisy Speech for Robust Speech Recognition

abstract: Incorporating invariances into a learning algorithm is a common problem in ma- chine learning. We provide a convex formulation which can deal with arbitrary loss functions and arbitrary losses. In addition, it is a drop-in replacement for most optimization algorithms for kernels, including solvers of the SVMStruct family. The advantage of our setting is that it relies on column generation instead of mod- ifying the underlying optimization problem directly.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to incorporate invariances into a learning algorithm. An invariance expresses that certain changes in an input should preserve the relevant prediction. The optimization challenge is to encode that requirement while retaining a formulation that can be handled by existing learning machinery.

The authors provide a convex formulation and state that it can accommodate arbitrary loss functions. Their approach relies on column generation rather than directly modifying the underlying optimization problem. This choice is central to the contribution: the mechanism for introducing invariance is designed to work with optimization machinery that is already available.

The formulation is presented as a drop-in replacement for most kernel optimization algorithms, including solvers in the SVMStruct family. Its stated value is therefore both mathematical and practical: it offers a convex treatment of invariance while maintaining broad compatibility with established solvers. The abstract emphasizes formulation and integration, making the contribution a general way to bring invariance requirements into learning systems across different choices of loss.
summary.tldr: A convex, column-generation formulation incorporates invariances while remaining compatible with most kernel optimization solvers.

title: Convex Learning with Invariances

abstract: We study a pattern classiﬁcation algorithm which has recently been proposed by Vapnik and coworkers. It builds on a new inductive principle which assumes that in addition to positive and negative data, a third class of data is available, termed the Universum. We assay the behavior of the algorithm by establishing links with Fisher discriminant analysis and oriented PCA, as well as with an SVM in a pro- jected subspace (or, equivalently, with a data-dependent reduced kernel). We also provide experimental results.

We assay the behavior of the algorithm by establishing links with Fisher discriminant analysis and oriented PCA, as well as with an SVM in a pro- jected subspace (or, equivalently, with a data-dependent reduced kernel). We also provide experimental results.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes a classification method that assumes access to three sources of data: positive examples, negative examples, and an additional collection called the Universum. The central question is how a learning principle built around this extra collection relates to more familiar ways of constructing a classifier. The contribution is an analysis of a previously proposed algorithm.

The authors establish connections with Fisher discriminant analysis and oriented principal component analysis. These links place the method alongside approaches concerned with selecting informative directions in the data. They also connect it to a support vector machine operating in a projected subspace. An equivalent description uses a reduced kernel whose form depends on the data.

These alternative views help explain the algorithm through its relationship to representation and classification. The projected-subspace description and the reduced-kernel description offer two ways to understand the same connection. The paper also supplies experimental results. Its stated contribution is therefore both conceptual and empirical: it clarifies the behavior of Universum-based inference while examining the method experimentally.
summary.tldr: The paper explains Universum-based classification through connections to discriminant analysis, oriented PCA, and SVMs in projected spaces.

title: An Analysis of Inference with the Universum

abstract: Many algorithms have been recently developed for reducing dimensionality by projecting data onto an intrinsic non-linear manifold. Unfortunately, existing algo- rithms often lose signiﬁcant precision in this transformation. Manifold Sculpting is a new algorithm that iteratively reduces dimensionality by simulating surface tension in local neighborhoods. We present several experiments that show Man- ifold Sculpting yields more accurate results than existing algorithms with both generated and natural data-sets. Manifold Sculpting is also able to beneﬁt from both prior dimensionality reduction efforts.
originalAbstract: Many algorithms have been recently developed for reducing dimensionality by projecting data onto an intrinsic non-linear manifold. We present several experiments that show Man- ifold Sculpting yields more accurate results than existing algorithms with both generated and natural data-sets. Manifold Sculpting is also able to beneﬁt from both prior dimensionality reduction efforts.

paragraphs: Dimensionality reduction seeks a lower-dimensional representation of data that may lie along a nonlinear manifold. The motivation here is that existing projection methods can lose substantial precision during that transformation. The paper introduces Manifold Sculpting as an iterative way to reduce dimensionality while addressing the accuracy of the resulting representation.

Its central mechanism simulates surface tension within local neighborhoods. This makes neighborhood-level structure part of the process that progressively reshapes the data into fewer dimensions. The method is described as iterative, so the dimensionality reduction develops through repeated adjustments. The surface-tension idea supplies the organizing principle for those adjustments.

Experiments on generated and natural datasets show more accurate results than existing algorithms in the reported comparisons. The paper also states that Manifold Sculpting can benefit from prior dimensionality-reduction efforts, giving earlier processing a role in the approach. The stated findings support an iterative, locally guided transformation as a useful alternative for obtaining accurate nonlinear representations, with evidence spanning both constructed data and naturally occurring datasets.
summary.tldr: Manifold Sculpting iteratively reduces dimensionality using simulated local surface tension and reports improved accuracy on generated and natural data.

title: Iterative Non-linear Dimensionality Reduction with Manifold Sculpting

abstract: In most cognitive and motor tasks, speed-accuracy tradeoffs are observed: Individuals can respond slowly and accurately, or quickly yet be prone to errors. Control mechanisms governing the initiation of behavioral responses are sensitive not only to task instructions and the stimulus being processed, but also to the recent stimulus history. When stimuli can be characterized on an easy-hard dimension (e.g., word frequency in a naming task), items preceded by easy trials are responded to more quickly, and with more errors, than items preceded by hard trials. We propose a rationally motivated mathematical model of this sequential adaptation of control, based on a diffusion model of the decision process in which difficulty corresponds to the drift rate for the correct response. The model assumes that responding is based on the posterior distribution over which response is correct, conditioned on the accumulated evidence. We derive this posterior as a function of the drift rate, and show that higher estimates of the drift rate lead to (normatively) faster responding. Trial-by-trial tracking of difficulty thus leads to sequential effects in speed and accuracy. Simulations show the model explains a variety of phenomena in human speeded decision making. We argue this passive statistical mechanism provides a more elegant and parsimonious account than extant theories based on elaborate control structures.

paragraphs: People often respond faster and make more mistakes after easy trials than after difficult ones. This paper explains that sequential pattern through a mathematical model of response initiation. It asks how recent experience changes expectations about task difficulty and, through those expectations, the tradeoff between speed and accuracy.

The model uses a diffusion decision process in which difficulty corresponds to the drift rate toward the correct response. It assumes that responding depends on the posterior probability of which response is correct, conditioned on accumulated evidence. The authors derive how that posterior depends on drift rate and show that a higher estimated drift rate normatively supports faster responding.

Tracking difficulty from trial to trial therefore produces changes in response speed and accuracy. Simulations show that the model explains several phenomena in human speeded decisions. The proposed account locates sequential adaptation in ongoing statistical estimation: recent trials change the interpretation of current evidence. The authors argue that this passive mechanism provides a more parsimonious explanation than accounts requiring elaborate control structures.
summary.tldr: A diffusion model explains sequential speed–accuracy effects through trial-by-trial estimates of task difficulty.

title: Optimal Response Initiation: Why Recent Experience Matters

abstract: We describe a novel stochastic process that can be used to construct a multidimensional generalization of the stick-breaking process and which is related to the classic stick breaking process described by Sethuraman1994 in one dimension. We describe how the process can be applied to relational data modeling using the de Finetti representation for infinitely and partially exchangeable arrays.
originalAbstract: We describe a novel stochastic process that can be used to construct a multidimensional generalization of the stick-breaking process and which is related to the classic stick breaking process described by Sethuraman1994 in one dimension. We describe how the process can be applied to relational data modeling using the de Finetti representation for infinitely and partially exchangeable arrays.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a stochastic process called the Mondrian process. Its central purpose is to construct a multidimensional generalization of stick breaking, carrying an idea associated with a one-dimensional construction into a setting with multiple dimensions. The authors also describe its relationship to the classical stick-breaking process in one dimension.

This connection gives the new construction a familiar mathematical reference point while expanding the kind of structure it can represent. The stated contribution is the definition of a stochastic process and its relationship to an existing construction. The abstract presents this as a modeling foundation rather than as a prediction algorithm with a reported performance comparison.

The authors describe an application to relational data modeling through the de Finetti representation for infinitely and partially exchangeable arrays. That representation supplies the stated mathematical link between the process and models of relationships. Taken together, the contributions connect multidimensional stick breaking with an exchangeability-based framework for relational data, establishing a route from a new probabilistic construction to a class of modeling problems.
summary.tldr: The Mondrian process generalizes stick breaking to multiple dimensions and supports relational modeling through exchangeable-array representations.

title: The Mondrian Process

abstract: There has been a recent push in extraction of 3D spatial layout of scenes. However, none of these approaches model the 3D interaction between objects and the spatial layout. In this paper, we argue for a parametric representation of objects in 3D, which allows us to incorporate volumetric constraints of the physical world. We show that augmenting current structured prediction techniques with volumetric reasoning significantly improves the performance of the state-of-the-art.
originalAbstract: There has been a recent push in extraction of 3D spatial layout of scenes. However, none of these approaches model the 3D interaction between objects and the spatial layout. In this paper, we argue for a parametric representation of objects in 3D, which allows us to incorporate volumetric constraints of the physical world. We show that augmenting current structured prediction techniques with volumetric reasoning significantly improves the performance of the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Estimating a room's three-dimensional layout involves understanding both its surfaces and the objects within it. This paper identifies a gap in the approaches it discusses: they recover spatial layout without modeling the three-dimensional interaction between objects and that layout. The authors argue that this interaction supplies useful information for scene interpretation.

Their approach represents objects parametrically in three dimensions. This representation makes it possible to incorporate volumetric constraints from the physical world into the prediction process. Objects are therefore described in terms that allow reasoning about the space they occupy and their relationship to the surrounding layout, bringing object geometry into the room-estimation problem.

The authors add this volumetric reasoning to existing structured prediction techniques and report a significant improvement over the state of the art. The finding supports the value of modeling objects and surfaces together when estimating spatial layout. The main contribution is the use of an explicit three-dimensional object representation to make physical constraints available to the prediction method.
summary.tldr: Adding volumetric constraints through parametric 3D object representations significantly improves room-layout estimation in the reported evaluation.

title: Estimating Spatial Layout of Rooms using Volumetric Reasoning about Objects and Surfaces

abstract: We show an application of a tree structure for approximate inference in graphical models using the expectation propagation algorithm. These approximations are typically used over graphs with short-range cycles. We demonstrate that these approximations also help in sparse graphs with long-range loops, as the ones used in coding theory to approach channel capacity. For asymptotically large sparse graph, the expectation propagation algorithm together with the tree structure yields a completely disconnected approximation to the graphical model but, for for finite-length practical sparse graphs, the tree structure approximation to the code graph provides accurate estimates for the marginal of each variable.
originalAbstract: We show an application of a tree structure for approximate inference in graphical models using the expectation propagation algorithm. These approximations are typically used over graphs with short-range cycles. We demonstrate that these approximations also help in sparse graphs with long-range loops, as the ones used in coding theory to approach channel capacity. For asymptotically large sparse graph, the expectation propagation algorithm together with the tree structure yields a completely disconnected approximation to the graphical model but, for for finite-length practical sparse graphs, the tree structure approximation to the code graph provides accurate estimates for the marginal of each variable.

paragraphs: Channel decoding can be represented as inference in a graphical model, where the task includes estimating the probabilities of individual variables. Loops in the graph complicate this calculation. The paper studies an approximation that combines expectation propagation with a tree structure, examining whether it helps on sparse graphs of the kind used in coding theory to approach channel capacity.

Tree-based approximations are typically applied to graphs containing short cycles. The contribution here is to demonstrate their usefulness when loops extend over longer ranges. Sparsity does not remove all dependencies, and a tree approximation can still capture relationships that matter for estimating individual variables in practical code graphs.

The results distinguish two regimes. For asymptotically large sparse graphs, the method produces an approximation in which all variables are disconnected. For practical graphs of finite length, however, the tree structure provides accurate marginal estimates. This distinction explains why the behavior in an infinite-size limit does not by itself describe the value of the approximation for finite channel-decoding problems.
summary.tldr: Tree-structured expectation propagation provides accurate variable marginals for practical finite sparse code graphs with long loops.

title: An Application of Tree-Structured Expectation Propagation for Channel Decoding

abstract: Warped Gaussian processes (WGP) [1] model output observations in regression tasks as a parametric nonlinear transformation of a Gaussian process (GP). The use of this nonlinear transformation, which is included as part of the probabilistic model, was shown to enhance performance by providing a better prior model on several data sets. In order to learn its parameters, maximum likelihood was used. In this work we show that it is possible to use a non-parametric nonlinear transformation in WGP and variationally integrate it out. The resulting Bayesian WGP is then able to work in scenarios in which the maximum likelihood WGP failed: Low data regime, data with censored values, classification, etc. We demonstrate the superior performance of Bayesian warped GPs on several real data sets.
originalAbstract: Warped Gaussian processes (WGP) [1] model output observations in regression tasks as a parametric nonlinear transformation of a Gaussian process (GP). The use of this nonlinear transformation, which is included as part of the probabilistic model, was shown to enhance performance by providing a better prior model on several data sets. In order to learn its parameters, maximum likelihood was used. In this work we show that it is possible to use a non-parametric nonlinear transformation in WGP and variationally integrate it out. The resulting Bayesian WGP is then able to work in scenarios in which the maximum likelihood WGP failed: Low data regime, data with censored values, classification, etc. We demonstrate the superior performance of Bayesian warped GPs on several real data sets.

paragraphs: Warped Gaussian processes model regression observations through a nonlinear transformation of a Gaussian process. This transformation is part of the probability model and can provide a better prior description of the data. Earlier warped Gaussian processes used a parametric transformation and learned its parameters by maximum likelihood.

This paper replaces that transformation with a nonparametric one and uses variational inference to integrate it out. The change concerns both flexibility and treatment of the transformation: instead of relying on a single maximum-likelihood fit of its parameters, the Bayesian construction incorporates it through approximate integration. The authors show that this combination is possible within the warped Gaussian process framework.

The resulting model works in settings where the maximum-likelihood version failed, including limited data, censored observations, and classification. The paper also reports superior performance on several real datasets. These findings support the value of changing how the nonlinear transformation is modeled and handled, with benefits demonstrated across the stated settings rather than asserted for every prediction problem.
summary.tldr: Bayesian warped Gaussian processes integrate out a nonparametric transformation and succeed in settings where maximum-likelihood warping failed.

title: Bayesian Warped Gaussian Processes

abstract: We consider the problem of independently sampling $s$ non-zero entries of a matrix $A$ in order to produce a sparse sketch of it, $B$, that minimizes $\|A-B\|_2$. For large $m \times n$ matrices, such that $n \gg m$ (for example, representing $n$ observations over $m$ attributes) we give distributions exhibiting four important properties. First, they have closed forms for the probability of sampling each item which are computable from minimal information regarding $A$. Second, they allow sketching of matrices whose non-zeros are presented to the algorithm in arbitrary order as a stream, with $O(1)$ computation per non-zero. Third, the resulting sketch matrices are not only sparse, but their non-zero entries are highly compressible. Lastly, and most importantly, under mild assumptions, our distributions are provably competitive with the optimal offline distribution. Note that the probabilities in the optimal offline distribution may be complex functions of all the entries in the matrix. Therefore, regardless of computational complexity, the optimal distribution might be impossible to compute in the streaming model.

paragraphs: A large matrix can be approximated by keeping a sampled collection of its nonzero entries. The challenge is choosing sampling probabilities that produce a small spectral-norm error while remaining practical when the whole matrix is unavailable. This paper focuses on matrices with many more columns than rows, such as many observations described by fewer attributes.

The authors give sampling distributions with explicit formulas that require little information about the matrix. Their approach supports nonzero entries arriving in arbitrary streaming order and requires constant computation per incoming nonzero. The resulting sketch is sparse, and its retained values are also highly compressible, addressing storage beyond simply reducing the number of entries.

Under mild assumptions, the distributions are provably competitive with the best offline sampling distribution. That comparison matters because an offline optimum may depend intricately on every matrix entry and may therefore be impossible to compute in a streaming setting, regardless of available computation. The result connects practical streaming constraints with a conditional guarantee against a much more informed sampling choice.
summary.tldr: Simple streaming sampling distributions produce compressible matrix sketches that are conditionally competitive with the optimal offline distribution.

title: Near-Optimal Entrywise Sampling for Data Matrices

abstract: Generative models can be seen as the swiss army knives of machine learning, as many problems can be written probabilistically in terms of the distribution of the data, including prediction, reconstruction, imputation and simulation. One of the most promising directions for unsupervised learning may lie in Deep Learning methods, given their success in supervised learning. However, one of the current problems with deep unsupervised learning methods, is that they often are harder to scale. As a result there are some easier, more scalable shallow methods, such as the Gaussian Mixture Model and the Student-t Mixture Model, that remain surprisingly competitive. In this paper we propose a new scalable deep generative model for images, called the Deep Gaussian Mixture Model, that is a straightforward but powerful generalization of GMMs to multiple layers. The parametrization of a Deep GMM allows it to efficiently capture products of variations in natural images. We propose a new EM-based algorithm that scales well to large datasets, and we show that both the Expectation and the Maximization steps can easily be distributed over multiple machines. In our density estimation experiments we show that deeper GMM architectures generalize better than more shallow ones, with results in the same ballpark as the state of the art.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a deep generative model for images that extends Gaussian mixture models across multiple layers. Its motivation is that scalable shallow mixture models remain competitive even as deeper approaches offer promising representations. The authors seek to combine a deeper model's ability to describe image variation with a training procedure suited to large datasets.

The Deep Gaussian Mixture Model is parameterized to capture products of variations in natural images efficiently. This gives the multilayer construction a specific modeling purpose: representing combinations of variation in the data. The paper also introduces an expectation-maximization training algorithm and shows that both its expectation and maximization stages can be distributed across machines.

In density estimation experiments, deeper versions generalize better than shallower versions, and their results are broadly comparable to the state of the art. These findings support depth within this mixture-model family while the distributed training design addresses scalability. The demonstrated outcome is improved modeling of the image distribution, which is the focus of the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: Deep Gaussian mixture models capture combinations of image variation and use distributable EM training, with deeper models generalizing better in density estimation experiments.

title: Factoring Variations in Natural Images with Deep Gaussian Mixture Models

abstract: Adaptive schemes, where tasks are assigned based on the data collected thus far, are widely used in practical crowdsourcing systems to efficiently allocate the budget. However, existing theoretical analyses of crowdsourcing systems suggest that the gain of adaptive task assignments is minimal. To bridge this gap, we investigate this question under a strictly more general probabilistic model, which has been recently introduced to model practical crowdsourcing data sets. Under this generalized Dawid-Skene model, we characterize the fundamental trade-off between budget and accuracy, and introduce a novel adaptive scheme that matches this fundamental limit. We further quantify the gain of adaptivity, by comparing the trade-off with the one for non-adaptive schemes, and confirm that the gain is significant and can be made arbitrarily large depending on the distribution of the difficulty level of the tasks at hand.
originalAbstract: Adaptive schemes, where tasks are assigned based on the data collected thus far, are widely used in practical crowdsourcing systems to efficiently allocate the budget. However, existing theoretical analyses of crowdsourcing systems suggest that the gain of adaptive task assignments is minimal. To bridge this gap, we investigate this question under a strictly more general probabilistic model, which has been recently introduced to model practical crowdsourcing data sets. Under this generalized Dawid-Skene model, we characterize the fundamental trade-off between budget and accuracy, and introduce a novel adaptive scheme that matches this fundamental limit. We further quantify the gain of adaptivity, by comparing the trade-off with the one for non-adaptive schemes, and confirm that the gain is significant and can be made arbitrarily large depending on the distribution of the difficulty level of the tasks at hand.

paragraphs: Crowdsourcing systems often assign new tasks using the answers already collected, so spending can respond to emerging evidence. Yet earlier theoretical analyses suggested that this adaptivity offered little benefit. The paper investigates whether that conclusion changes under a more general probabilistic model designed to describe practical crowdsourcing data.

Working within a generalized Dawid-Skene model, the authors characterize the fundamental relationship between available budget and achievable accuracy. They then construct an adaptive assignment scheme that matches this limit. Budget optimality here is a statement within that model: the scheme reaches the performance boundary established by the analysis.

The authors compare this boundary with the corresponding one for assignments fixed without adaptation. They find that the advantage of adaptivity can be significant and can become arbitrarily large, depending on the distribution of task difficulty. This dependence is central to the result. It explains how adaptive allocation can have substantial value in some crowdsourcing settings even when less general analyses predict only small gains.
summary.tldr: Under a generalized crowdsourcing model, an adaptive assignment scheme attains the optimal budget–accuracy trade-off and can greatly outperform non-adaptive allocation.

title: Achieving budget-optimality with adaptive schemes in crowdsourcing

abstract: We propose and study a new class of submodular functions called deep submodular functions (DSFs). We define DSFs and situate them within the broader context of classes of submodular functions in relationship both to various matroid ranks and sums of concave composed with modular functions (SCMs). Notably, we find that DSFs constitute a strictly broader class than SCMs, thus motivating their use, but that they do not comprise all submodular functions. Interestingly, some DSFs can be seen as special cases of certain deep neural networks (DNNs), hence the name. Finally, we provide a method to learn DSFs in a max-margin framework, and offer preliminary results applying this both to synthetic and real-world data instances.

We define DSFs and situate them within the broader context of classes of submodular functions in relationship both to various matroid ranks and sums of concave composed with modular functions (SCMs). Notably, we find that DSFs constitute a strictly broader class than SCMs, thus motivating their use, but that they do not comprise all submodular functions. Interestingly, some DSFs can be seen as special cases of certain deep neural networks (DNNs), hence the name. Finally, we provide a method to learn DSFs in a max-margin framework, and offer preliminary results applying this both to synthetic and real-world data instances.

paragraphs: Submodular functions describe set-valued objectives with a diminishing-returns structure. This paper introduces a new family called deep submodular functions and investigates what that family can represent. The central question is how to gain expressive power while retaining submodularity, rather than treating every possible set function as equally suitable.

The authors compare the new family with matroid rank functions and with sums of concave functions composed with modular functions, abbreviated SCMs. They prove that deep submodular functions strictly extend SCMs, meaning that the new family can represent functions the older family cannot. They also establish a boundary: it still does not include every submodular function.

Some deep submodular functions can be represented as special cases of certain deep neural networks, which motivates the name. The paper also provides a max-margin method for learning them and reports preliminary applications to synthetic and real-world data. Together, these contributions supply both a representation theory and an initial practical route for fitting this more expressive family.
summary.tldr: Deep submodular functions expand a known representational family while preserving submodularity and support learning through a max-margin framework.

title: Deep Submodular Functions: Definitions and Learning

abstract: We introduce the general and powerful scheme of predicting information re-use in optimization algorithms. This allows us to devise a computationally efficient algorithm for bandit convex optimization with new state-of-the-art guarantees for both Lipschitz loss functions and loss functions with Lipschitz gradients. This is the first algorithm admitting both a polynomial time complexity and a regret that is polynomial in the dimension of the action space that improves upon the original regret bound for Lipschitz loss functions, achieving a regret of $\widetilde O(T^{11/16}d^{3/8})$. Our algorithm further improves upon the best existing polynomial-in-dimension bound (both computationally and in terms of regret) for loss functions with Lipschitz gradients, achieving a regret of $\widetilde O(T^{8/13} d^{5/3})$.
originalAbstract: We introduce the general and powerful scheme of predicting information re-use in optimization algorithms. This allows us to devise a computationally efficient algorithm for bandit convex optimization with new state-of-the-art guarantees for both Lipschitz loss functions and loss functions with Lipschitz gradients. This is the first algorithm admitting both a polynomial time complexity and a regret that is polynomial in the dimension of the action space that improves upon the original regret bound for Lipschitz loss functions, achieving a regret of $\widetilde O(T^{11/16}d^{3/8})$. Our algorithm further improves upon the best existing polynomial-in-dimension bound (both computationally and in terms of regret) for loss functions with Lipschitz gradients, achieving a regret of $\widetilde O(T^{8/13} d^{5/3})$.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a scheme for predicting how information can be reused within optimization algorithms. It applies this idea to bandit convex optimization, where decisions must be made with limited feedback about losses. The central contribution combines improved regret guarantees with computational efficiency, addressing both decision quality and the cost of producing decisions.

For Lipschitz loss functions, the algorithm achieves regret Õ(T^(11/16)d^(3/8)), where T is the number of rounds and d is the action-space dimension. The abstract identifies it as the first algorithm to improve the original regret bound while having both polynomial runtime and regret that is polynomial in dimension. The tilde notation suppresses logarithmic factors.

For the more structured case of losses with Lipschitz gradients, the stated bound is Õ(T^(8/13)d^(5/3)). This improves the best existing polynomial-in-dimension bound described in the abstract in both computational and regret terms. The two results apply to different regularity conditions, so their importance is the improved guarantee within each setting rather than a single bound claimed for all losses.
summary.tldr: Predicting information reuse yields efficient bandit convex optimization with improved regret bounds for Lipschitz losses and losses with Lipschitz gradients.

title: Optimistic Bandit Convex Optimization

abstract: We discover a screening rule for l1-regularized Ising model estimation. The simple closed-form screening rule is a necessary and sufficient condition for exactly recovering the blockwise structure of a solution under any given regularization parameters. With enough sparsity, the screening rule can be combined with various optimization procedures to deliver solutions efficiently in practice. The screening rule is especially suitable for large-scale exploratory data analysis, where the number of variables in the dataset can be thousands while we are only interested in the relationship among a handful of variables within moderate-size clusters for interpretability. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the efficiency and insights gained from the introduction of the screening rule.
originalAbstract: We discover a screening rule for l1-regularized Ising model estimation. The simple closed-form screening rule is a necessary and sufficient condition for exactly recovering the blockwise structure of a solution under any given regularization parameters. With enough sparsity, the screening rule can be combined with various optimization procedures to deliver solutions efficiently in practice. The screening rule is especially suitable for large-scale exploratory data analysis, where the number of variables in the dataset can be thousands while we are only interested in the relationship among a handful of variables within moderate-size clusters for interpretability. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the efficiency and insights gained from the introduction of the screening rule.

paragraphs: Estimating relationships among thousands of variables can be computationally demanding and difficult to interpret. This paper addresses that problem for l1-regularized Ising models by identifying the block structure of a solution. The blocks group variables into separate parts of the fitted relationship structure, making moderate-size clusters available for closer examination.

The main contribution is a simple screening rule with a closed-form expression. For any specified regularization parameters, its condition is both necessary and sufficient to recover the solution's block structure exactly. This is stronger than a heuristic for finding plausible clusters: the rule characterizes the actual block structure of the regularized solution.

When the solution is sufficiently sparse, the screening rule can work with different optimization procedures to make estimation efficient in practice. This is particularly useful for exploratory analysis focused on a small set of interpretable relationships within a much larger dataset. Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate computational efficiency and analytical insights from using the rule.
summary.tldr: A closed-form screening rule exactly identifies blocks in l1-regularized Ising solutions and can accelerate estimation when sufficient sparsity is present.

title: A Screening Rule for l1-Regularized Ising Model Estimation

abstract: The remarkable successes of deep learning in speech recognition and computer vision have motivated efforts to adapt similar techniques to other problem domains, including reinforcement learning (RL). Consequently, RL methods have produced rich motor behaviors on simulated robot tasks, with their success largely attributed to the use of multi-layer neural networks. This work is among the first to carefully study what might be responsible for these recent advancements. Our main result calls this emerging narrative into question by showing that much simpler architectures -- based on linear and RBF parameterizations -- achieve comparable performance to state of the art results. We not only study different policy representations with regard to performance measures at hand, but also towards robustness to external perturbations. We again find that the learned neural network policies --- under the standard training scenarios --- are no more robust than linear (or RBF) policies; in fact, all three are remarkably brittle. Finally, we then directly modify the training scenarios in order to favor more robust policies, and we again do not find a compelling case to favor multi-layer architectures. Overall, this study suggests that multi-layer architectures should not be the default choice, unless a side-by-side comparison to simpler architectures shows otherwise. More generally, we hope that these results lead to more interest in carefully studying the architectural choices, and associated trade-offs, for training generalizable and robust policies.

They argue that complex policy networks should earn their place through direct comparison with simpler choices. summary.tldr: Simple linear and RBF policies match strong continuous-control results, challenging the assumed advantage of multilayer networks.

title: Towards Generalization and Simplicity in Continuous Control

abstract: Mechanistic models of single-neuron dynamics have been extensively studied in computational neuroscience. However, identifying which models can quantitatively reproduce empirically measured data has been challenging. We propose to overcome this limitation by using likelihood-free inference approaches (also known as Approximate Bayesian Computation, ABC) to perform full Bayesian inference on single-neuron models. Our approach builds on recent advances in ABC by learning a neural network which maps features of the observed data to the posterior distribution over parameters. We learn a Bayesian mixture-density network approximating the posterior over multiple rounds of adaptively chosen simulations. Furthermore, we propose an efficient approach for handling missing features and parameter settings for which the simulator fails, as well as a strategy for automatically learning relevant features using recurrent neural networks. On synthetic data, our approach efficiently estimates posterior distributions and recovers ground-truth parameters. On in-vitro recordings of membrane voltages, we recover multivariate posteriors over biophysical parameters, which yield model-predicted voltage traces that accurately match empirical data. Our approach will enable neuroscientists to perform Bayesian inference on complex neuron models without having to design model-specific algorithms, closing the gap between mechanistic and statistical approaches to single-neuron modelling.

paragraphs: Mechanistic neuron models describe how a neuron's dynamics arise from biophysical parameters, but identifying parameters that reproduce measured activity is challenging. This paper develops a Bayesian approach that estimates a distribution over plausible parameter settings. It uses likelihood-free inference, allowing simulations to support inference without requiring a directly evaluated likelihood.

A Bayesian mixture-density network learns to map features of observed activity to an approximate posterior distribution over parameters. Training proceeds through several rounds of adaptively selected simulations. The method also handles missing features and parameter settings where simulation fails. A recurrent neural network provides a way to learn relevant data features automatically, reducing the need to specify all of them manually.

On synthetic data, the approach efficiently estimates posterior distributions and recovers the generating parameters. On recorded membrane voltages from in-vitro experiments, it obtains joint distributions over biophysical parameters whose predicted voltage traces closely match observations. These results support a flexible route for connecting mechanistic neuron simulations with statistical inference, without designing a separate inference algorithm for each model.
summary.tldr: An adaptively trained neural density model estimates Bayesian parameter distributions for neuron simulators and reproduces measured voltage dynamics.

title: Flexible statistical inference for mechanistic models of neural dynamics

abstract: In recent years, deep generative models have been shown to 'imagine' convincing high-dimensional observations such as images, audio, and even video, learning directly from raw data. In this work, we ask how to imagine goal-directed visual plans -- a plausible sequence of observations that transition a dynamical system from its current configuration to a desired goal state, which can later be used as a reference trajectory for control. We focus on systems with high-dimensional observations, such as images, and propose an approach that naturally combines representation learning and planning. Our framework learns a generative model of sequential observations, where the generative process is induced by a transition in a low-dimensional planning model, and an additional noise. By maximizing the mutual information between the generated observations and the transition in the planning model, we obtain a low-dimensional representation that best explains the causal nature of the data. We structure the planning model to be compatible with efficient planning algorithms, and we propose several such models based on either discrete or continuous states. Finally, to generate a visual plan, we project the current and goal observations onto their respective states in the planning model, plan a trajectory, and then use the generative model to transform the trajectory to a sequence of observations. We demonstrate our method on imagining plausible visual plans of rope manipulation.

High-dimensional inputs such as images make learning a useful planning representation central to this task.

The result connects representation learning to an explicit planning process, making the learned representation useful for constructing goal-directed observation sequences.
summary.tldr: Causal InfoGAN learns compact planning states and renders planned trajectories as plausible visual sequences, demonstrated on rope manipulation.

title: Learning Plannable Representations with Causal InfoGAN

abstract: Learning to cooperate with friends and compete with foes is a key component of multi-agent reinforcement learning. Typically to do so, one requires access to either a model of or interaction with the other agent(s). Here we show how to learn effective strategies for cooperation and competition in an asymmetric information game with no such model or interaction. Our approach is to encourage an agent to reveal or hide their intentions using an information-theoretic regularizer. We consider both the mutual information between goal and action given state, as well as the mutual information between goal and state. We show how to stochastically optimize these regularizers in a way that is easy to integrate with policy gradient reinforcement learning. Finally, we demonstrate that cooperative (competitive) policies learned with our approach lead to more (less) reward for a second agent in two simple asymmetric information games.

paragraphs: In games with asymmetric information, an agent's behavior can reveal or conceal what it is trying to accomplish. This paper uses that idea to learn cooperative or competitive strategies without a model of the other agent or interaction with it during learning. The agent is encouraged to make its intentions more or less informative through an information-theoretic regularizer.

The authors consider two quantities: the mutual information between goal and action given the current state, and the mutual information between goal and state. These capture different ways behavior can carry information about an agent's objective. The paper develops stochastic methods for optimizing both regularizers that can be integrated into policy-gradient reinforcement learning.

In two simple asymmetric-information games, policies trained to cooperate lead to greater reward for a second agent, while policies trained to compete lead to lower reward for that agent. The experiments show that controlling how much goal information an agent exposes can affect another agent's success, even when the learning procedure does not directly model or interact with that other agent.
summary.tldr: Information regularization teaches agents to reveal or hide their goals, helping or hindering another agent in two asymmetric-information games.

title: Learning to Share and Hide Intentions using Information Regularization

abstract: We address the problem of learning semantic representation of questions to measure similarity between pairs as a continuous distance metric. Our work naturally extends Word Mover’s Distance (WMD) [1] by representing text documents as normal distributions instead of bags of embedded words. Our learned metric measures the dissimilarity between two questions as the minimum amount of distance the intent (hidden representation) of one question needs to "travel" to match the intent of another question. We first learn to repeat, reformulate questions to infer intents as normal distributions with a deep generative model [2] (variational auto encoder). Semantic similarity between pairs is then learned discriminatively as an optimal transport distance metric (Wasserstein 2) with our novel variational siamese framework. Among known models that can read sentences individually, our proposed framework achieves competitive results on Quora duplicate questions dataset. Our work sheds light on how deep generative models can approximate distributions (semantic representations) to effectively measure semantic similarity with meaningful distance metrics from Information Theory.

paragraphs: Determining whether two questions have similar meanings requires a representation of their intent and a way to compare those representations. This paper represents each question as a normal distribution in a continuous hidden space. It extends the idea behind Word Mover's Distance, replacing collections of embedded words with distributions that represent entire questions.

A variational autoencoder first learns to repeat and reformulate questions, using those tasks to infer distributions over their hidden intents. A variational siamese framework then learns semantic similarity discriminatively through the Wasserstein-2 distance. The comparison is framed as the minimum transport needed to move one question's intent distribution into agreement with the other's.

The resulting method achieves competitive performance on the Quora duplicate-questions dataset among models that process sentences individually. That qualification defines the comparison group for the reported result. More broadly, the work demonstrates a way to combine generative representation learning with a meaningful distance between distributions, so semantic similarity is expressed through the geometry of learned intent distributions.
summary.tldr: The method represents question intents as normal distributions and learns semantic similarity through Wasserstein-2 transport distance.

title: Learning semantic similarity in a continuous space

abstract: Inverse Problems in medical imaging and computer vision are traditionally solved using purely model-based methods. Among those variational regularization models are one of the most popular approaches. We propose a new framework for applying data-driven approaches to inverse problems, using a neural network as a regularization functional. The network learns to discriminate between the distribution of ground truth images and the distribution of unregularized reconstructions. Once trained, the network is applied to the inverse problem by solving the corresponding variational problem. Unlike other data-based approaches for inverse problems, the algorithm can be applied even if only unsupervised training data is available. Experiments demonstrate the potential of the framework for denoising on the BSDS dataset and for computer tomography reconstruction on the LIDC dataset.

paragraphs: Inverse problems reconstruct an image from measurements, as in denoising or medical imaging. A regularizer helps guide reconstruction by expressing which candidate images are preferable. This paper proposes learning that regularizer with a neural network, bringing information from image data into the variational optimization framework traditionally used for these problems.

The network learns to distinguish the distribution of ground-truth images from the distribution of reconstructions produced without regularization. This discrimination task supplies a learned criterion for assessing reconstructed images. After training, the network becomes the regularization functional in the corresponding variational problem, and solving that problem produces the reconstruction. The learned component therefore participates directly in the reconstruction objective.

An important feature is that the framework can operate with unsupervised training data, broadening the circumstances in which learned regularization can be used. Experiments address image denoising on BSDS and computed tomography reconstruction on LIDC. These results demonstrate the framework's potential across two reconstruction tasks, supporting the idea that distribution-based learning can improve the guidance supplied to an inverse-problem solver.
summary.tldr: A neural network learns an image regularizer from distributions and then guides variational reconstruction, even with unsupervised training data.

title: Adversarial Regularizers in Inverse Problems

abstract: Many structured prediction problems admit a natural loss function for evaluation such as the edit-distance or $n$-gram loss. However, existing learning algorithms are typically designed to optimize alternative objectives such as the cross-entropy. This is because a na\"{i}ve implementation of the natural loss functions often results in intractable gradient computations. In this paper, we design efficient gradient computation algorithms for two broad families of structured prediction loss functions: rational and tropical losses. These families include as special cases the $n$-gram loss, the edit-distance loss, and many other loss functions commonly used in natural language processing and computational biology tasks that are based on sequence similarity measures. Our algorithms make use of weighted automata and graph operations over appropriate semirings to design efficient solutions. They facilitate efficient gradient computation and hence enable one to train learning models such as neural networks with complex structured losses.
