paragraphs: Structured prediction tasks often have evaluation measures that reflect the actual errors users care about, such as edit distance or n-gram mismatch. Training commonly uses a different objective, such as cross-entropy, because directly computing gradients for these structured losses can become intractable. The paper addresses this computational obstacle to aligning training with evaluation.

The authors develop efficient gradient algorithms for two broad loss families, called rational and tropical losses. These include edit-distance and n-gram losses as well as other sequence-similarity measures used in natural language processing and computational biology. The contribution therefore covers a collection of related objectives rather than a single specialized loss.

The algorithms organize computation using weighted automata and graph operations over suitable semirings. These mathematical structures provide a way to carry out the gradient calculations efficiently. As a result, models including neural networks can be trained with complex structured losses from the supported families. The stated advance is computational feasibility for these objectives, enabling training to use losses that would be difficult to handle through a naive implementation.
summary.tldr: Efficient gradient algorithms make broad families of structured losses, including edit-distance and n-gram losses, usable for model training.

title: Efficient Gradient Computation for Structured Output Learning with Rational and Tropical Losses

abstract: Transformer architectures show significant promise for natural language processing. Given that a single pretrained model can be fine-tuned to perform well on many different tasks, these networks appear to extract generally useful linguistic features. A natural question is how such networks represent this information internally. This paper describes qualitative and quantitative investigations of one particularly effective model, BERT. At a high level, linguistic features seem to be represented in separate semantic and syntactic subspaces. We find evidence of a fine-grained geometric representation of word senses. We also present empirical descriptions of syntactic representations in both attention matrices and individual word embeddings, as well as a mathematical argument to explain the geometry of these representations.

paragraphs: BERT’s usefulness across language tasks raises a question about what its internal representations contain. This paper investigates that question through both qualitative and quantitative analysis. Its focus is the geometry of linguistic information: how meaning and grammatical structure appear in the model’s internal representations.

The authors find that semantic and syntactic features seem to occupy separate subspaces. They also identify evidence of a fine-grained geometric representation of word senses, suggesting that distinctions in meaning have structure within the representation space. These observations are presented as evidence about BERT’s organization, preserving the exploratory character of the findings.

The study examines syntax in both attention matrices and individual word embeddings, giving empirical descriptions at two different locations within the model. A mathematical argument accompanies those descriptions to help explain their geometry. Together, the analyses connect visible patterns with quantitative measurements and theoretical reasoning. The contribution is a more concrete account of how a successful language model may internally organize meaning and syntax.
summary.tldr: Geometric analyses of BERT find evidence of structured word senses and apparently separate semantic and syntactic subspaces.

title: Visualizing and Measuring the Geometry of BERT

abstract: We study the problem of inverting a deep generative model with ReLU activations. Inversion corresponds to finding a latent code vector that explains observed measurements as much as possible. In most prior works this is performed by attempting to solve a non-convex optimization problem involving the generator. In this paper we obtain several novel theoretical results for the inversion problem. We show that for the realizable case, single layer inversion can be performed exactly in polynomial time, by solving a linear program. Further, we show that for two layers, inversion is NP-hard to recover binary latent code (even for the realizable case) and the pre-image set can be non-convex. For generative models of arbitrary depth, we show that exact recovery is possible in polynomial time with high probability, if the layers are expanding and the weights are randomly selected. Very recent work analyzed the same problem for gradient descent inversion. Their analysis requires significantly higher expansion (logarithmic in the latent dimension) while our proposed algorithm can provably reconstruct even with constant factor expansion. We also provide provable error bounds for different norms for reconstructing noisy observations. Our empirical validation demonstrates that we obtain better reconstructions when the latent dimension is large.

paragraphs: Inverting a generative network means finding a latent input that explains an observed output. This paper studies generators with ReLU activations and develops recovery results that distinguish easy cases from computationally difficult ones. Its approach examines inversion through individual layers rather than relying solely on a nonconvex optimization over the entire generator.

For a single layer, an exactly explainable observation can be inverted in polynomial time using a linear program. With two layers, however, recovering a binary latent code is NP-hard even when an exact explanation exists, and the set of possible inputs can be nonconvex. These results show that exact explainability alone does not make inversion computationally easy.

For arbitrary depth, the authors prove high-probability polynomial-time exact recovery when layers expand and weights are randomly chosen. Their algorithm permits constant-factor expansion, whereas the compared gradient-descent analysis requires substantially greater expansion. They also provide reconstruction-error bounds for noisy observations under different norms. Empirical results show better reconstructions in the reported comparisons when the latent dimension is large.
summary.tldr: Layerwise inversion gives efficient recovery guarantees for expanding random ReLU generators, alongside hardness results for more general inversion settings.

title: Inverting Deep Generative models, One layer at a time

abstract: Transportation cost is an attractive similarity measure between probability distributions due to its many useful theoretical properties. However, solving optimal transport exactly can be prohibitively expensive. Therefore, there has been significant effort towards the design of scalable approximation algorithms. Previous combinatorial results [Sharathkumar, Agarwal STOC '12, Agarwal, Sharathkumar STOC '14] have focused primarily on the design of near-linear time multiplicative approximation algorithms. There has also been an effort to design approximate solutions with additive errors [Cuturi NIPS '13, Altschuler \etal\ NIPS '17, Dvurechensky \etal\, ICML '18, Quanrud, SOSA '19] within a time bound that is linear in the size of the cost matrix and polynomial in $C/\delta$; here $C$ is the largest value in the cost matrix and $\delta$ is the additive error. We present an adaptation of the classical graph algorithm of Gabow and Tarjan and provide a novel analysis of this algorithm that bounds its execution time by $\BigO(\frac{n^2 C}{\delta}+ \frac{nC^2}{\delta^2})$. Our algorithm is extremely simple and executes, for an arbitrarily small constant $\eps$, only $\lfloor \frac{2C}{(1-\eps)\delta}\rfloor + 1$ iterations, where each iteration consists only of a Dijkstra-type search followed by a depth-first search. We also provide empirical results that suggest our algorithm is competitive with respect to a sequential implementation of the Sinkhorn algorithm in execution time. Moreover, our algorithm quickly computes a solution for very small values of $\delta$ whereas Sinkhorn algorithm slows down due to numerical instability.

This paper studies an additive approximation: the computed transport cost may exceed the optimum by a specified amount, delta. That makes the relationship between accuracy and computation central to the method.

The authors also report that their method quickly obtains solutions for very small additive errors, where the compared Sinkhorn algorithm slows because of numerical instability. These findings support the algorithm as a practical option when tight additive accuracy matters.
summary.tldr: A graph-search algorithm approximates optimal transport with a proved additive-error runtime bound and promising performance at tight error tolerances.

title: A Graph Theoretic Additive Approximation of Optimal Transport

abstract: Low-rank matrix factorization is a problem of broad importance, owing to the ubiquity of low-rank models in machine learning contexts. In spite of its non- convexity, this problem has a well-behaved geometric landscape, permitting local search algorithms such as gradient descent to converge to global minimizers. In this paper, we study low-rank matrix factorization in the distributed setting, where local variables at each node encode parts of the overall matrix factors, and consensus is encouraged among certain such variables. We identify conditions under which this new problem also has a well-behaved geometric landscape, and we propose an extension of distributed gradient descent (DGD) to solve this problem. The favorable landscape allows us to prove convergence to global optimality with exact consensus, a stronger result than what is provided by off-the-shelf DGD theory.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix factorization represents a matrix through smaller factors. Although its optimization is nonconvex, favorable geometry can allow local search methods to reach global minimizers. This paper asks whether comparable guarantees survive when the factorization is distributed across multiple computing nodes, each holding variables that encode portions of the overall factors.

Distribution adds a coordination requirement: certain local variables must agree across nodes. The authors study a formulation that encourages this consensus and identify conditions under which its optimization landscape remains well behaved. Those conditions are essential to the result; distributing a factorization problem does not by itself establish the favorable geometry.

Using that structure, the paper proposes an extension of distributed gradient descent and proves convergence to global optimality with exact consensus. The guarantee addresses both the quality of the factorization and agreement among the relevant local variables. This strengthens what off-the-shelf distributed gradient descent theory provides and connects the geometry of the distributed problem directly to an algorithmic convergence result.
summary.tldr: Under identified landscape conditions, an extended distributed gradient method reaches a globally optimal low-rank factorization with exact consensus.

title: Distributed Low-rank Matrix Factorization With Exact Consensus

abstract: Modern machine learning systems are susceptible to adversarial examples; inputs which clearly preserve the characteristic semantics of a given class, but whose classification is (usually confidently) incorrect. Existing approaches to adversarial defense generally rely on modifying the input, e.g. quantization, or the learned model parameters, e.g. via adversarial training. However, recent research has shown that most such approaches succumb to adversarial examples when different norms or more sophisticated adaptive attacks are considered. In this paper, we propose a fundamentally different approach which instead changes the way the output is represented and decoded. This simple approach achieves state-of-the-art robustness to adversarial examples for L 2 and L ∞ based adversarial perturbations on MNIST and CIFAR10. In addition, even under strong white-box attacks, we find that our model often assigns adversarial examples a low probability; those with high probability are usually interpretable, i.e. perturbed towards the perceptual boundary between the original and adversarial class. Our approach has several advantages: it yields more meaningful probability estimates, is extremely fast during training and testing, requires essentially no architectural changes to existing discriminative learning pipelines, is wholly complementary to other defense approaches including adversarial training, and does not sacrifice benign test set performance

paragraphs: Adversarial examples can preserve an input’s apparent class while causing a classifier to make a confident mistake. This paper approaches the problem through the model’s output representation. It uses error-correcting output codes and changes how outputs are decoded, offering a defense that can fit into existing discriminative learning pipelines with essentially no architectural changes.

The authors report state-of-the-art robustness on MNIST and CIFAR10 against perturbations measured using L2 and L-infinity norms. They also examine probability estimates under strong white-box attacks. Adversarial inputs often receive low probabilities, while high-probability examples usually move perceptually toward the boundary between the original class and the adversarial class.

These findings connect robustness with how meaningfully the model expresses confidence. The abstract also reports fast training and testing, no loss of benign test performance, and compatibility with defenses such as adversarial training. The qualifications around confidence matter: low probability is common rather than guaranteed, and perceptual interpretability describes the usual high-probability examples. The reported benefits are demonstrated in the stated evaluation settings.
summary.tldr: Changing output coding and decoding improves reported adversarial robustness and confidence estimates while preserving benign test performance.

title: Error Correcting Output Codes Improve Probability Estimation and Adversarial Robustness of Deep Neural Networks

abstract: We propose Episodic Backward Update (EBU) – a novel deep reinforcement learning algorithm with a direct value propagation. In contrast to the conventional use of the experience replay with uniform random sampling, our agent samples a whole episode and successively propagates the value of a state to its previous states. Our computationally efficient recursive algorithm allows sparse and delayed rewards to propagate directly through all transitions of the sampled episode. We theoretically prove the convergence of the EBU method and experimentally demonstrate its performance in both deterministic and stochastic environments. Especially in 49 games of Atari 2600 domain, EBU achieves the same mean and median human normalized performance of DQN by using only 5% and 10% of samples, respectively.

Especially in 49 games of Atari 2600 domain, EBU achieves the same mean and median human normalized performance of DQN by using only 5% and 10% of samples, respectively.

paragraphs: Sparse or delayed rewards make reinforcement learning difficult because useful information must reach decisions made well before a reward arrives. Episodic Backward Update addresses this problem by changing how stored experience is used. Instead of uniformly sampling individual experiences, it samples an entire episode and carries value information backward through its sequence of states.

The method uses a computationally efficient recursive procedure to pass a state's value to preceding states. This allows reward information to propagate directly through all transitions in the sampled episode. The episode's temporal structure becomes part of the update process, providing a direct route for connecting later outcomes to earlier experiences.

The authors prove convergence of EBU and evaluate it in both deterministic and stochastic environments. Across 49 Atari 2600 games, it reaches DQN's mean human-normalized performance using 5% of the samples and its median performance using 10%. Those are distinct aggregate comparisons, rather than a claim about identical savings in every game. The results support backward episode-level propagation as a way to obtain substantially more learning from the sampled experience.
summary.tldr: Episodic Backward Update propagates values backward through whole episodes and reaches DQN-level aggregate Atari performance with far fewer samples.

title: Sample-Efficient Deep Reinforcement Learning via Episodic Backward Update

abstract: We study the problem of estimating a $p$-dimensional $s$-sparse vector in a linear model with Gaussian design. In the case where the labels are contaminated by at most $o$ adversarial outliers, we prove that the $\ell_1$-penalized Huber's $M$-estimator based on $n$ samples attains the optimal rate of convergence $(s/n)^{1/2} + (o/n)$, up to a logarithmic factor. For more general design matrices, our results highlight the importance of two properties: the transfer principle and the incoherence property. These properties with suitable constants are shown to yield the optimal rates of robust estimation with adversarial contamination.

paragraphs: The paper studies linear regression when only a small subset of the model's coefficients are nonzero and some observed labels may be adversarially corrupted. The target is a vector with p coordinates and s nonzero entries, estimated from n samples. This combines the challenge of finding a sparse model with resistance to deliberately misleading outcomes.

The estimator combines an l1 penalty with Huber's estimation criterion. Under a Gaussian design and at most o corrupted labels, the authors prove an optimal convergence rate of sqrt(s/n) + o/n, up to a logarithmic factor. The expression separates the contribution associated with sparse estimation from the contribution associated with the fraction of contaminated labels.

The analysis also considers more general design matrices. It identifies the transfer principle and an incoherence property as sufficient for optimal robust-estimation rates when their constants are suitable. This extends the theoretical message beyond the Gaussian setting through explicit structural conditions. The result explains when this estimator can achieve optimal accuracy despite adversarial label contamination.
summary.tldr: Under Gaussian design, l1-penalized Huber estimation achieves optimal sparse-regression rates up to logarithmic factors despite adversarial label outliers.

title: Outlier-robust estimation of a sparse linear model using $\ell_1$-penalized Huber's $M$-estimator

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning setting where many devices collaboratively train a machine learning model while keeping the training data decentralized. In most of the current training schemes the central model is refined by averaging the parameters of the server model and the updated parameters from the client side. However, directly averaging model parameters is only possible if all models have the same structure and size, which could be a restrictive constraint in many scenarios. In this work we investigate more powerful and more flexible aggregation schemes for FL. Specifically, we propose ensemble distillation for model fusion, i.e. training the central classifier through unlabeled data on the outputs of the models from the clients. This knowledge distillation technique mitigates privacy risk and cost to the same extent as the baseline FL algorithms, but allows flexible aggregation over heterogeneous client models that can differ e.g. in size, numerical precision or structure. We show in extensive empirical experiments on various CV/NLP datasets (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, AG News, SST2) and settings (heterogeneous models/data) that the server model can be trained much faster, requiring fewer communication rounds than any existing FL technique so far.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets devices collaborate while keeping their training data decentralized. A common aggregation method averages model parameters, which requires participating models to share the same structure and size. This paper investigates a more flexible way to combine client learning when those architectural requirements would be restrictive.

The proposed method uses ensemble distillation. Client models produce outputs on unlabeled data, and those outputs train the central classifier. Knowledge is combined through predictions, allowing client models to differ in size, numerical precision, or structure. The authors state that the approach mitigates privacy risk and cost to the same extent as baseline federated learning algorithms.

Experiments span computer vision and language datasets, including CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, AG News, and SST2, with heterogeneous models and data. The authors report faster server-model training and fewer communication rounds than existing federated techniques in their comparisons. The findings make prediction-based fusion attractive when devices need different models and communication efficiency is an important part of collaborative training.
summary.tldr: Ensemble distillation combines heterogeneous client models through their predictions and reduces communication rounds in federated-learning experiments.

title: Ensemble Distillation for Robust Model Fusion in Federated Learning

abstract: The Information Bottleneck (IB) objective uses information theory to formulate a task-performance versus robustness trade-off. It has been successfully applied in the standard discriminative classification setting. We pose the question whether the IB can also be used to train generative likelihood models such as normalizing flows. Since normalizing flows use invertible network architectures (INNs), they are information-preserving by construction. This seems contradictory to the idea of a bottleneck. In this work, firstly, we develop the theory and methodology of IB-INNs, a class of conditional normalizing flows where INNs are trained using the IB objective: Introducing a small amount of controlled information loss allows for an asymptotically exact formulation of the IB, while keeping the INN's generative capabilities intact. Secondly, we investigate the properties of these models experimentally, specifically used as generative classifiers. This model class offers advantages such as improved uncertainty quantification and out-of-distribution detection, but traditional generative classifier solutions suffer considerably in classification accuracy. We find the trade-off parameter in the IB controls a mix of generative capabilities and accuracy close to standard classifiers. Empirically, our uncertainty estimates in this mixed regime compare favourably to conventional generative and discriminative classifiers. Code is provided in the supplement.

paragraphs: The information bottleneck objective expresses a trade-off between task performance and robustness. Applying it to normalizing flows creates an apparent conflict: flows use invertible networks that preserve information, whereas a bottleneck involves discarding information. This paper develops IB-INNs, conditional normalizing flows trained with an information-bottleneck objective, to reconcile those requirements.

The method introduces a small, controlled amount of information loss. This permits an asymptotically exact formulation of the bottleneck while preserving the network’s ability to generate data. The authors then investigate these models as generative classifiers, a setting where uncertainty estimation and out-of-distribution detection are attractive capabilities but traditional approaches suffer in classification accuracy.

Experiments show that the bottleneck trade-off parameter controls a mixture of generative capabilities and classification accuracy close to that of standard classifiers. In this mixed regime, uncertainty estimates compare favorably with conventional generative and discriminative classifiers. The findings support using a single training trade-off to retain generation while obtaining competitive classification and useful uncertainty estimates in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: Controlled information loss lets invertible generative models use an information bottleneck to balance generation, classification accuracy, and uncertainty estimation.

title: Training Normalizing Flows with the Information Bottleneck for Competitive Generative Classification

abstract: We consider the parameter estimation problem of a probabilistic generative model prescribed using a natural exponential family of distributions. For this problem, the typical maximum likelihood estimator usually overfits under limited training sample size, is sensitive to noise and may perform poorly on downstream predictive tasks. To mitigate these issues, we propose a distributionally robust maximum likelihood estimator that minimizes the worst-case expected log-loss uniformly over a parametric Kullback-Leibler ball around a parametric nominal distribution. Leveraging the analytical expression of the Kullback-Leibler divergence between two distributions in the same natural exponential family, we show that the min-max estimation problem is tractable in a broad setting, including the robust training of generalized linear models. Our novel robust estimator also enjoys statistical consistency and delivers promising empirical results in both regression and classification tasks.

To mitigate these issues, we propose a distributionally robust maximum likelihood estimator that minimizes the worst-case expected log-loss uniformly over a parametric Kullback-Leibler ball around a parametric nominal distribution. paragraphs: The paper considers parameter estimation for probabilistic generative models in a natural exponential family. Ordinary maximum likelihood can overfit with limited data and can be sensitive to noise, harming later predictions. The proposed estimator addresses these issues by allowing uncertainty about the distribution used to evaluate a candidate model.

Rather than minimizing expected log-loss for just one nominal distribution, the method minimizes the worst expected log-loss within a parametric neighborhood of that distribution. Kullback–Leibler divergence defines the neighborhood. This makes the fitting objective account for a collection of nearby distributions, so a parameter choice is assessed against the least favorable distribution in that collection.

The authors exploit an analytical expression for divergence between distributions in the same natural exponential family to make this min-max problem tractable in a broad setting, including generalized linear models. They also establish statistical consistency and report promising regression and classification results. The contribution combines a structured robustness objective with computational tractability and statistical justification within the model family studied.
summary.tldr: A robust maximum likelihood estimator fits exponential-family models against nearby worst-case distributions while retaining tractability and statistical consistency.

title: Distributionally Robust Parametric Maximum Likelihood Estimation

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning, wherein one uses off-policy data logged by a fixed behavior policy to evaluate and learn new policies, is crucial in applications where experimentation is limited such as medicine. We study the estimation of policy value and gradient of a deterministic policy from off-policy data when actions are continuous. Targeting deterministic policies, for which action is a deterministic function of state, is crucial since optimal policies are always deterministic (up to ties). In this setting, standard importance sampling and doubly robust estimators for policy value and gradient fail because the density ratio does not exist. To circumvent this issue, we propose several new doubly robust estimators based on different kernelization approaches. We analyze the asymptotic mean-squared error of each of these under mild rate conditions for nuisance estimators. Specifically, we demonstrate how to obtain a rate that is independent of the horizon length.

Targeting deterministic policies, for which action is a deterministic function of state, is crucial since optimal policies are always deterministic (up to ties). In this setting, standard importance sampling and doubly robust estimators for policy value and gradient fail because the density ratio does not exist. To circumvent this issue, we propose several new doubly robust estimators based on different kernelization approaches. paragraphs: The paper studies how to evaluate and improve a deterministic policy using data collected by a different, fixed behavior policy. Actions are continuous, and the target policy selects one specific action for each state. This offline setting matters when collecting new experimental data is constrained, because policy learning must depend on previously logged experience.

A central obstacle is that standard importance-sampling and doubly robust estimators require a density ratio that does not exist in this setting. Consequently, those usual value and gradient estimators cannot be applied directly. The authors develop several new doubly robust estimators using different kernelization approaches, introducing a way to handle the mismatch created by deterministic target actions.

The paper analyzes each estimator's asymptotic mean-squared error under mild conditions on the convergence rates of auxiliary, or nuisance, estimators. It also shows how to obtain a rate that does not depend on horizon length. This result concerns the estimation rate under the stated conditions, providing a theoretical route to evaluating deterministic policies without a rate that worsens with longer horizons.
summary.tldr: Kernel-based doubly robust estimators enable off-policy value and gradient estimation for deterministic continuous-action policies, with a horizon-independent rate under stated conditions.

title: Doubly Robust Off-Policy Value and Gradient Estimation for Deterministic Policies

abstract: We study locally differentially private (LDP) bandits learning in this paper. First, we propose simple black-box reduction frameworks that can solve a large family of context-free bandits learning problems with LDP guarantee. Based on our frameworks, we can improve previous best results for private bandits learning with one-point feedback, such as private Bandits Convex Optimization etc, and obtain the first results for Bandits Convex Optimization (BCO) with multi-point feedback under LDP. LDP guarantee and black-box nature make our frameworks more attractive in real applications compared with previous specifically designed and relatively weaker differentially private (DP) algorithms. Further, we also extend our algorithm to Generalized Linear Bandits with regret bound $\tilde{\mc{O}}(T^{3/4}/\varepsilon)$ under $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-LDP and it is conjectured to be optimal. Note given existing $\Omega(T)$ lower bound for DP contextual linear bandits (Shariff & Sheffet, NeurIPS 2018), our result shows a fundamental difference between LDP and DP for contextual bandits.

paragraphs: Bandit learning makes sequential decisions using limited feedback about their outcomes. This paper develops frameworks for doing so under local differential privacy. Its initial contribution is a set of black-box reductions for a broad family of context-free bandit problems, allowing privacy guarantees to be incorporated through a reusable framework.

These reductions improve previous results for private bandit learning with one-point feedback, including bandit convex optimization. They also provide the first stated results for bandit convex optimization with multi-point feedback under local differential privacy. The combination of reusable reductions and local privacy is presented as attractive for practical applications compared with specially designed algorithms using weaker privacy guarantees.

The authors extend their method to generalized linear bandits, obtaining a regret bound of approximately T to the three-quarter power divided by epsilon, with logarithmic factors suppressed, under (epsilon, delta) local differential privacy. Optimality is conjectured rather than proved. They also contrast this result with an existing linear lower bound for a differentially private contextual linear bandit setting, highlighting a distinction between the privacy formulations studied.
summary.tldr: Reusable reductions provide locally private bandit algorithms, including a generalized linear bandit extension with a conjecturally optimal regret bound.

title: Locally Differentially Private (Contextual) Bandits Learning

abstract: We address the question of repeatedly learning linear classifiers against agents who are \emph{strategically} trying to \emph{game} the deployed classifiers, and we use the \emph{Stackelberg regret} to measure the performance of our algorithms. First, we show that Stackelberg and external regret for the problem of strategic classification are \emph{strongly incompatible}: i.e., there exist worst-case scenarios, where \emph{any} sequence of actions providing \emph{sublinear} external regret might result in \emph{linear} Stackelberg regret and vice versa. Second, we present a strategy-aware algorithm for minimizing the Stackelberg regret for which we prove nearly matching upper and lower regret bounds. Finally, we provide simulations to complement our theoretical analysis. Our results advance the growing literature of learning from revealed preferences, which has so far focused on ``smoother'' assumptions from the perspective of the learner and the agents respectively.

First, we show that Stackelberg and external regret for the problem of strategic classification are \emph{strongly incompatible}: i.e., there exist worst-case scenarios, where \emph{any} sequence of actions providing \emph{sublinear} external regret might result in \emph{linear} Stackelberg regret and vice versa. Finally, we provide simulations to complement our theoretical analysis. Our results advance the growing literature of learning from revealed preferences, which has so far focused on ``smoother'' assumptions from the perspective of the learner and the agents respectively.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated learning of linear classifiers when the people or agents being classified strategically try to obtain favorable decisions. The deployed classifier can influence their behavior, so evaluating a learner requires attention to those responses. The authors use Stackelberg regret to measure performance in this strategic setting.

Their first result shows a strong conflict between Stackelberg regret and external regret. In worst-case scenarios, any sequence of decisions with sublinear external regret can have linear Stackelberg regret, and the reverse conflict can also occur. Thus, success according to one criterion need not translate into success according to the other when agents respond strategically.

The authors then design an algorithm that explicitly accounts for strategy and minimizes Stackelberg regret. They prove upper and lower regret bounds that nearly match, helping characterize the achievable performance for the problem. Simulations complement the theoretical analysis. The main implication is that learning against strategic behavior requires a performance criterion and algorithm that account for that behavior, rather than assuming ordinary regret control will automatically suffice.
summary.tldr: Strategic classification can make standard and Stackelberg regret incompatible, motivating an algorithm with nearly matching Stackelberg regret bounds.

title: Learning Strategy-Aware Linear Classifiers

abstract:
The Transformer and its variants have been proven to be efficient sequence learners in many different domains. Despite their staggering success, a critical issue has been the enormous number of parameters that must be trained (ranging from $10^7$ to $10^{11}$) along with the quadratic complexity of dot-product attention. In this work, we investigate the problem of approximating the two central components of the Transformer --- multi-head self-attention and point-wise feed-forward transformation, with reduced parameter space and computational complexity. We build upon recent developments in analyzing deep neural networks as numerical solvers of ordinary differential equations. Taking advantage of an analogy between Transformer stages and the evolution of a dynamical system of multiple interacting particles, we formulate a temporal evolution scheme, 
ame, to bypass costly dot-product attention over multiple stacked layers. We perform exhaustive experiments with 
ame\ on well-known encoder-decoder as well as encoder-only tasks. We observe that the degree of approximation (or inversely, the degree of parameter reduction) has different effects on the performance, depending on the task. While in the encoder-decoder regime, 
ame\ delivers performances comparable to the original Transformer, in encoder-only tasks it consistently outperforms Transformer along with several subsequent variants.

paragraphs: Transformers can require enormous parameter counts, while dot-product attention has quadratic computational complexity. This paper investigates approximating their two central components, multi-head self-attention and point-wise feed-forward transformations, with fewer parameters and less computation. The approach draws on the interpretation of deep networks as numerical solvers of ordinary differential equations.

The authors use an analogy between transformer stages and the evolution of a system of interacting particles. They develop a temporal evolution scheme that bypasses costly dot-product attention across multiple stacked layers. This dynamical perspective supplies a way to redesign the repeated transformations, with the degree of approximation tied to the extent of parameter reduction.

Experiments cover both encoder-decoder and encoder-only tasks. The effect of approximation differs by task: the proposed scheme achieves performance comparable to the original transformer in the encoder-decoder setting, while consistently outperforming it and several later variants on the tested encoder-only tasks. These results make task dependence central to understanding how much approximation is useful.
summary.tldr: A dynamical-systems-inspired transformer approximation reduces parameters and computation, with task-dependent results across encoder-decoder and encoder-only settings.

title: Redesigning the Transformer Architecture with Insights from Multi-particle Dynamical Systems

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (offline RL), which aims to find an optimal policy from a previously collected static dataset, bears algorithmic difficulties due to function approximation errors from out-of-distribution (OOD) data points. To this end, offline RL algorithms adopt either a constraint or a penalty term that explicitly guides the policy to stay close to the given dataset. However, prior methods typically require accurate estimation of the behavior policy or sampling from OOD data points, which themselves can be a non-trivial problem. Moreover, these methods under-utilize the generalization ability of deep neural networks and often fall into suboptimal solutions too close to the given dataset. In this work, we propose an uncertainty-based offline RL method that takes into account the confidence of the Q-value prediction and does not require any estimation or sampling of the data distribution. We show that the clipped Q-learning, a technique widely used in online RL, can be leveraged to successfully penalize OOD data points with high prediction uncertainties. Surprisingly, we find that it is possible to substantially outperform existing offline RL methods on various tasks by simply increasing the number of Q-networks along with the clipped Q-learning. Based on this observation, we propose an ensemble-diversified actor-critic algorithm that reduces the number of required ensemble networks down to a tenth compared to the naive ensemble while achieving state-of-the-art performance on most of the D4RL benchmarks considered.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns a policy from a fixed dataset, but value estimates can be unreliable for decisions outside that dataset's coverage. Existing approaches often constrain the policy to remain near observed behavior. The paper argues that these methods can require difficult distribution-estimation steps and can also keep the policy unnecessarily close to the data.

The proposed approach uses confidence in Q-value predictions to guide conservatism without estimating or sampling the data distribution. The authors show that clipped Q-learning can penalize out-of-distribution points whose predictions are highly uncertain. They also find that simply increasing the number of Q-networks alongside clipping can substantially outperform existing offline methods on various tasks.

It reduces the required ensemble size to one tenth of the naive ensemble while achieving state-of-the-art performance on most evaluated D4RL benchmarks. The results connect uncertainty-based penalties with a more economical ensemble design, supporting improved use of neural-network generalization without imposing an explicit requirement to reproduce the behavior represented in the dataset.
summary.tldr: Diversifying Q-network ensembles enables uncertainty-based offline reinforcement learning with one tenth the naive ensemble size and strong reported benchmark performance.

title: Uncertainty-Based Offline Reinforcement Learning with Diversified Q-Ensemble

abstract: Theoretical results show that neural networks can be approximated by Gaussian processes in the infinite-width limit. However, for fully connected networks, it has been previously shown that for any fixed network width, $n$, the Gaussian approximation gets worse as the network depth, $d$, increases. Given that modern networks are deep, this raises the question of how well modern architectures, like ResNets, are captured by the infinite-width limit. To provide a better approximation, we study ReLU ResNets in the infinite-depth-and-width limit, where \emph{both} depth and width tend to infinity as their ratio, $d/n$, remains constant. In contrast to the Gaussian infinite-width limit, we show theoretically that the network exhibits log-Gaussian behaviour at initialization in the infinite-depth-and-width limit, with parameters depending on the ratio $d/n$. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we demonstrate that even basic properties of standard ResNet architectures are poorly captured by the Gaussian limit, but remarkably well captured by our log-Gaussian limit. Moreover, our analysis reveals that ReLU ResNets at initialization are hypoactivated: fewer than half of the ReLUs are activated. Additionally, we calculate the interlayer correlations, which have the effect of exponentially increasing the variance of the network output. Based on our analysis, we introduce \emph{Balanced ResNets}, a simple architecture modification, which eliminates hypoactivation and interlayer correlations and is more amenable to theoretical analysis.

title: The future is log-Gaussian: ResNets and their infinite-depth-and-width limit at initialization

abstract: Backpropagation (BP) uses detailed, unit-specific feedback to train deep neural networks (DNNs) with remarkable success. That biological neural circuits appear to perform credit assignment, but cannot implement BP, implies the existence of other powerful learning algorithms. Here, we explore the extent to which a globally broadcast learning signal, coupled with local weight updates, enables training of DNNs. We present both a learning rule, called global error-vector broadcasting (GEVB), and a class of DNNs, called vectorized nonnegative networks (VNNs), in which this learning rule operates. VNNs have vector-valued units and nonnegative weights past the first layer. The GEVB learning rule generalizes three-factor Hebbian learning, updating each weight by an amount proportional to the inner product of the presynaptic activation and a globally broadcast error vector when the postsynaptic unit is active. We prove that these weight updates are matched in sign to the gradient, enabling accurate credit assignment. Moreover, at initialization, these updates are exactly proportional to the gradient in the limit of infinite network width. GEVB matches the performance of BP in VNNs, and in some cases outperforms direct feedback alignment (DFA) applied in conventional networks. Unlike DFA, GEVB successfully trains convolutional layers. Altogether, our theoretical and empirical results point to a surprisingly powerful role for a global learning signal in training DNNs.

paragraphs: Backpropagation supplies detailed feedback to individual units so that each weight can be updated appropriately. This paper investigates how much learning is possible when all units instead receive a shared error vector and weights are updated locally. The authors introduce global error-vector broadcasting, or GEVB, together with vectorized nonnegative networks, the architecture in which their rule operates.

These networks use vector-valued units and nonnegative weights beyond the first layer. When a postsynaptic unit is active, its incoming weight update depends on the inner product between the presynaptic activation and the broadcast error. The authors prove that these updates have the same signs as the gradient. At initialization, they are exactly proportional to the gradient in the infinite-width limit.

The combination of theoretical alignment and experimental performance shows that a global signal can support effective credit assignment in the proposed architecture, with exact gradient proportionality requiring the stated initialization and width conditions.
summary.tldr: A shared error vector supports gradient-aligned local learning in vectorized nonnegative networks and empirically matches backpropagation within that architecture.

title: Credit Assignment Through Broadcasting a Global Error Vector

abstract: Tensor network methods have been a key ingredient of advances in condensed matter physics and have recently sparked interest in the machine learning community for their ability to compactly represent very high-dimensional objects. Tensor network methods can for example be used to efficiently learn linear models in exponentially large feature spaces [Stoudenmire and Schwab, 2016]. In this work, we derive upper and lower bounds on the VC dimension and pseudo-dimension of a large class of tensor network models for classification, regression and completion. Our upper bounds hold for linear models parameterized by arbitrary tensor network structures, and we derive lower bounds for common tensor decomposition models~(CP, Tensor Train, Tensor Ring and Tucker) showing the tightness of our general upper bound. These results are used to derive a generalization bound which can be applied to classification with low rank matrices as well as linear classifiers based on any of the commonly used tensor decomposition models. As a corollary of our results, we obtain a bound on the VC dimension of the matrix product state classifier introduced in [Stoudenmire and Schwab, 2016] as a function of the so-called bond dimension~(i.e. tensor train rank), which answers an open problem listed by Cirac, Garre-Rubio and Pérez-García in [Cirac et al., 2019].

paragraphs: Tensor networks can represent very high-dimensional objects compactly, making them attractive for learning models in enormous feature spaces. This paper asks how expressive such models are from a statistical learning perspective. It derives upper and lower bounds on VC dimension and pseudo-dimension, capacity measures relevant to classification and real-valued prediction.

The upper bounds cover linear models parameterized by arbitrary tensor network structures. Lower bounds for CP, Tensor Train, Tensor Ring, and Tucker decompositions establish the tightness of the general upper bound. Together, these results connect the structured representation of a model with how rich a collection of predictions it can express.

The authors use the capacity bounds to derive a generalization bound for classifiers based on low-rank matrices and common tensor decompositions. They also obtain a VC-dimension bound for the matrix product state classifier as a function of bond dimension, or tensor train rank, resolving a stated open problem. The contribution provides theoretical control over model capacity rather than an empirical comparison of predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Capacity bounds for tensor network models yield generalization guarantees and resolve an open question about matrix product state classifiers.

title: Lower and Upper Bounds on the Pseudo-Dimension of Tensor Network Models

abstract: Humans perceive the world by concurrently processing and fusing high-dimensional inputs from multiple modalities such as vision and audio. Machine perception models, in stark contrast, are typically modality-specific and optimised for unimodal benchmarks.A common approach for building multimodal models is to simply combine multiple of these modality-specific architectures using late-stage fusion of final representations or predictions ('late-fusion').Instead, we introduce a novel transformer based architecture that uses 'attention bottlenecks' for modality fusion at multiple layers. Compared to traditional pairwise self-attention, these bottlenecks force information between different modalities to pass through a small number of '`bottleneck' latent units, requiring the model to collate and condense the most relevant information in each modality and only share what is necessary. We find that such a strategy improves fusion performance, at the same time reducing computational cost. We conduct thorough ablation studies, and achieve state-of-the-art results on multiple audio-visual classification benchmarks including Audioset, Epic-Kitchens and VGGSound. All code and models will be released.

paragraphs: Combining sound and vision requires deciding how information from the two streams should interact. A common approach processes each modality separately and combines only the final representations or predictions. This paper instead introduces a transformer architecture that lets modalities exchange information at multiple layers, making fusion part of representation learning itself.

The exchange passes through a small set of shared latent units called attention bottlenecks. Rather than using unrestricted pairwise attention across modalities, the architecture requires each stream to condense relevant information before sharing it. This gives the model a restricted communication channel through which audio and visual information can inform one another.

The authors find that this restriction improves fusion performance while reducing computation. Their evaluation includes ablation studies and reports state-of-the-art results on audio-visual classification benchmarks including Audioset, Epic-Kitchens, and VGGSound. The findings show that limiting cross-modal communication can be useful: in the reported experiments, a compact channel supports stronger predictions as well as cheaper processing.
summary.tldr: Attention bottlenecks let audio and visual streams exchange condensed information across layers, improving reported classification performance while reducing computation.

title: Attention Bottlenecks for Multimodal Fusion

abstract: We present Deep Region Competition (DRC), an algorithm designed to extract foreground objects from images in a fully unsupervised manner. Foreground extraction can be viewed as a special case of generic image segmentation that focuses on identifying and disentangling objects from the background. In this work, we rethink the foreground extraction by reconciling energy-based prior with generative image modeling in the form of Mixture of Experts (MoE), where we further introduce the learned pixel re-assignment as the essential inductive bias to capture the regularities of background regions. With this modeling, the foreground-background partition can be naturally found through Expectation-Maximization (EM). We show that the proposed method effectively exploits the interaction between the mixture components during the partitioning process, which closely connects to region competition, a seminal approach for generic image segmentation. Experiments demonstrate that DRC exhibits more competitive performances on complex real-world data and challenging multi-object scenes compared with prior methods. Moreover, we show empirically that DRC can potentially generalize to novel foreground objects even from categories unseen during training.

paragraphs: Foreground extraction separates objects from their surrounding background. Deep Region Competition tackles this task without supervision, using a generative model to explain image regions. The central idea is to let different model components interact during partitioning, so the foreground-background split emerges from their competing explanations of the image.

The model combines an energy-based prior with a mixture-of-experts formulation of image generation. It also learns pixel reassignment, which supplies an inductive bias for capturing regularities in background regions. Expectation-Maximization finds the partition within this formulation. The interaction among mixture components connects the method to region competition, an earlier approach to image segmentation.

Experiments report more competitive performance than prior methods on complex real-world images and challenging scenes containing multiple objects. The authors also find empirical evidence that the method can potentially extend to foreground objects from categories absent during training. That result suggests useful generalization beyond familiar categories, while remaining an observed possibility rather than a guarantee for every unseen object.
summary.tldr: Deep Region Competition learns foreground-background partitions without supervision through interacting generative components and learned pixel reassignment.

title: Unsupervised Foreground Extraction via Deep Region Competition

abstract: In this paper, we provide theoretical results of estimation bounds and excess risk upper bounds for support vector machine (SVM) with sparse multi-kernel representation. These convergence rates for multi-kernel SVM are established by analyzing a Lasso-type regularized learning scheme within composite multi-kernel spaces. It is shown that the oracle rates of convergence of classifiers depend on the complexity of multi-kernels, the sparsity, a Bernstein condition and the sample size, which significantly improves on previous results even for the additive or linear cases. In summary, this paper not only provides unified theoretical results for multi-kernel SVMs, but also enriches the literature on high-dimensional nonparametric classification.

These convergence rates for multi-kernel SVM are established by analyzing a Lasso-type regularized learning scheme within composite multi-kernel spaces. It is shown that the oracle rates of convergence of classifiers depend on the complexity of multi-kernels, the sparsity, a Bernstein condition and the sample size, which significantly improves on previous results even for the additive or linear cases. In summary, this paper not only provides unified theoretical results for multi-kernel SVMs, but also enriches the literature on high-dimensional nonparametric classification.

paragraphs: This paper studies the theoretical accuracy of support vector machines built from sparse combinations of multiple kernels. The central question is how reliably such classifiers learn as the amount of data grows, and how that reliability depends on the complexity and sparsity of their representation. The contribution consists of mathematical guarantees about learning.

The authors analyze a Lasso-type regularized learning procedure in composite multi-kernel spaces. They derive both estimation bounds and upper bounds on excess risk, addressing how closely the learned model approaches its target and how much additional predictive risk remains. Their oracle convergence rates depend on kernel complexity, sparsity, sample size, and a Bernstein condition.

Those dependencies matter because the guarantees reflect more than the number of available examples: they also account for structure in the learning problem. The paper reports substantially improved rates over previous results, including additive and linear cases. Its unified analysis covers multi-kernel SVMs while contributing to the theory of high-dimensional nonparametric classification.
summary.tldr: The paper derives improved convergence guarantees for sparse multi-kernel SVMs under conditions involving complexity, sparsity, and sample size.

title: Improved Learning Rates of a Functional Lasso-type SVM with Sparse Multi-Kernel Representation

abstract: We study data corruption attacks on stochastic multi arm bandit algorithms. Existing attack methodologies assume that the attacker can observe the multi arm bandit algorithm's realized behavior which is in contrast to the adversaries modeled in the robust multi arm bandit algorithms literature. To the best of our knowledge, we develop the first data corruption attack on stochastic multi arm bandit algorithms which works without observing the algorithm's realized behavior. Through this attack, we also discover a sufficient condition for a stochastic multi arm bandit algorithm to be susceptible to adversarial data corruptions. We show that any bandit algorithm that makes decisions just using the empirical mean reward, and the number of times that arm has been pulled in the past can suffer from linear regret under data corruption attacks. We further show that various popular stochastic multi arm bandit algorithms such UCB, $\epsilon$-greedy and Thompson Sampling satisfy this sufficient condition and are thus prone to data corruption attacks. We further analyze the behavior of our attack for these algorithms and show that using only $o(T)$ corruptions, our attack can force these algorithms to select a potentially non-optimal target arm preferred by the attacker for all but $o(T)$ rounds.

paragraphs: This paper studies how corrupted reward data can mislead stochastic multi-armed bandit algorithms. Earlier attack methods assumed access to the learner’s realized behavior. The authors develop an attack that works without that observation, bringing the attacker’s information requirements closer to those considered in research on robust bandit algorithms.

The analysis identifies a sufficient condition for vulnerability: an algorithm that bases decisions only on empirical mean rewards and past arm-pull counts can suffer linear regret under corruption. This is a sufficient condition, not a complete classification of all vulnerable algorithms. The authors show that popular methods including UCB, epsilon-greedy, and Thompson Sampling satisfy the condition in their analysis.

For these algorithms, the attack uses only o(T) corruptions while inducing selection of an attacker-preferred target arm for all but o(T) rounds. Both exceptional quantities grow sublinearly with the horizon T. The target can be suboptimal, making the result consequential for learning performance: a vanishing fraction of corrupted observations can influence almost the entire sequence of decisions without monitoring the learner’s realized behavior.
summary.tldr: An observation-free corruption attack can steer several popular bandit algorithms toward a target arm for almost all rounds using sublinear corruptions.

title: Observation-Free Attacks on Stochastic Bandits

abstract: During typical gradient-based training of deep neural networks, all of the model's parameters are updated at each iteration. Recent work has shown that it is possible to update only a small subset of the model's parameters during training, which can alleviate storage and communication requirements. In this paper, we show that it is possible to induce a fixed sparse mask on the model’s parameters that selects a subset to update over many iterations. Our method constructs the mask out of the $k$ parameters with the largest Fisher information as a simple approximation as to which parameters are most important for the task at hand. In experiments on parameter-efficient transfer learning and distributed training, we show that our approach matches or exceeds the performance of other methods for training with sparse updates while being more efficient in terms of memory usage and communication costs. We release our code publicly to promote further applications of our approach.

paragraphs: Typical neural-network training updates every parameter at every iteration. Updating only a small subset can reduce the storage and communication associated with those updates. This paper studies how to choose a sparse subset that can remain fixed over many training iterations, rather than requiring continual changes to the selection.

The method selects the k parameters with the largest Fisher information and uses them to construct a binary update mask. Fisher information serves as a simple approximation of which parameters matter most for the task. The mask determines which parameters receive updates, making the contribution a method for sparse training updates rather than a claim about removing the remaining model parameters.

Experiments cover parameter-efficient transfer learning and distributed training. The approach matches or exceeds other sparse-update methods while reducing memory usage and communication costs. These findings suggest that a task-informed, fixed selection can retain useful training capacity with fewer resources devoted to updates. The abstract reports these advantages in the evaluated settings without claiming that the same subset is best for every task.
summary.tldr: Fixed masks based on Fisher information select a small parameter subset for efficient training with competitive sparse-update performance.

title: Training Neural Networks with Fixed Sparse Masks

abstract: We propose a self-supervised capsule architecture for 3D point clouds. We compute capsule decompositions of objects through permutation-equivariant attention, and self-supervise the process by training with pairs of randomly rotated objects. Our key idea is to aggregate the attention masks into semantic keypoints, and use these to supervise a decomposition that satisfies the capsule invariance/equivariance properties. This not only enables the training of a semantically consistent decomposition, but also allows us to learn a canonicalization operation that enables object-centric reasoning. To train our neural network we require neither classification labels nor manually-aligned training datasets. Yet, by learning an object-centric representation in a self-supervised manner, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art on 3D point cloud reconstruction, canonicalization, and unsupervised classification.

paragraphs: An object represented as a 3D point cloud can appear in many orientations, even though its meaningful parts remain the same. This paper learns to decompose such objects into capsules while also learning a consistent reference pose. Training uses pairs of randomly rotated objects, so the supervision comes from transformations of the data itself.

The architecture uses permutation-equivariant attention, allowing its decomposition to respect changes in the ordering of input points. It combines attention masks into semantic keypoints and uses those keypoints to supervise capsule behavior under rotation. The aim is to preserve relevant part identity while allowing pose-related quantities to transform appropriately, producing a semantically consistent decomposition.

Learning this decomposition also enables canonicalization: expressing objects in an object-centered reference frame that supports reasoning about their structure. The method needs neither classification labels nor manually aligned training examples. The authors report performance beyond the state of the art on point-cloud reconstruction, canonicalization, and unsupervised classification, showing that the learned representation is useful across these evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Canonical Capsules learns consistent object parts and reference poses from randomly rotated point clouds without labels or manual alignment.

title: Canonical Capsules: Self-Supervised Capsules in Canonical Pose

abstract: This paper presents a novel image dataset with high intrinsic ambiguity specifically built for evaluating and comparing set-valued classifiers. This dataset, built from the database of Pl@ntnet citizen observatory, consists of 306,146 images covering 1,081 species. We highlight two particular features of the dataset, inherent to the way the images are acquired and to the intrinsic diversity of plants morphology: i) The dataset has a strong class imbalance, meaning that a few species account for most of the images. ii) Many species are visually similar, making identification difficult even for the expert eye.These two characteristics make the present dataset well suited for the evaluation of set-valued classification methods and algorithms. Therefore, we recommend two set-valued evaluation metrics associated with the dataset (mean top-k accuracy and mean average-k accuracy) and we provide the results of a baseline approach based on a deep neural network trained with the cross-entropy loss.

paragraphs: Pl@ntNet-300K is designed to evaluate classifiers that can return a set of candidate labels. Plant identification provides a demanding setting because different species can look very similar. The dataset comes from the Pl@ntNet citizen observatory and contains 306,146 images representing 1,081 species.

Two properties shape the challenge. First, a small number of species account for most images, leaving an uneven distribution of examples across classes. Second, visual resemblance between species can make identification difficult even for experts. These characteristics make the dataset useful for investigating predictions that retain several possible species when the image is ambiguous.

The authors recommend mean top-k accuracy and mean average-k accuracy as evaluation measures for this setting. They also provide a baseline using a deep neural network trained with cross-entropy loss. Together, the data, proposed metrics, and baseline establish a comparison point for set-valued classification methods under both strong class imbalance and substantial visual ambiguity.
summary.tldr: Pl@ntNet-300K tests set-valued plant classification using visually ambiguous species and a strongly imbalanced image distribution.

title: Pl@ntNet-300K: a plant image dataset with high label ambiguity and a long-tailed distribution

abstract: Object manipulation from 3D visual inputs poses many challenges on building generalizable perception and policy models. However, 3D assets in existing benchmarks mostly lack the diversity of 3D shapes that align with real-world intra-class complexity in topology and geometry. Here we propose SAPIEN Manipulation Skill Benchmark (ManiSkill) to benchmark manipulation skills over diverse objects in a full-physics simulator. 3D assets in ManiSkill include large intra-class topological and geometric variations. Tasks are carefully chosen to cover distinct types of manipulation challenges. Latest progress in 3D vision also makes us believe that we should customize the benchmark so that the challenge is inviting to researchers working on 3D deep learning. To this end, we simulate a moving panoramic camera that returns ego-centric point clouds or RGB-D images. In addition, we would like ManiSkill to serve a broad set of researchers interested in manipulation research. Besides supporting the learning of policies from interactions, we also support learning-from-demonstrations (LfD) methods, by providing a large number of high-quality demonstrations (~36,000 successful trajectories, ~1.5M point cloud/RGB-D frames in total). We provide baselines using 3D deep learning and LfD algorithms. All code of our benchmark (simulator, environment, SDK, and baselines) is open-sourced (\href{https://github.com/haosulab/ManiSkill}{Github repo}), and a challenge facing interdisciplinary researchers will be held based on the benchmark.

Besides supporting the learning of policies from interactions, we also support learning-from-demonstrations (LfD) methods, by providing a large number of high-quality demonstrations (~36,000 successful trajectories, ~1.5M point cloud/RGB-D frames in total). We provide baselines using 3D deep learning and LfD algorithms. All code of our benchmark (simulator, environment, SDK, and baselines) is open-sourced (\href{https://github.com/haosulab/ManiSkill}{Github repo}), and a challenge facing interdisciplinary researchers will be held based on the benchmark.

paragraphs: Learning to manipulate objects from 3D visual input requires coping with variation among objects of the same class. ManiSkill addresses a weakness in existing benchmarks: their assets often lack the geometric and topological diversity found within real-world object categories. It provides diverse objects in a full-physics simulator, with tasks selected to cover different manipulation challenges.

A moving panoramic camera supplies observations as point clouds or RGB-D images from the agent's perspective. This makes the benchmark suitable for studying policies that work from 3D visual information. Its combination of varied object shapes and visual observations connects the manipulation challenge directly to learning useful representations of the objects being handled.

ManiSkill supports learning through interaction and learning from demonstrations. The release includes approximately 36,000 successful trajectories and 1.5 million point-cloud or RGB-D frames, alongside baselines using 3D deep learning and demonstration-based methods. By providing the simulator, environments, software tools, and baselines, the authors create a shared resource for investigating generalizable manipulation across diverse objects.
summary.tldr: ManiSkill benchmarks visually guided manipulation across diverse objects and supplies about 36,000 successful demonstrations.

title: ManiSkill: Generalizable Manipulation Skill Benchmark with Large-Scale Demonstrations

abstract: This work studies online zero-order optimization of convex and Lipschitz functions. We present a novel gradient estimator based on two function evaluations and randomization on the $\ell_1$-sphere. Considering different geometries of feasible sets and Lipschitz assumptions we analyse online dual averaging algorithm with our estimator in place of the usual gradient. We consider two types of assumptions on the noise of the zero-order oracle: canceling noise and adversarial noise. We provide an anytime and completely data-driven algorithm, which is adaptive to all parameters of the problem. In the case of canceling noise that was previously studied in the literature, our guarantees are either comparable or better than state-of-the-art bounds obtained by~\citet{duchi2015} and \citet{Shamir17} for non-adaptive algorithms. Our analysis is based on deriving a new weighted Poincaré type inequality for the uniform measure on the $\ell_1$-sphere with explicit constants, which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: The paper studies online optimization when an algorithm can evaluate a function but cannot directly obtain its gradient. The functions are assumed to be convex and Lipschitz, meaning their values change at a bounded rate. The central contribution is a gradient estimator that uses two function evaluations and a random direction drawn from the l1 sphere.

The authors insert this estimator into online dual averaging and analyze different combinations of feasible-set geometry and Lipschitz assumptions. They also consider two noise models: canceling noise and adversarial noise. Their algorithm is anytime and fully data-driven, adapting to the problem parameters instead of requiring them to be specified beforehand.

For the canceling-noise setting, the resulting guarantees match or improve on the cited leading bounds for non-adaptive algorithms. The proof develops a weighted Poincaré-type inequality with explicit constants for the uniform distribution on the l1 sphere. This mathematical result supports the estimator analysis and may also be useful independently. The contribution therefore combines an adaptive optimization procedure with a new tool for understanding its randomized estimates.
summary.tldr: A two-evaluation gradient estimator enables adaptive online optimization with competitive guarantees under canceling noise.

title: A gradient estimator via L1-randomization for online zero-order optimization with two point feedback

abstract: Existing benchmark datasets for recommender systems (RS) either are created at a small scale or involve very limited forms of user feedback. RS models evaluated on such datasets often lack practical values for large-scale real-world applications. In this paper, we describe Tenrec, a novel and publicly available data collection for RS that records various user feedback from four different recommendation scenarios. To be specific, Tenrec has the following five characteristics: (1) it is large-scale, containing around 5 million users and 140 million interactions; (2) it has not only positive user feedback, but also true negative feedback (vs. one-class recommendation); (3) it contains overlapped users and items across four different scenarios; (4) it contains various types of user positive feedback, in forms of clicking, liking, sharing, and following, etc; (5) it contains additional features beyond the user IDs and item IDs. We verify Tenrec on ten diverse recommendation tasks by running several classical baseline models per task. Tenrec has the potential to become a useful benchmark dataset for a majority of popular recommendation tasks. Our source codes and datasets will be included in supplementary materials.

paragraphs: Recommendation benchmarks can be limited by small datasets or narrow records of user behavior. Tenrec addresses both concerns with a publicly available collection covering four recommendation scenarios. It contains approximately five million users and 140 million interactions, providing a setting for evaluating recommendation methods at a substantial scale.

The collection includes positive feedback such as clicks, likes, shares, and follows, together with true negative feedback. It also provides features beyond user and item identifiers. Users and items overlap across the four scenarios, making the relationships between scenarios part of the data. These properties support a wider range of questions than a dataset recording only one kind of positive interaction.

The authors evaluate Tenrec on ten recommendation tasks, running several classical baseline models for each. This demonstrates its use across multiple tasks rather than establishing a single recommendation method as the contribution. The paper presents Tenrec as a potentially useful benchmark for many popular recommendation problems, with its breadth coming from the combination of scale, varied feedback, and overlapping scenarios.
summary.tldr: Tenrec provides large-scale, varied recommendation feedback across four overlapping scenarios and is evaluated on ten tasks.

title: Tenrec: A Large-scale Multipurpose Benchmark Dataset for Recommender Systems

abstract: Modern pre-trained transformers have rapidly advanced the state-of-the-art in machine learning, but have also grown in parameters and computational complexity, making them increasingly difficult to deploy in resource-constrained environments. Binarization of the weights and activations of the network can significantly alleviate these issues, however, is technically challenging from an optimization perspective. In this work, we identify a series of improvements that enables binary transformers at a much higher accuracy than what was possible previously. These include a two-set binarization scheme, a novel elastic binary activation function with learned parameters, and a method to quantize a network to its limit by successively distilling higher precision models into lower precision students. These approaches allow for the first time, fully binarized transformer models that are at a practical level of accuracy, approaching a full-precision BERT baseline on the GLUE language understanding benchmark within as little as 5.9%. Code and models are available at:https://github.com/facebookresearch/bit.
