paragraphs: Large pretrained transformers are difficult to deploy when memory and computation are limited. Representing their weights and activations with binary values can reduce those demands, but training such restricted models is challenging. This paper studies how to improve the accuracy of fully binarized transformers enough to make the approach practically useful.

BiT combines several changes to the training and representation scheme. These include a two-set binarization method and an elastic binary activation function whose parameters are learned. It also uses successive knowledge distillation: models operating at higher precision teach students operating at lower precision. This creates a sequence of training transfers toward increasingly restrictive numerical representations.

The authors report substantially higher accuracy than previously possible for binary transformers. On the GLUE language-understanding benchmark, a fully binarized model comes within as little as 5.9% of a full-precision BERT baseline. The result indicates that coordinated changes to binarization, activations, and distillation can narrow the accuracy gap associated with extreme numerical compression, although the reported binary model still differs from its full-precision reference.
summary.tldr: BiT combines learned binary activations, a binarization scheme, and successive distillation to bring fully binary transformers closer to full-precision BERT accuracy.

title: BiT: Robustly Binarized Multi-distilled Transformer

abstract: Neural network models trained on text data have been found to encode undesirable linguistic or sensitive concepts in their representation. Removing such concepts is non-trivial because of a complex relationship between the concept, text input, and the learnt representation. Recent work has proposed post-hoc and adversarial methods to remove such unwanted concepts from a model's representation. Through an extensive theoretical and empirical analysis, we show that these methods can be counter-productive: they are unable to remove the concepts entirely, and in the worst case may end up destroying all task-relevant features. The reason is the methods' reliance on a probing classifier as a proxy for the concept. Even under the most favorable conditions for learning a probing classifier when a concept's relevant features in representation space alone can provide 100% accuracy, we prove that a probing classifier is likely to use non-concept features and thus post-hoc or adversarial methods will fail to remove the concept correctly. These theoretical implications are confirmed by experiments on models trained on synthetic, Multi-NLI, and Twitter datasets. For sensitive applications of concept removal such as fairness, we recommend caution against using these methods and propose a spuriousness metric to gauge the quality of the final classifier.

paragraphs: Text models can encode sensitive or unwanted concepts in their internal representations. Some removal methods train a probing classifier to detect the concept, then alter representations using that probe as a guide. This paper investigates whether a probe reliably identifies the information that actually belongs to the concept.

The theoretical analysis shows that a probe is likely to use features unrelated to the concept even when concept-relevant features alone allow perfect classification. Consequently, methods relying on the probe can remove the wrong information while leaving the unwanted concept incompletely removed. In the worst case, the analyzed approaches may destroy all features relevant to the main task.

Experiments with synthetic data, Multi-NLI, and Twitter data confirm the theoretical implications. The authors recommend caution when using these removal methods in sensitive applications such as fairness, and propose a spuriousness metric for assessing the final classifier. The key lesson is that accurate prediction of a concept does not establish that the probe uses the concept's own features, which undermines its role as a removal target.
summary.tldr: Probes can predict unwanted concepts using unrelated features, causing probe-based removal methods to retain the concept or damage task-relevant information.

title: Probing Classifiers are Unreliable for Concept Removal and Detection

abstract: Rationale extraction can be considered as a straightforward method of improving the model explainability, where rationales are a subsequence of the original inputs, and can be extracted to support the prediction results. Existing methods are mainly cascaded with the selector which extracts the rationale tokens, and the predictor which makes the prediction based on selected tokens. Since previous works fail to fully exploit the original input, where the information of non-selected tokens is ignored, in this paper, we propose a Disentanglement-Augmented Rationale Extraction (DARE) method, which encapsulates more information from the input to extract rationales. Specifically, it first disentangles the input into the rationale representations and the non-rationale ones, and then learns more comprehensive rationale representations for extracting by minimizing the mutual information (MI) between the two disentangled representations. Besides, to improve the performance of MI minimization, we develop a new MI estimator by exploring existing MI estimation methods. Extensive experimental results on three real-world datasets and simulation studies clearly validate the effectiveness of our proposed method. Code is released at https://github.com/yuelinan/DARE.

paragraphs: Rationale extraction explains a prediction by selecting a subsequence of the original input that supports it. A common design uses one component to choose tokens and another to predict from those tokens. The paper identifies a weakness in this setup: information contained in the unselected portion of the input is ignored.

DARE addresses this by separating the input into representations of rationale information and non-rationale information. It then minimizes the mutual information between those representations, reducing the information they share. This separation is used to learn more comprehensive rationale representations for extraction while taking account of information across the original input.

Because the method depends on estimating mutual information, the authors also develop a new estimator by examining existing estimation approaches. Experiments on three real-world datasets and simulation studies support the method’s effectiveness. The contribution is therefore both a different way to organize information for rationale selection and an estimation technique that supports the separation objective, with the goal of improving the extracted support for predictions.
summary.tldr: DARE improves rationale extraction by separating rationale and non-rationale representations and minimizing their shared information.

title: DARE: Disentanglement-Augmented Rationale Extraction

abstract: Open-vocabulary models like CLIP achieve high accuracy across many image classification tasks. However, there are still settings where their zero-shot performance is far from optimal. We study model patching, where the goal is to improve accuracy on specific tasks without degrading accuracy on tasks where performance is already adequate. Towards this goal, we introduce PAINT, a patching method that uses interpolations between the weights of a model before fine-tuning and the weights after fine-tuning on a task to be patched. On nine tasks where zero-shot CLIP performs poorly, PAINT increases accuracy by 15 to 60 percentage points while preserving accuracy on ImageNet within one percentage point of the zero-shot model. PAINT also allows a single model to be patched on multiple tasks and improves with model scale. Furthermore, we identify cases of broad transfer, where patching on one task increases accuracy on other tasks even when the tasks have disjoint classes. Finally, we investigate applications beyond common benchmarks such as counting or reducing the impact of typographic attacks on CLIP. Our findings demonstrate that it is possible to expand the set of tasks on which open-vocabulary models achieve high accuracy without re-training them from scratch.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary models such as CLIP perform well across many classification tasks, but some tasks remain difficult in the zero-shot setting. This paper studies patching: improving those weak areas while preserving performance where the model already works adequately. The challenge is to make a targeted improvement without giving up the usefulness of the original model.

PAINT interpolates between the model's original weights and its weights after fine-tuning on a task needing improvement. On nine tasks with poor zero-shot CLIP performance, this approach raises accuracy by 15 to 60 percentage points while keeping ImageNet accuracy within one percentage point of the original. These results demonstrate the desired balance on the evaluated tasks.

Additional applications investigate counting and typographic attacks. Together, the findings show that task coverage can be expanded without retraining the model from scratch.
summary.tldr: PAINT mixes original and fine-tuned weights to improve weak CLIP tasks while largely preserving ImageNet accuracy in the reported evaluations.

title: Patching open-vocabulary models by interpolating weights

abstract: Topological features based on persistent homology capture high-order structural information so as to augment graph neural network methods. However, computing extended persistent homology summaries remains slow for large and dense graphs and can be a serious bottleneck for the learning pipeline. Inspired by recent success in neural algorithmic reasoning, we propose a novel graph neural network to estimate extended persistence diagrams (EPDs) on graphs efficiently. Our model is built on algorithmic insights, and benefits from better supervision and closer alignment with the EPD computation algorithm. We validate our method with convincing empirical results on approximating EPDs and downstream graph representation learning tasks. Our method is also efficient; on large and dense graphs, we accelerate the computation by nearly 100 times.

paragraphs: Topological summaries can give graph neural networks information about higher-order graph structure. However, computing extended persistent homology can be slow, especially for large, dense graphs. This paper targets that bottleneck by learning to estimate extended persistence diagrams, the summaries used to represent these topological features.

The authors design a graph neural network around insights from the algorithm that computes the diagrams. The model benefits from improved supervision and a closer match between its design and the computation being approximated. This applies the idea of neural algorithmic reasoning to a specific costly step in graph learning: estimating a structural summary that would otherwise need to be computed directly.

Experiments evaluate both the quality of the diagram approximations and their usefulness in downstream graph representation learning. The authors report supportive results in both settings, alongside a speedup of nearly 100 times on large, dense graphs. The contribution is an efficient learned approximation whose value is assessed through both the target summaries and the learning tasks that use them.
summary.tldr: An algorithm-informed graph neural network approximates topological summaries, reporting nearly a hundredfold speedup on large, dense graphs.

title: Neural Approximation of Graph Topological Features

abstract: In real-world federated learning scenarios, participants could have their own personalized labels incompatible with those from other clients, due to using different label permutations or tackling completely different tasks or domains. However, most existing FL approaches cannot effectively tackle such extremely heterogeneous scenarios since they often assume that (1) all participants use a synchronized set of labels, and (2) they train on the same tasks from the same domain. In this work, to tackle these challenges, we introduce Factorized-FL, which allows to effectively tackle label- and task-heterogeneous federated learning settings by factorizing the model parameters into a pair of rank-1 vectors, where one captures the common knowledge across different labels and tasks and the other captures knowledge specific to the task for each local model. Moreover, based on the distance in the client-specific vector space, Factorized-FL performs a selective aggregation scheme to utilize only the knowledge from the relevant participants for each client. We extensively validate our method on both label- and domain-heterogeneous settings, on which it outperforms the state-of-the-art personalized federated learning methods. The code is available at https://github.com/wyjeong/Factorized-FL.

paragraphs: Federated learning becomes difficult when participants disagree about label meanings or work on different tasks and domains. Labels may be permuted between clients, or their prediction problems may be entirely different. This paper addresses such heterogeneity, challenging the shared-label and shared-task assumptions made by many existing federated-learning approaches.

Factorized-FL represents model parameters through a pair of rank-one vectors. One captures knowledge shared across labels and tasks, while the other represents knowledge specific to each local task. The client-specific vectors also provide a way to compare participants. Distances in that space guide selective aggregation, so each client draws on knowledge from participants judged relevant to it.

The authors evaluate the method in settings with heterogeneous labels and domains, where it outperforms the compared leading personalized federated-learning methods. The results support combining a separation of shared and local knowledge with selective collaboration. This matters because deciding whose information to combine becomes part of the learning problem when clients no longer share a common interpretation of their prediction targets.
summary.tldr: Factorized-FL separates shared and client-specific parameters and selectively combines relevant clients to handle heterogeneous federated-learning tasks.

title: Factorized-FL: Personalized Federated Learning with Parameter Factorization & Similarity Matching

abstract: We study the first gradient descent step on the first-layer parameters $\boldsymbol{W}$ in a two-layer neural network: $f(\boldsymbol{x}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\boldsymbol{a}^\top\sigma(\boldsymbol{W}^\top\boldsymbol{x})$, where $\boldsymbol{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}, \boldsymbol{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$ are randomly initialized, and the training objective is the empirical MSE loss: $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (f(\boldsymbol{x}_i)-y_i)^2$. In the proportional asymptotic limit where $n,d,N\to\infty$ at the same rate, and an idealized student-teacher setting where the teacher $f^*$ is a single-index model, we compute the prediction risk of ridge regression on the conjugate kernel after one gradient step on $\boldsymbol{W}$ with learning rate $\eta$. We consider two scalings of the first step learning rate $\eta$. For small $\eta$, we establish a Gaussian equivalence property for the trained feature map, and prove that the learned kernel improves upon the initial random features model, but cannot defeat the best linear model on the input. Whereas for sufficiently large $\eta$, we prove that for certain $f^*$, the same ridge estimator on trained features can go beyond this ``linear regime'' and outperform a wide range of (fixed) kernels. Our results demonstrate that even one gradient step can lead to a considerable advantage over random features, and highlight the role of learning rate scaling in the initial phase of training.

paragraphs: This paper isolates the effect of a single training step on the features of a randomly initialized two-layer neural network. The first-layer weights receive one gradient update using mean squared error, after which ridge regression is analyzed on the resulting features. This separates the value of changing the representation from the effects of a long training process.

The theory assumes an idealized student–teacher problem with a single-index teacher, while sample size, input dimension, and network width grow proportionally. For a small first-step learning rate, the authors establish a Gaussian equivalence property. The updated representation improves on the initial random features, but its prediction performance cannot surpass that of the best linear model on the original input.

With a sufficiently large learning rate, the conclusion changes for certain teacher functions: ridge regression on the updated features can outperform a broad range of fixed kernels. The results show that one step can already provide substantial representational benefits under the analyzed conditions. They also identify learning-rate scaling as a key factor in whether early feature learning remains within a linear performance regime.
summary.tldr: Under a proportional asymptotic model, one feature-learning step improves prediction, and sufficiently large steps can beat fixed kernels for certain targets.

title: High-dimensional Asymptotics of Feature Learning: How One Gradient Step Improves the Representation

abstract: Nanophotonic structures have versatile applications including solar cells, anti-reflective coatings, electromagnetic interference shielding, optical filters, and light emitting diodes. To design and understand these nanophotonic structures, electrodynamic simulations are essential. These simulations enable us to model electromagnetic fields over time and calculate optical properties. In this work, we introduce frameworks and benchmarks to evaluate nanophotonic structures in the context of parametric structure design problems. The benchmarks are instrumental in assessing the performance of optimization algorithms and identifying an optimal structure based on target optical properties. Moreover, we explore the impact of varying grid sizes in electrodynamic simulations, shedding light on how evaluation fidelity can be strategically leveraged in enhancing structure designs.

paragraphs: Nanophotonic design seeks structures with useful optical properties for applications such as solar cells, coatings, filters, and light-emitting diodes. Evaluating a candidate requires electrodynamic simulation, which models electromagnetic fields over time and calculates the resulting optical behavior. These evaluations are central to deciding whether a proposed design meets its target.

The paper introduces frameworks and benchmarks for design problems expressed through structural parameters. They provide a setting in which optimization algorithms can be assessed according to their ability to identify structures with desired optical properties. This connects algorithm evaluation to the actual design objective: finding a suitable physical structure through simulation.

The authors also investigate how changing the simulation grid size affects evaluation fidelity. This brings the resolution of the evaluation itself into the design problem, alongside the parameters of the structure being optimized. Their exploration examines how fidelity can be used strategically to improve designs. The contribution combines benchmarks for comparing optimization methods with an investigation of how the simulation choices supporting those comparisons influence the design process.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces nanophotonic design benchmarks and investigates how simulation grid size and evaluation fidelity can support better structure optimization.

title: Datasets and Benchmarks for Nanophotonic Structure and Parametric Design Simulations

abstract: We study the infinite-horizon restless bandit problem with the average reward criterion, in both discrete-time and continuous-time settings.A fundamental goal is to efficiently compute policies that achieve a diminishing optimality gap as the number of arms, $N$, grows large. Existing results on asymptotic optimality all rely on the uniform global attractor property (UGAP), a complex and challenging-to-verify assumption. In this paper, we propose a general, simulation-based framework, Follow-the-Virtual-Advice, that converts any single-armed policy into a policy for the original $N$-armed problem. This is done by simulating the single-armed policy on each arm and carefully steering the real state towards the simulated state. Our framework can be instantiated to produce a policy with an $O(1/\sqrt{N})$ optimality gap. In the discrete-time setting, our result holds under a simpler synchronization assumption, which covers some problem instances that violate UGAP. More notably, in the continuous-time setting, we do not require \emph{any} additional assumptions beyond the standard unichain condition. In both settings, our work is the first asymptotic optimality result that does not require UGAP.

paragraphs: This paper studies restless bandits over an unlimited time horizon, with performance measured by average reward. Earlier asymptotic optimality results depended on the uniform global attractor property, an assumption that is difficult to verify.

title: Restless Bandits with Average Reward: Breaking the Uniform Global Attractor Assumption

abstract: We propose a learning problem involving adapting a pre-trained source model to the target domain for classifying all classes that appeared in the source data, using target data that covers only a partial label space. This problem is practical, as it is unrealistic for the target end-users to collect data for all classes prior to adaptation. However, it has received limited attention in the literature. To shed light on this issue, we construct benchmark datasets and conduct extensive experiments to uncover the inherent challenges. We found a dilemma --- on the one hand, adapting to the new target domain is important to claim better performance; on the other hand, we observe that preserving the classification accuracy of classes missing in the target adaptation data is highly challenging, let alone improving them. To tackle this, we identify two key directions: 1) disentangling domain gradients from classification gradients, and 2) preserving class relationships. We present several effective solutions that maintain the accuracy of the missing classes and enhance the overall performance, establishing solid baselines for holistic transfer of pre-trained models with partial target data.

paragraphs: Holistic transfer asks how to adapt a pretrained classifier to a new domain when the available target data contain only some of its classes. The adapted model must still recognize every class from the source data. This reflects a practical situation in which end users cannot collect target examples for the full classification task.

The authors construct benchmarks and investigate the resulting tension. Adapting to the new domain matters for performance, but maintaining accuracy on classes absent from the adaptation data is difficult. Evaluating only the classes represented during adaptation would therefore miss an essential part of the intended behavior.

The paper identifies two directions for addressing the problem: separating domain-related gradients from classification-related gradients, and preserving relationships among classes. It presents several solutions that maintain accuracy for missing classes while improving overall performance in the experiments. These methods establish baselines for adaptation that accounts for the complete original label space, including classes for which the user supplies no target examples.
summary.tldr: Holistic transfer adapts classifiers using partial target-class data while seeking to preserve accuracy on the classes missing from adaptation.

title: Holistic Transfer: Towards Non-Disruptive Fine-Tuning with Partial Target Data

abstract: Interpreting time series models is uniquely challenging because it requires identifying both the location of time series signals that drive model predictions and their matching to an interpretable temporal pattern. While explainers from other modalities can be applied to time series, their inductive biases do not transfer well to the inherently challenging interpretation of time series. We present TimeX, a time series consistency model for training explainers. TimeX trains an interpretable surrogate to mimic the behavior of a pretrained time series model. It addresses the issue of model faithfulness by introducing model behavior consistency, a novel formulation that preserves relations in the latent space induced by the pretrained model with relations in the latent space induced by TimeX. TimeX provides discrete attribution maps and, unlike existing interpretability methods, it learns a latent space of explanations that can be used in various ways, such as to provide landmarks to visually aggregate similar explanations and easily recognize temporal patterns. We evaluate TimeX on eight synthetic and real-world datasets and compare its performance against state-of-the-art interpretability methods. We also conduct case studies using physiological time series. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate that TimeX achieves the highest or second-highest performance in every metric compared to baselines across all datasets. Through case studies, we show that the novel components of TimeX show potential for training faithful, interpretable models that capture the behavior of pretrained time series models.

paragraphs: Explaining a time-series prediction involves both locating influential signals and recognizing the temporal patterns they form. The contribution combines strong reported attribution performance with a way to compare explanations across examples.
summary.tldr: TimeX learns attribution maps and an explanation space by preserving relationships in a pretrained time-series model's internal representations.

title: Encoding Time-Series Explanations through Self-Supervised Model Behavior Consistency

abstract: Neural networks are capable of translating between languages—in some cases even between two languages where there is little or no access to parallel translations, in what is known as Unsupervised Machine Translation (UMT). Given this progress, it is intriguing to ask whether machine learning tools can ultimately enable understanding animal communication, particularly that of highly intelligentanimals. We propose a theoretical framework for analyzing UMT when no parallel translations are available and when it cannot be assumed that the source and target corpora address related subject domains or posses similar linguistic structure. Weexemplify this theory with two stylized models of language, for which our framework provides bounds on necessary sample complexity; the bounds are formally proven and experimentally verified on synthetic data. These bounds show that the error rates are inversely related to the language complexity and amount of common ground. This suggests that unsupervised translation of animal communication may be feasible if the communication system is sufficiently complex.

paragraphs: Unsupervised translation attempts to connect languages without examples showing how particular messages translate. This paper asks what can be established when the problem is harder still: the two collections of communication need not discuss similar subjects or share similar linguistic structure. Animal communication motivates this broader theoretical setting.

The authors develop a framework for studying this problem and apply it to two simplified models of language. For these models, they prove bounds on the amount of data needed and check the theoretical results using synthetic data. This connects translation difficulty to properties of the communication systems, rather than assuming the similarities that make human-language translation easier.

The bounds associate lower error with greater language complexity and more common ground between the systems. Within this framework, complexity can therefore help make translation possible. The results suggest that sufficiently complex animal communication might support unsupervised translation; they do not establish successful translation of an actual animal communication system.
summary.tldr: A theoretical framework suggests that unsupervised animal communication translation may be feasible when communication is sufficiently complex.

title: A Theory of Unsupervised Translation Motivated by Understanding Animal Communication

abstract: The increasing availability of graph-structured data motivates the task of optimising over functions defined on the node set of graphs. Traditional graph search algorithms can be applied in this case, but they may be sample-inefficient and do not make use of information about the function values; on the other hand, Bayesian optimisation is a class of promising black-box solvers with superior sample efficiency, but it has scarcely been applied to such novel setups. To fill this gap, we propose a novel Bayesian optimisation framework that optimises over functions defined on generic, large-scale and potentially unknown graphs. Through the learning of suitable kernels on graphs, our framework has the advantage of adapting to the behaviour of the target function. The local modelling approach further guarantees the efficiency of our method. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world graphs demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed optimisation framework.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to find good values of a function whose possible inputs are the nodes of a graph. Ordinary graph search can explore this space, but may spend evaluations inefficiently and fail to exploit information from function values already observed. The authors bring Bayesian optimisation to this setting to make the search more informed.

Their framework learns suitable graph kernels: mathematical descriptions of relationships between nodes that help model the target function. Learning these relationships lets the search adapt to how the function behaves, rather than relying only on the graph's fixed structure. The method also uses local modelling to keep optimisation efficient on large graphs, including settings where the graph may initially be unknown.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world graphs demonstrate the framework's effectiveness. The contribution combines adaptation to observed function values with an approach designed for computational efficiency. This matters because searching a graph involves both deciding where to evaluate next and keeping the model that guides those decisions manageable.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian optimisation framework learns relationships between graph nodes and uses local models to search large, potentially unknown graphs efficiently.

title: Bayesian Optimisation of Functions on Graphs

abstract: Adapting models deployed to test distributions can mitigate the performance degradation caused by distribution shifts. However, privacy concerns may render model parameters inaccessible. One promising approach involves utilizing zeroth-order optimization (ZOO) to train a data adaptor to adapt the test data to fit the deployed models. Nevertheless, the data adaptor trained with ZOO typically brings restricted improvements due to the potential corruption of data features caused by the data adaptor. To address this issue, we revisit ZOO in the context of test-time data adaptation. We find that the issue directly stems from the unreliable estimation of the gradients used to optimize the data adaptor, which is inherently due to the unreliable nature of the pseudo-labels assigned to the test data. Based on this observation, we propose pseudo-label-robust data adaptation (SODA) to improve the performance of data adaptation. Specifically, SODA leverages high-confidence predicted labels as reliable labels to optimize the data adaptor with ZOO for label prediction. For data with low-confidence predictions, SODA encourages the adaptor to preserve data information to mitigate data corruption. Empirical results indicate that SODA can significantly enhance the performance of deployed models in the presence of distribution shifts without requiring access to model parameters.

paragraphs: A deployed model can lose accuracy when its input distribution changes, yet its parameters may be inaccessible. One response is to train a data adaptor that changes incoming examples to better fit the model. This paper examines why training such adaptors with zeroth-order optimization can yield limited improvements and even corrupt useful input features.

The authors trace the problem to unreliable gradient estimates arising from unreliable pseudo-labels assigned to test examples. SODA responds differently according to prediction confidence. It uses high-confidence predicted labels to optimize the adaptor for label prediction, while encouraging preservation of information for examples whose predictions have low confidence.

This distinction lets the adaptor use stronger predictive signals where available and reduce damaging changes where those signals are uncertain. Empirical results show substantial improvements for deployed models facing distribution shifts without access to their parameters. The contribution is a confidence-sensitive adaptation strategy that addresses both the learning signal and the risk of losing useful data information during adaptation.
summary.tldr: SODA improves parameter-inaccessible models under distribution shift by adapting confident examples and preserving information in uncertain ones.

title: SODA: Robust Training of Test-Time Data Adaptors

abstract: 3D visual grounding, the task of identifying visual objects in 3D scenes based on natural language inputs, plays a critical role in enabling machines to understand and engage with the real-world environment. However, this task is challenging due to the necessity to capture 3D contextual information to distinguish target objects from complex 3D scenes. The absence of annotations for contextual objects and relations further exacerbates the difficulties. In this paper, we propose a novel model, CORE-3DVG, to address these challenges by explicitly learning about contextual objects and relations. Our method accomplishes 3D visual grounding via three sequential modular networks, including a text-guided object detection network, a relation matching network, and a target identification network. During training, we introduce a pseudo-label self-generation strategy and a weakly-supervised method to facilitate the learning of contextual objects and relations, respectively. The proposed techniques allow the networks to focus more effectively on referred objects within 3D scenes by understanding their context better. We validate our model on the challenging Nr3D, Sr3D, and ScanRefer datasets and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. Our code will be public at https://github.com/yangli18/CORE-3DVG.

paragraphs: Identifying an object in a 3D scene from a language description can require understanding other objects and their relationships. The target’s own appearance may not provide enough information to distinguish it within a complex scene. CORE-3DVG addresses this contextual reasoning problem while also handling the absence of annotations for contextual objects and relations.

The model divides grounding into three sequential networks. A text-guided object detector identifies relevant objects, a relation-matching network considers their relationships, and a target-identification network selects the referred object. This modular sequence makes context an explicit part of the path from a description to its intended target.

During training, the system generates pseudo-labels to help learn contextual objects and uses weak supervision to learn relations. These techniques provide learning signals where direct contextual annotations are unavailable. Evaluations on Nr3D, Sr3D, and ScanRefer report state-of-the-art performance. The findings support explicitly learning contextual objects and relationships as a way to improve language-guided object identification in 3D scenes.
summary.tldr: CORE-3DVG improves language-guided object identification in 3D scenes by explicitly learning contextual objects and their relationships.

title: Exploiting Contextual Objects and Relations for 3D Visual Grounding

abstract: Pre-training on massive video datasets has become essential to achieve high action recognition performance on smaller downstream datasets. However, most large-scale video datasets contain images of people and hence are accompanied with issues related to privacy, ethics, and data protection, often preventing them from being publicly shared for reproducible research. Existing work has attempted to alleviate these problems by blurring faces, downsampling videos, or training on synthetic data. On the other hand, analysis on the {\em transferability} of privacy-preserving pre-trained models to downstream tasks has been limited. In this work, we study this problem by first asking the question: can we pre-train models for human action recognition with data that does not include real humans? To this end, we present, for the first time, a benchmark that leverages real-world videos with {\em humans removed} and synthetic data containing virtual humans to pre-train a model. We then evaluate the transferability of the representation learned on this data to a diverse set of downstream action recognition benchmarks. Furthermore, we propose a novel pre-training strategy, called Privacy-Preserving MAE-Align, to effectively combine synthetic data and human-removed real data. Our approach outperforms previous baselines by up to 5\% and closes the performance gap between human and no-human action recognition representations on downstream tasks, for both linear probing and fine-tuning. Our benchmark, code, and models are available at https://github.com/howardzh01/PPMA.

paragraphs: Large video datasets help models learn representations for recognizing human actions, but recordings of real people raise privacy and data-sharing concerns. This paper investigates whether useful action-recognition representations can be pretrained without real humans appearing in the training data. Its emphasis is on how well those representations transfer to downstream tasks.

The authors introduce a benchmark combining two sources: real-world videos with humans removed and synthetic videos containing virtual humans. They evaluate models pretrained on these sources across a diverse collection of action-recognition benchmarks. They also propose Privacy-Preserving MAE-Align, a pretraining strategy designed to combine the two sources effectively.

The approach improves on previous baselines by up to 5% in the reported experiments and closes the performance gap between representations learned with and without real humans. The results cover both linear probing and fine-tuning. This makes transfer quality a central part of evaluating the proposed alternative, connecting the choice of pretraining data to its usefulness for later action-recognition tasks.
summary.tldr: Combining human-removed videos with synthetic people improves action-recognition pretraining without images of real humans.

title: Learning Human Action Recognition Representations Without Real Humans

abstract: Learning rich skills under the option framework without supervision of external rewards is at the frontier of reinforcement learning research. Existing works mainly fall into two distinctive categories: variational option discovery that maximizes the diversity of the options through a mutual information loss (while ignoring coverage) and Laplacian-based methods that focus on improving the coverage of options by increasing connectivity of the state space (while ignoring diversity). In this paper, we show that diversity and coverage in unsupervised option discovery can indeed be unified under the same mathematical framework. To be specific, we explicitly quantify the diversity and coverage of the learned options through a novel use of Determinantal Point Process (DPP) and optimize these objectives to discover options with both superior diversity and coverage. Our proposed algorithm, ODPP, has undergone extensive evaluation on challenging tasks created with Mujoco and Atari. The results demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both diversity- and coverage-driven categories.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a reinforcement learning agent can discover useful skills without external rewards. Within the option framework, the challenge is to learn behaviors that differ from one another while also reaching broadly across the available states. These goals are related, but optimizing one does not automatically address the other.

The authors identify a split in existing approaches. Variational methods encourage diversity through mutual information, while Laplacian methods emphasize coverage by improving connectivity across the state space. They propose a shared mathematical treatment using a determinantal point process, or DPP, to explicitly quantify both diversity and coverage. Their algorithm, ODPP, optimizes these quantities together.

Evaluations on challenging Mujoco and Atari tasks show ODPP outperforming leading methods from both categories. The contribution is therefore both conceptual and empirical: diversity and coverage can be expressed within one framework, and jointly pursuing them produced better results in the reported evaluations. This gives unsupervised skill discovery a way to address both objectives within the same learning procedure.
summary.tldr: ODPP uses determinantal point processes to jointly optimize skill diversity and state-space coverage without external rewards.

title: A Unified Algorithm Framework for Unsupervised Discovery of Skills based on Determinantal Point Process

abstract: Deriving reliable region-word alignment from image-text pairs is critical to learnobject-level vision-language representations for open-vocabulary object detection.Existing methods typically rely on pre-trained or self-trained vision-languagemodels for alignment, which are prone to limitations in localization accuracy orgeneralization capabilities. In this paper, we propose CoDet, a novel approachthat overcomes the reliance on pre-aligned vision-language space by reformulatingregion-word alignment as a co-occurring object discovery problem. Intuitively, bygrouping images that mention a shared concept in their captions, objects corresponding to the shared concept shall exhibit high co-occurrence among the group.CoDet then leverages visual similarities to discover the co-occurring objects andalign them with the shared concept. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoDethas superior performances and compelling scalability in open-vocabulary detection,e.g., by scaling up the visual backbone, CoDet achieves 37.0 $AP^m_{novel}$ and 44.7 $AP^m_{all}$ on OV-LVIS, surpassing the previous SoTA by 4.2 $AP^m_{novel}$ and 9.8 $AP^m_{all}$. Code is available at https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/CoDet.

paragraphs: CoDet studies how to connect words in captions with the image regions they describe. This alignment is important for learning object representations in open-vocabulary detection. Existing approaches rely on vision-language models to establish the connection, which can introduce problems with localization accuracy or generalization.

The proposed approach turns alignment into a search for objects that recur across related images. It groups images whose captions mention a shared concept, then uses visual similarities to identify recurring objects within the group. Those objects are aligned with the shared concept. The key intuition is that repeated mentions across images can provide evidence about which visual regions correspond to a word, without requiring a previously aligned vision-language space.

Experiments report strong detection performance and benefits from scaling the visual backbone. On OV-LVIS, the scaled model reaches 37.0 APᵐ for novel categories and 44.7 APᵐ overall, exceeding the previous state of the art by 4.2 and 9.8 respectively. These results support co-occurrence as a useful source of region-word supervision.
summary.tldr: CoDet aligns caption concepts with image regions by finding visually recurring objects across images that mention the same concept.

title: CoDet: Co-occurrence Guided Region-Word Alignment for Open-Vocabulary Object Detection

abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm is the method of choice in many machine learning tasks thanks to its scalability and efficiency in dealing with large-scale problems. In this paper, we focus on the shuffling version of SGD which matches the mainstream practical heuristics. We show the convergence to a global solution of shuffling SGD for a class of non-convex functions under over-parameterized settings. Our analysis employs more relaxed non-convex assumptions than previous literature. Nevertheless, we maintain the desired computational complexity as shuffling SGD has achieved in the general convex setting.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent is widely used because it can handle large learning problems efficiently. This paper studies its shuffling variant, reflecting a common practical training procedure. The central theoretical question is whether that procedure can converge to a global solution when the objective is non-convex, rather than only having the simpler structure of a convex problem.

The authors establish global convergence for a particular class of non-convex functions in over-parameterized settings. Their analysis uses more relaxed non-convex assumptions than previous work. Both qualifications matter: the result concerns the specified function class and parameterization regime, rather than asserting that shuffling resolves arbitrary non-convex optimization problems.

Despite relaxing the assumptions, the analysis retains the computational complexity that shuffling SGD had achieved in the general convex setting. This links a stronger understanding of non-convex training to an established efficiency standard. The contribution is a convergence guarantee for a practically relevant optimization procedure, showing that global-solution results and favorable complexity can coexist under the conditions studied.
summary.tldr: Shuffling SGD provably reaches global solutions for a class of over-parameterized non-convex problems while retaining favorable computational complexity.

title: On the Convergence to a Global Solution of Shuffling-Type Gradient Algorithms

abstract: We study the problem, where given a dataset of $n$ i.i.d. samples from an unknown distribution $P$, we seek to generate a sample from a distribution that is close to $P$ in total variation distance, under the constraint of differential privacy. We study the settings where $P$ is a multi-dimensional Gaussian distribution with different assumptions: known covariance, unknown bounded covariance, and unknown unbounded covariance. We present new differentially private sampling algorithms, and show that they achieve near-optimal sample complexity in the first two settings. Moreover, when $P$ is a product distribution on the binary hypercube, we obtain a pure-DP algorithm whereas only an approximate-DP algorithm (with slightly worse sample complexity) was previously known.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to generate a new sample resembling an unknown distribution while protecting the privacy of the dataset used to produce it. The input consists of independent samples drawn from that distribution. The target is a sampling distribution close to the original in total variation distance, subject to differential privacy.

The authors develop algorithms for multidimensional Gaussian distributions under three information settings: known covariance, unknown but bounded covariance, and unknown unbounded covariance. Covariance describes how the coordinates vary together. The distinction matters because the available information changes what the private sampling procedure must accomplish from the observed data.

The paper establishes nearly optimal sample complexity for the known-covariance and unknown-bounded-covariance settings. It also studies product distributions over binary vectors and gives a pure differential privacy algorithm where an approximate differential privacy algorithm had previously been known, with slightly worse sample complexity. These results sharpen both the data requirements and privacy guarantees available for sampling from the specified distribution families.
summary.tldr: New private sampling algorithms improve guarantees for Gaussian and binary product distributions, with nearly optimal data requirements in two Gaussian settings.

title: On Differentially Private Sampling from Gaussian and Product Distributions

abstract: We consider the problem of sampling transition paths between two given metastable states of a molecular system, eg. a folded and unfolded protein or products and reactants of a chemical reaction. Due to the existence of high energy barriers separating the states, these transition paths are unlikely to be sampled with standard Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulation. Traditional methods to augment MD with a bias potential to increase the probability of the transition rely on a dimensionality reduction step based on Collective Variables (CVs). Unfortunately, selecting appropriate CVs requires chemical intuition and traditional methods are therefore not always applicable to larger systems. Additionally, when incorrect CVs are used, the bias potential might not be minimal and bias the system along dimensions irrelevant to the transition. Showing a formal relation between the problem of sampling molecular transition paths, the Schrodinger bridge problem and stochastic optimal control with neural network policies, we propose a machine learning method for sampling said transitions. Unlike previous non-machine learning approaches our method, named PIPS, does not depend on CVs. We show that our method successful generates low energy transitions for Alanine Dipeptide as well as the larger Polyproline and Chignolin proteins.

Choosing suitable variables requires chemical intuition and becomes difficult for larger systems.

Poorly chosen collective variables can direct the bias along dimensions irrelevant to the transition. This paper develops PIPS, a machine-learning method that avoids requiring those variables. Its foundation is a formal relationship between transition-path sampling, the Schrödinger bridge problem, and stochastic optimal control with neural-network policies.

The theoretical connection supplies the basis for the method, while the molecular examples show its ability to produce transitions across the systems studied.
summary.tldr: PIPS uses neural stochastic optimal control to sample molecular transition paths without hand-selected collective variables.

title: Stochastic Optimal Control for Collective Variable Free Sampling of Molecular Transition Paths

abstract: Collaborative filtering (CF) has exhibited prominent results for recommender systems and been broadly utilized for real-world applications.A branch of research enhances CF methods by message passing (MP) used in graph neural networks, due to its strong capabilities of extracting knowledge from graph-structured data, like user-item bipartite graphs that naturally exist in CF. They assume that MP helps CF methods in a manner akin to its benefits for graph-based learning tasks in general (e.g., node classification). However, even though MP empirically improves CF, whether or not this assumption is correct still needs verification. To address this gap, we formally investigate why MP helps CF from multiple perspectives and show that many assumptions made by previous works are not entirely accurate. With our curated ablation studies and theoretical analyses, we discover that (i) MP improves the CF performance primarily by additional representations passed from neighbors during the forward pass instead of additional gradient updates to neighbor representations during the model back-propagation and (ii) MP usually helps low-degree nodes more than high-degree nodes.}Utilizing these novel findings, we present Test-time Aggregation for Collaborative Filtering, namely TAG-CF, a test-time augmentation framework that only conducts MP once at inference time. The key novelty of TAG-CF is that it effectively utilizes graph knowledge while circumventing most of notorious computational overheads of MP. Besides, TAG-CF is extremely versatile can be used as a plug-and-play module to enhance representations trained by different CF supervision signals. Evaluated on six datasets (i.e., five academic benchmarks and one real-world industrial dataset), TAG-CF consistently improves the recommendation performance of CF methods without graph by up to 39.2% on cold users and 31.7% on all users, with little to no extra computational overheads. Furthermore, compared with trending graph-enhanced CF methods, TAG-CF delivers comparable or even better performance with less than 1% of their total training times. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/snap-research/Test-time-Aggregation-for-CF.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering can use a graph connecting users and items, with message passing allowing neighboring representations to contribute information. Although this often improves recommendations, the paper questions whether it helps for the same reasons assumed in other graph-learning tasks. The authors investigate the mechanism through theoretical analysis and targeted ablation studies.

They find that the main benefit comes from neighboring representations added during the forward pass, rather than extra gradient updates to neighbors during backpropagation. They also find that message passing usually helps nodes with fewer connections more. These observations motivate TAG-CF, which performs message passing just once at inference time and can augment representations trained with different collaborative-filtering supervision signals.

Across six datasets, TAG-CF improves nongraph collaborative filtering by up to 39.2% for cold users and 31.7% across all users, with little or no extra computational overhead. These empirical results support extracting useful graph information at inference without repeatedly incorporating message passing throughout training.
summary.tldr: TAG-CF turns findings about message passing into a single inference-time aggregation step that improves collaborative filtering at low computational cost.

title: How Does Message Passing Improve Collaborative Filtering?

abstract: Images produced by diffusion models are increasingly popular in digital artwork and visual marketing. However, such generated images might replicate content from existing ones and pose the challenge of content originality. Existing Image Copy Detection (ICD) models, though accurate in detecting hand-crafted replicas, overlook the challenge from diffusion models. This motivates us to introduce ICDiff, the first ICD specialized for diffusion models. To this end, we construct a Diffusion-Replication (D-Rep) dataset and correspondingly propose a novel deep embedding method. D-Rep uses a state-of-the-art diffusion model (Stable Diffusion V1.5) to generate 40, 000 image-replica pairs, which are manually annotated into 6 replication levels ranging from 0 (no replication) to 5 (total replication). Our method, PDF-Embedding, transforms the replication level of each image-replica pair into a probability density function (PDF) as the supervision signal. The intuition is that the probability of neighboring replication levels should be continuous and smooth. Experimental results show that PDF-Embedding surpasses protocol-driven methods and non-PDF choices on the D-Rep test set. Moreover, by utilizing PDF-Embedding, we find that the replication ratios of well-known diffusion models against an open-source gallery range from 10% to 20%. The project is publicly available at https://icdiff.github.io/.

The paper introduces ICDiff to study this problem with a dedicated dataset and detection method.

The authors also use it to assess well-known diffusion models against an open-source gallery, finding replication ratios between 10% and 20%. Those figures describe the reported gallery-based assessment; the broader contribution is a graded representation of replication tailored to diffusion outputs.
summary.tldr: ICDiff introduces a diffusion-replication dataset and a detector trained with smooth supervision over degrees of image copying.

title: Image Copy Detection for Diffusion Models

abstract: Restless multi-armed bandits (RMAB) extend multi-armed bandits so arm pulls impact future arm states. Despite the success of RMABs, a key limiting assumption is the separability of rewards into a sum across arms. We address this deficiency by proposing restless-multi-armed bandit with global rewards (RMAB-G), a generalization of RMABs to global non-separable rewards. To solve RMAB-G, we develop the Linear-Whittle and Shapley-Whittle indices, which extend Whittle indices from RMABs to RMAB-Gs. We prove approximation bounds which demonstrate how Linear and Shapley-Whittle indices fail for non-linear rewards. To overcome this limitation, we propose two sets of adaptive policies: the first computes indices iteratively and the second combines indices with Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). Empirically, we demonstrate that adaptive policies outperform both pre-computed index policies and baselines in synthetic and real-world food rescue datasets.

paragraphs: The paper extends restless multi-armed bandits to settings where rewards depend jointly on multiple arms. In these problems, choosing an arm affects its future state. The usual assumption that total reward is a sum of separate arm rewards limits the interactions that the model can represent, motivating the proposed global-reward formulation, RMAB-G.

The authors first develop Linear-Whittle and Shapley-Whittle indices as extensions of Whittle indices. Their approximation bounds also reveal how these extensions can fail with nonlinear rewards. This analysis motivates policies that adapt their decisions rather than relying entirely on indices computed in advance.

Two families of adaptive policies follow: one recomputes indices iteratively, and the other combines indices with Monte-Carlo Tree Search. On synthetic datasets and real-world food rescue datasets, these adaptive policies outperform precomputed index policies and the evaluated baselines. The findings show the practical value of accounting for joint rewards during decision-making, while the theoretical analysis explains a limitation of directly extending index-based methods to nonlinear objectives.
summary.tldr: The paper extends restless bandits to joint rewards and develops adaptive policies that outperform precomputed indices in experiments.

title: Global Rewards in Restless Multi-Armed Bandits

abstract: We develop and analyze algorithms for instrumental variable regression by viewing the problem as a conditional stochastic optimization problem. In the context of least-squares instrumental variable regression, our algorithms neither require matrix inversions nor mini-batches thereby providing a fully online approach for performing instrumental variable regression with streaming data. When the true model is linear, we derive rates of convergence in expectation, that are of order $\mathcal{O}(\log T/T)$ and $\mathcal{O}(1/T^{1-\epsilon})$ for any $\epsilon>0$, respectively under the availability of two-sample and one-sample oracles respectively. Importantly, under the availability of the two-sample oracle, the aforementioned rate is actually agnostic to the relationship between confounder and the instrumental variable demonstrating the flexibility of the proposed approach in alleviating the need for explicit model assumptions required in recent works based on reformulating the problem as min-max optimization problems. Experimental validation is provided to demonstrate the advantages of the proposed algorithms over classical approaches like the 2SLS method.

paragraphs: This paper develops instrumental-variable regression algorithms suited to data arriving as a stream. It casts the regression problem as conditional stochastic optimization. For the least-squares setting, the resulting methods avoid both matrix inversions and minibatches, allowing updates in a fully online manner.

When the true model is linear, the authors prove expected convergence rates that depend on the sampling access available. A two-sample oracle gives a rate of O(log T/T), while a one-sample oracle gives O(1/T^(1−epsilon)) for any positive epsilon. These are distinct guarantees associated with different oracle settings, rather than interchangeable rates for the same access conditions.

Under the two-sample oracle, the stated rate does not depend on the relationship between the confounder and instrumental variable. The authors emphasize that this relaxes explicit modeling requirements used in recent min-max reformulations. Experiments demonstrate advantages over classical approaches such as two-stage least squares. Together, the results connect an online computational design with convergence theory under clearly identified assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper provides fully online instrumental-variable regression algorithms without matrix inversions or minibatches, with convergence guarantees for linear true models.

title: Stochastic Optimization Algorithms for Instrumental Variable Regression with Streaming Data

abstract: We propose a novel approach to molecular simulations using neural network reparametrization, which offers a flexible alternative to traditional coarse-graining methods. Unlike conventional techniques that strictly reduce degrees of freedom, the complexity of the system can be adjusted in our model, sometimes increasing it to simplify the optimization process. Our approach also maintains continuous access to fine-grained modes and eliminates the need for force-matching, enhancing both the efficiency and accuracy of energy minimization.Importantly, our framework allows for the use of potentially arbitrary neural networks (e.g., Graph Neural Networks (GNN)) to perform the reparametrization, incorporating CG modes as needed. In fact, our experiments using very weak molecular forces (Lennard-Jones potential) the GNN-based model is the sole model to find the correct configuration. Similarly, in protein-folding scenarios, our GNN-based CG method consistently outperforms traditional optimization methods. It not only recovers the target structures more accurately but also achieves faster convergence to the deepest energy states.This work demonstrates significant advancements in molecular simulations by optimizing energy minimization and convergence speeds, offering a new, efficient framework for simulating complex molecular systems.

paragraphs: Molecular energy minimization depends on how a system's configurations are represented during optimization. Traditional coarse-graining reduces the number of degrees of freedom. This paper proposes a neural-network reparametrization that can adjust complexity more flexibly, including sometimes increasing it when doing so makes the optimization problem easier to solve.

The approach retains continuous access to fine-grained modes and avoids force-matching. Its framework allows potentially arbitrary neural-network architectures to define the reparametrization, including graph neural networks, while incorporating coarse-grained modes as needed. The central idea is to improve the representation through which optimization proceeds without requiring a strict reduction in the system's available detail.

In experiments with weak Lennard-Jones forces, the graph-neural-network version is the only tested model to find the correct configuration. In the reported protein-folding scenarios, it recovers target structures more accurately and converges faster to the deepest energy states than traditional optimization methods. These findings support flexible reparametrization as a useful route to improved energy minimization in the molecular settings studied.
summary.tldr: Neural-network reparametrization improves molecular energy optimization by flexibly changing the representation while preserving access to fine-grained modes.

title: Neural Network Reparametrization for Accelerated Optimization in Molecular Simulations

abstract: Studying the interplay between the geometry of the loss landscape and the optimization trajectories of simple neural networks is a fundamental step for understanding their behavior in more complex settings.This paper reveals the presence of topological obstruction in the loss landscape of shallow ReLU neural networks trained using gradient flow. We discuss how the homogeneous nature of the ReLU activation function constrains the training trajectories to lie on a product of quadric hypersurfaces whose shape depends on the particular initialization of the network's parameters. When the neural network's output is a single scalar, we prove that these quadrics can have multiple connected components, limiting the set of reachable parameters during training. We analytically compute the number of these components and discuss the possibility of mapping one to the other through neuron rescaling and permutation. In this simple setting, we find that the non-connectedness results in a topological obstruction, which, depending on the initialization, can make the global optimum unreachable. We validate this result with numerical experiments.

paragraphs: A training trajectory can be restricted by the geometry of parameter space, not just by the values of the loss it encounters. This paper studies such restrictions for shallow ReLU networks trained with gradient flow. It shows how the scaling structure of the activation constrains which parameter values training can reach.

Specifically, ReLU homogeneity keeps trajectories on a product of quadric hypersurfaces whose shapes depend on initialization. For networks with a single scalar output, the authors prove that these surfaces can have multiple disconnected components. They calculate the number of components and discuss whether neuron rescaling and permutation can map between them.

Disconnectedness matters because a continuous training trajectory cannot freely move between separate components of its permitted surface. Depending on initialization, this can make the global optimum unreachable. Numerical experiments validate the theoretical result in the studied setting. The claim is therefore a possible, initialization-dependent obstruction for shallow scalar-output networks under gradient flow, rather than a universal assertion that ReLU training cannot find global optima.
summary.tldr: For shallow scalar-output ReLU networks, initialization-dependent disconnected constraints can prevent gradient flow from reaching a global optimum.

title: Topological obstruction to the training of shallow ReLU neural networks

abstract: Despite the abundance of datasets available for assessing large language models (LLMs), the scarcity of continuous and reliable difficulty labels for individual data points, in most cases, curtails their capacity to benchmark model generalization performance across different levels of complexity. Addressing this limitation, we present Easy2Hard, an innovative collection of 6 benchmark datasets featuring standardized difficulty labels spanning a wide range of domains, such as mathematics and programming problems, chess puzzles, and reasoning questions, providing a much-needed tool for those in demand of a dataset with varying degrees of difficulty for LLM assessment. We estimate the difficulty of individual problems by leveraging the performance data of many human subjects and LLMs on prominent leaderboards. Harnessing the rich human performance data, we employ widely recognized difficulty ranking systems, including the Item Response Theory (IRT) and Glicko-2 models, to uniformly assign difficulty scores to problems. The Easy2Hard datasets distinguish themselves from previous collections by incorporating a significantly higher proportion of challenging problems, presenting a novel and demanding test for state-of-the-art LLMs. Through extensive experiments conducted with six state-of-the-art LLMs on the Easy2Hard datasets, we offer valuable insights into their performance and generalization capabilities across varying degrees of difficulty, setting the stage for future research in LLM generalization.

paragraphs: An overall benchmark score can leave unclear how a language model performs as problems become harder. Many existing datasets lack reliable, continuous difficulty labels for individual questions. Easy2Hard addresses this measurement gap with six benchmark datasets covering domains that include mathematics, programming, chess puzzles, and reasoning.

The authors estimate difficulty using performance records from many people and language models on established leaderboards. They apply recognized ranking approaches, including Item Response Theory and Glicko-2, to assign standardized problem scores. Difficulty is therefore grounded in observed performance, giving researchers a basis for examining model behavior across a range of challenge levels.

The collection includes a substantially greater proportion of difficult problems than previous collections, making it a demanding evaluation resource. Experiments with six state-of-the-art language models examine performance and generalization across the difficulty range. The contribution is a way to profile where models succeed and struggle more precisely, rather than treating all questions in a dataset as equally informative about their capabilities.
summary.tldr: Easy2Hard provides six datasets with performance-derived difficulty scores for evaluating how language-model capabilities change as problems become harder.

title: Easy2Hard-Bench: Standardized Difficulty Labels for Profiling LLM Performance and Generalization

abstract: Long-tailed semi-supervised learning poses a significant challenge in training models with limited labeled data exhibiting a long-tailed label distribution. Current state-of-the-art LTSSL approaches heavily rely on high-quality pseudo-labels for large-scale unlabeled data. However, these methods often neglect the impact of representations learned by the neural network and struggle with real-world unlabeled data, which typically follows a different distribution than labeled data. This paper introduces a novel probabilistic framework that unifies various recent proposals in long-tail learning. Our framework derives the class-balanced contrastive loss through Gaussian kernel density estimation. We introduce a continuous contrastive learning method, CCL, extending our framework to unlabeled data using *reliable* and *smoothed* pseudo-labels. By progressively estimating the underlying label distribution and optimizing its alignment with model predictions, we tackle the diverse distribution of unlabeled data in real-world scenarios. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets with varying unlabeled data distributions demonstrate that CCL consistently outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods, achieving over 4% improvement on the ImageNet-127 dataset. The supplementary material includes the source code for reproducibility.

paragraphs: Learning from a small labeled dataset becomes particularly difficult when some classes have many examples and others have very few. Adding unlabeled data can help, but its class frequencies may differ from those of the labeled examples. Methods that depend heavily on model-generated labels must therefore deal with both unreliable predictions and mismatched distributions.

The paper develops a probabilistic framework that connects several existing approaches to learning with uneven class frequencies. It derives a class-balanced contrastive objective through Gaussian kernel density estimation, linking the learned representation to class balancing. Continuous Contrastive Learning, or CCL, extends this framework to unlabeled examples using reliable, smoothed pseudo-labels.

CCL progressively estimates the underlying label distribution and adjusts its alignment with model predictions. This explicitly addresses the possibility that unlabeled data has a different class distribution. Across experiments with varying unlabeled distributions, the method consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art approaches, including a reported improvement exceeding 4% on ImageNet-127. The results support jointly addressing representation learning, pseudo-label quality, and distribution mismatch.
summary.tldr: CCL combines class-balanced contrastive learning with smoothed pseudo-labels and distribution estimation to improve long-tailed semi-supervised recognition.

title: Continuous Contrastive Learning for Long-Tailed Semi-Supervised Recognition

abstract: Sequential memory, the ability to form and accurately recall a sequence of events or stimuli in the correct order, is a fundamental prerequisite for biological and artificial intelligence as it underpins numerous cognitive functions (e.g., language comprehension, planning, episodic memory formation, etc.) However, existing methods of sequential memory suffer from catastrophic forgetting, limited capacity, slow iterative learning procedures, low-order Markov memory, and, most importantly, the inability to represent and generate multiple valid future possibilities stemming from the same context. Inspired by biologically plausible neuroscience theories of cognition, we propose Predictive Attractor Models (PAM), a novel sequence memory architecture with desirable generative properties. PAM is a streaming model that learns a sequence in an online, continuous manner by observing each input only once. Additionally, we find that PAM avoids catastrophic forgetting by uniquely representing past context through lateral inhibition in cortical minicolumns, which prevents new memories from overwriting previously learned knowledge. PAM generates future predictions by sampling from a union set of predicted possibilities; this generative ability is realized through an attractor model trained alongside the predictor. We show that PAM is trained with local computations through Hebbian plasticity rules in a biologically plausible framework. Other desirable traits (e.g., noise tolerance, CPU-based learning, capacity scaling) are discussed throughout the paper. Our findings suggest that PAM represents a significant step forward in the pursuit of biologically plausible and computationally efficient sequential memory models, with broad implications for cognitive science and artificial intelligence research. Illustration videos and code are available on our project page: https://ramymounir.com/publications/pam.

paragraphs: Sequential memory must preserve event order while allowing the same past context to lead to multiple plausible futures. Predictive Attractor Models address this combination through a biologically inspired architecture. PAM learns continuously from a stream, observing each input only once, rather than depending on repeated passes through a sequence.

The model represents past context using lateral inhibition in cortical minicolumns. The authors find that these distinct context representations prevent new memories from overwriting learned knowledge, avoiding catastrophic forgetting. Alongside the predictor, an attractor model learns to generate future outcomes by sampling from a combined set of predicted possibilities, giving the memory a branching generative capability.

Training uses local computations governed by Hebbian plasticity rules, which the authors present as biologically plausible. The paper also discusses noise tolerance, CPU-based learning, and how capacity scales. Its central contribution is a unified approach to retaining sequential knowledge and generating alternative futures, with findings suggesting progress toward computationally efficient memory models inspired by biological learning.
summary.tldr: PAM learns sequences in a single online pass, preserves distinct past contexts, and generates multiple possible futures through a companion attractor model.

title: Predictive Attractor Models

abstract: Autoformalization, the task of automatically translating natural language descriptions into a formal language, poses a significant challenge across various domains, especially in mathematics. Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have unveiled their promising capabilities to formalize even competition-level math problems. However, we observe a considerable discrepancy between pass@1 and pass@k accuracies in LLM-generated formalizations. To address this gap, we introduce a novel framework that scores and selects the best result from k autoformalization candidates based on two complementary self-consistency methods: symbolic equivalence and semantic consistency. Elaborately, symbolic equivalence identifies the logical homogeneity among autoformalization candidates using automated theorem provers, and semantic consistency evaluates the preservation of the original meaning by informalizing the candidates and computing the similarity between the embeddings of the original and informalized texts. Our extensive experiments on the MATH and miniF2F datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances autoformalization accuracy, achieving up to 0.22-1.35x relative improvements across various LLMs and baseline methods.
