paragraphs: Autoformalization translates mathematical statements written in ordinary language into a formal language. Language models can produce promising translations, but their first attempt is considerably less reliable than obtaining a correct result somewhere among several attempts. This paper targets that selection problem: given multiple candidate formalizations, how can a system choose the best one?

The proposed framework combines two kinds of consistency. Symbolic equivalence uses automated theorem provers to identify candidates that express the same logical content. Semantic consistency translates a candidate back into informal language and compares its text embedding with that of the original statement. These checks examine complementary relationships: agreement between formal candidates and preservation of the source statement's meaning.

Experiments on MATH and miniF2F show significant accuracy improvements across several language models and baseline methods. The contribution is a way to make better use of a model's collection of proposed answers through scoring and selection. Logical agreement alone and similarity to the original wording provide different evidence, and the framework uses both to guide its choice.
summary.tldr: The framework selects mathematical formalizations by combining theorem-prover checks of logical agreement with checks that the original meaning is preserved.

title: Autoformalize Mathematical Statements by Symbolic Equivalence and Semantic Consistency

abstract: Interpreting the decisions of deep learning models, including audio classifiers, is crucial for ensuring the transparency and trustworthiness of this technology. In this paper, we introduce LMAC-ZS (Listenable Maps for Zero-Shot Audio Classifiers), which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first decoder-based post-hoc explanation method for explaining the decisions of zero-shot audio classifiers. The proposed method utilizes a novel loss function that aims to closely reproduce the original similarity patterns between text-and-audio pairs in the generated explanations. We provide an extensive evaluation using the Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP) model to showcase that our interpreter remains faithful to the decisions in a zero-shot classification context. Moreover, we qualitatively show that our method produces meaningful explanations that correlate well with different text prompts.

paragraphs: Zero-shot audio classifiers make decisions using relationships between sounds and text descriptions. Explaining those decisions requires preserving what the classifier finds relevant to the supplied text. This paper introduces LMAC-ZS, a post-hoc method that uses a decoder to produce explanations that can be listened to.

The central design is a loss function intended to reproduce the original similarity patterns between audio and text pairs. This gives the explanation process a direct connection to the classifier’s decision mechanism: the generated explanation should retain the relationships that made particular descriptions match the original audio. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first decoder-based post-hoc explanation method for zero-shot audio classification.

An extensive evaluation with the CLAP model supports the interpreter’s faithfulness to classification decisions in the zero-shot setting. Qualitative results also show meaningful explanations that correspond well to different text prompts. Together, these findings support listenable explanations as a way to inspect both a model’s audio decisions and their dependence on the accompanying language.
summary.tldr: LMAC-ZS generates listenable explanations that aim to preserve the text–audio similarity patterns behind zero-shot audio classifications.

title: Listenable Maps for Zero-Shot Audio Classifiers

abstract: Bird's-eye-view (BEV) map layout estimation requires an accurate and full understanding of the semantics for the environmental elements around the ego car to make the results coherent and realistic. Due to the challenges posed by occlusion, unfavourable imaging conditions and low resolution, \emph{generating} the BEV semantic maps corresponding to corrupted or invalid areas in the perspective view (PV) is appealing very recently. \emph{The question is how to align the PV features with the generative models to facilitate the map estimation}. In this paper, we propose to utilize a generative model similar to the Vector Quantized-Variational AutoEncoder (VQ-VAE) to acquire prior knowledge for the high-level BEV semantics in the tokenized discrete space. Thanks to the obtained BEV tokens accompanied with a codebook embedding encapsulating the semantics for different BEV elements in the groundtruth maps, we are able to directly align the sparse backbone image features with the obtained BEV tokens from the discrete representation learning based on a specialized token decoder module, and finally generate high-quality BEV maps with the BEV codebook embedding serving as a bridge between PV and BEV. We evaluate the BEV map layout estimation performance of our model, termed VQ-Map, on both the nuScenes and Argoverse benchmarks, achieving 62.2/47.6 mean IoU for surround-view/monocular evaluation on nuScenes, as well as 73.4 IoU for monocular evaluation on Argoverse, which all set a new record for this map layout estimation task. The code and models are available on \url{https://github.com/Z1zyw/VQ-Map}.

paragraphs: Estimating a bird's-eye-view map from vehicle cameras requires coherent interpretation of the surrounding environment, including regions obscured or poorly captured in the images. VQ-Map addresses how image features can be connected to a generative model that supplies prior knowledge about plausible map layouts and their semantic elements.

The method learns a discrete representation of ground-truth maps using a generative model similar to a vector-quantized variational autoencoder. This produces map tokens and a codebook embedding that captures semantics of different map elements. A specialized token decoder aligns sparse image features with the learned map tokens, and the codebook bridges perspective-view information and bird's-eye-view map generation.

Evaluations report mean IoU values of 62.2 for surround-view and 47.6 for monocular estimation on nuScenes, plus 73.4 IoU for monocular estimation on Argoverse. The authors report these as new records for the task. The findings support using discrete map representations as the interface between incomplete visual evidence and a model of high-level map structure.
summary.tldr: VQ-Map aligns camera features with learned discrete map tokens to generate bird's-eye-view layouts with reported benchmark-record accuracy.

title: VQ-Map: Bird's-Eye-View Map Layout Estimation in Tokenized Discrete Space via Vector Quantization

abstract: Variational regularization is a classical technique to solve statistical inference tasks and inverse problems, with modern data-driven approaches parameterizing regularizers via deep neural networks showcasing impressive empirical performance. Recent works along these lines learn task-dependent regularizers. This is done by integrating information about the measurements and ground-truth data in an unsupervised, critic-based loss function, where the regularizer attributes low values to likely data and high values to unlikely data. However, there is little theory about the structure of regularizers learned via this process and how it relates to the two data distributions. To make progress on this challenge, we initiate a study of optimizing critic-based loss functions to learn regularizers over a particular family of regularizers: gauges (or Minkowski functionals) of star-shaped bodies. This family contains regularizers that are commonly employed in practice and shares properties with regularizers parameterized by deep neural networks. We specifically investigate critic-based losses derived from variational representations of statistical distances between probability measures. By leveraging tools from star geometry and dual Brunn-Minkowski theory, we illustrate how these losses can be interpreted as dual mixed volumes that depend on the data distribution. This allows us to derive exact expressions for the optimal regularizer in certain cases. Finally, we identify which neural network architectures give rise to such star body gauges and when do such regularizers have favorable properties for optimization. More broadly, this work highlights how the tools of star geometry can aid in understanding the geometry of unsupervised regularizer learning.

Critic-based training can learn these penalties from measurements and ground-truth distributions, but their resulting structure is poorly understood. This paper studies that structure through a geometric family of regularizers.

The family consists of gauges, also called Minkowski functionals, of star-shaped bodies. It includes regularizers used in practice and shares properties with neural-network parameterizations. The authors examine critic losses derived from variational formulations of statistical distances. Using star geometry and dual Brunn-Minkowski theory, they interpret these losses as geometric quantities called dual mixed volumes that depend on the data distributions.

This interpretation yields exact formulas for optimal regularizers in certain cases. The paper also identifies neural-network architectures that produce star-body gauges and examines when these regularizers have favorable optimization properties. Its contribution is a mathematical bridge between training distributions, critic objectives, and regularizer geometry, with exact solutions established for specific cases within the studied family.
summary.tldr: Star geometry explains the structure of a family of critic-trained regularizers and yields exact optima in certain cases.

title: The Star Geometry of Critic-Based Regularizer Learning

abstract: Disentangled representation learning (DRL) aims to identify and decompose underlying factors behind observations, thus facilitating data perception and generation. However, current DRL approaches often rely on the unrealistic assumption that semantic factors are statistically independent. In reality, these factors may exhibit correlations, which off-the-shelf solutions have yet to properly address. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a bidirectional weighted graph-based framework, to learn factorized attributes and their interrelations within complex data. Specifically, we propose a $\beta$-VAE based module to extract factors as the initial nodes of the graph, and leverage the multimodal large language model (MLLM) to discover and rank latent correlations, thereby updating the weighted edges. By integrating these complementary modules, our model successfully achieves fine-grained, practical and unsupervised disentanglement. Experiments demonstrate our method's superior performance in disentanglement and reconstruction. Furthermore, the model inherits enhanced interpretability and generalizability from MLLMs.

paragraphs: Disentangled representation learning seeks to separate observations into underlying factors that make data easier to understand and generate. Many methods assume these semantic factors are statistically independent. This paper addresses situations where meaningful factors are correlated, so separating them should also preserve an account of how they relate to one another.

The proposed framework represents factors and their relationships in a bidirectional weighted graph. A beta-VAE module extracts factors that become the initial graph nodes. A multimodal large language model then discovers and ranks latent correlations, updating the edge weights. The two modules provide complementary information: candidate attributes and estimates of their interrelationships.

This design makes factorization and relationship modeling part of the same unsupervised system. Experiments report superior disentanglement and reconstruction performance, alongside enhanced interpretability and generalizability inherited from the multimodal language model. The central idea is that useful factor representations can distinguish attributes while explicitly describing correlations, instead of relying on statistical independence.
summary.tldr: A beta-VAE and multimodal language model jointly learn separate attributes and a weighted graph of their correlations.

title: Graph-based Unsupervised Disentangled Representation Learning via Multimodal Large Language Models

abstract: We study cultural and socioeconomic diversity in contrastive vision-language models (VLMs). Using a broad range of benchmark datasets and evaluation metrics, we bring to attention several important findings. First, the common filtering of training data to English image-text pairs disadvantages communities of lower socioeconomic status and negatively impacts cultural understanding. Notably, this performance gap is not captured by - and even at odds with - the currently popular evaluation metrics derived from the Western-centric ImageNet and COCO datasets. Second, pretraining with global, unfiltered data before fine-tuning on English content can improve cultural understanding without sacrificing performance on said popular benchmarks. Third, we introduce the task of geo-localization as a novel evaluation metric to assess cultural diversity in VLMs. Our work underscores the value of using diverse data to create more inclusive multimodal systems and lays the groundwork for developing VLMs that better represent global perspectives.

paragraphs: This paper studies how training-data choices affect cultural and socioeconomic coverage in contrastive vision-language models. Across a broad collection of datasets and evaluation measures, it finds that restricting image-text training pairs to English disadvantages lower-socioeconomic-status communities and weakens cultural understanding. The effect makes language filtering consequential for which communities a model represents well.

The authors also find that commonly used metrics based on ImageNet and COCO fail to capture this gap and can even point in the opposite direction. Consequently, favorable results on those Western-centric benchmarks can coexist with weaker performance on broader cultural coverage. The study connects the training-data issue with a separate issue in how progress is measured.

A proposed training sequence first uses global, unfiltered data and then fine-tunes on English content. The reported findings show that this can improve cultural understanding without sacrificing performance on the popular benchmarks. The paper additionally introduces geolocation as an evaluation task for cultural diversity. Together, these contributions support broader training data and evaluations that expose differences hidden by standard benchmark scores.
summary.tldr: English-only data filtering can weaken cultural coverage, while global pretraining can improve it without reducing performance on common benchmarks.

title: No Filter: Cultural and Socioeconomic Diversity in Contrastive Vision-Language Models

abstract: In the 1990s, the constant error carousel and gating were introduced as the central ideas of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM). Since then, LSTMs have stood the test of time and contributed to numerous deep learning success stories, in particular they constituted the first Large Language Models (LLMs). However, the advent of the Transformer technology with parallelizable self-attention at its core marked the dawn of a new era, outpacing LSTMs at scale. We now raise a simple question: How far do we get in language modeling when scaling LSTMs to billions of parameters, leveraging the latest techniques from modern LLMs, but mitigating known limitations of LSTMs? Firstly, we introduce exponential gating with appropriate normalization and stabilization techniques. Secondly, we modify the LSTM memory structure, obtaining: (i) sLSTM with a scalar memory, a scalar update, and new memory mixing, (ii) mLSTM that is fully parallelizable with a matrix memory and a covariance update rule. Integrating these LSTM extensions into residual block backbones yields xLSTM blocks that are then residually stacked into xLSTM architectures. Exponential gating and modified memory structures boost xLSTM capabilities to perform favorably when compared to state-of-the-art Transformers and State Space Models, both in performance and scaling.

paragraphs: The paper revisits whether LSTM-based language models can remain competitive when scaled using modern language-model design techniques. Its starting point is that Transformers overtook earlier LSTMs at scale, but established LSTM mechanisms may still be useful if their limitations are addressed. xLSTM changes both the gates controlling memory and the structure of memory itself.

The first change introduces exponential gating, accompanied by normalization and stabilization. The second produces two variants: sLSTM uses scalar memory, scalar updates, and new memory mixing, while mLSTM uses matrix memory with a covariance update rule and is fully parallelizable. These extensions are placed inside residual blocks, which are stacked to build the full xLSTM architectures.

The authors report that exponential gating and the revised memory structures allow xLSTM to compare favorably with state-of-the-art Transformers and state space models in performance and scaling. The contribution is therefore a concrete modernization of LSTM architectures for large-scale language modeling. The findings support their competitiveness in the reported comparisons, without asserting that one architecture is universally best across all language-modeling settings.
summary.tldr: xLSTM updates LSTM gating and memory structures to achieve favorable performance and scaling comparisons with Transformers and state space models.

title: xLSTM: Extended Long Short-Term Memory

abstract: The advent of foundation models (FMs) in healthcare offers unprecedented opportunities to enhance medical diagnostics through automated classification and segmentation tasks. However, these models also raise significant concerns about their fairness, especially when applied to diverse and underrepresented populations in healthcare applications. Currently, there is a lack of comprehensive benchmarks, standardized pipelines, and easily adaptable libraries to evaluate and understand the fairness performance of FMs in medical imaging, leading to considerable challenges in formulating and implementing solutions that ensure equitable outcomes across diverse patient populations. To fill this gap, we introduce FairMedFM, a fairness benchmark for FM research in medical imaging. FairMedFM integrates with 17 popular medical imaging datasets, encompassing different modalities, dimensionalities, and sensitive attributes. It explores 20 widely used FMs, with various usages such as zero-shot learning, linear probing, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and prompting in various downstream tasks -- classification and segmentation. Our exhaustive analysis evaluates the fairness performance over different evaluation metrics from multiple perspectives, revealing the existence of bias, varied utility-fairness trade-offs on different FMs, consistent disparities on the same datasets regardless FMs, and limited effectiveness of existing unfairness mitigation methods. Furthermore, FairMedFM provides an open-sourced codebase at https://github.com/FairMedFM/FairMedFM, supporting extendible functionalities and applications and inclusive for studies on FMs in medical imaging over the long term.

paragraphs: FairMedFM addresses a measurement problem in medical imaging: foundation models may perform differently across patient populations, yet researchers lack consistent infrastructure for evaluating those differences. The paper introduces a benchmark and adaptable codebase for studying fairness alongside performance in automated image classification and segmentation.

The benchmark covers 17 medical imaging datasets with different imaging modalities, dimensionalities, and sensitive attributes. It examines 20 foundation models under several ways of using them, including zero-shot learning, linear probing, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and prompting. This breadth allows fairness to be examined across both model choices and downstream usage choices.

The analysis finds bias, different trade-offs between predictive utility and fairness, and disparities that recur on the same datasets across foundation models. Existing unfairness mitigation methods also show limited effectiveness in the evaluation. These findings indicate that changing the model alone may leave recurring disparities unresolved. The extensible benchmark provides a common basis for investigating those patterns and comparing efforts to address them.
summary.tldr: FairMedFM benchmarks medical imaging foundation models and reveals recurring population disparities, varied fairness trade-offs, and limited mitigation effectiveness.

title: FairMedFM: Fairness Benchmarking for Medical Imaging Foundation Models

abstract: Recent advances in AI music (AIM) generation services are currently transforming the music industry. Given these advances, understanding how humans perceive AIM is crucial both to educate users on identifying AIM songs, and, conversely, to improve current models. We present results from a listener-focused experiment aimed at understanding how humans perceive AIM. In a blind, Turing-like test, participants were asked to distinguish, from a pair, the AIM and human-made song. We contrast with other studies by utilizing a randomized controlled crossover trial that controls for pairwise similarity and allows for a causal interpretation. We are also the first study to employ a novel, author-uncontrolled dataset of AIM songs from real-world usage of commercial models (i.e., Suno). We establish that listeners' reliability in distinguishing AIM causally increases when pairs are similar. Lastly, we conduct a mixed-methods content analysis of listeners’ free-form feedback, revealing a focus on vocal and technical cues in their judgments.

paragraphs: Echoes of Humanity investigates how listeners distinguish AI-generated songs from human-made music. Participants hear pairs of songs in a blind, Turing-like test and identify which song was generated by AI. The study focuses on the conditions shaping that judgment as well as the musical cues people describe using.

The researchers use a randomized controlled crossover design that controls for similarity within each song pair. This design supports a causal interpretation of the effect of pairwise similarity. They also use AI songs drawn from real-world use of the commercial service Suno, with a dataset whose generation was not controlled by the study’s authors.

The central finding is that listeners become more reliable at identifying the AI song when the paired songs are similar. This makes the construction of comparison pairs consequential for interpreting listening tests. A mixed-methods analysis of participants’ written feedback finds that vocal and technical cues feature prominently in their decisions. These observations can inform both education about recognizing AI music and efforts to improve music generation models.
summary.tldr: A controlled listening study finds that similar song pairs causally improve listeners’ ability to distinguish AI music from human-made music.

title: Echoes of Humanity: Exploring the Perceived Humanness of AI Music

abstract: Explaining complex machine learning models is a fundamental challenge when developing safe and trustworthy deep learning applications. To date, a broad selection of explainable AI (XAI) algorithms exist. One popular choice is SmoothGrad, which has been conceived to alleviate the well-known shattered gradient problem by smoothing gradients through convolution. SmoothGrad proposes to solve this high-dimensional convolution integral by sampling -- typically approximating the convolution with limited precision. Higher numbers of samples would amount to higher precision in approximating the convolution but also to higher computing demand, therefore in practice only few samples are used in SmoothGrad. In this work we propose a well founded novel method _SmoothDiff_ to resolve this tradeoff yielding a _speedup of over two orders of magnitude_. Specifically, _SmoothDiff_ leverages automatic differentiation to decompose the expected values of Jacobians across a network architecture, directly targeting only the non-linearities responsible for shattered gradients and making it easy to implement. We demonstrate SmoothDiff's excellent speed and performance in a number of experiments and benchmarks. Thus, SmoothDiff greatly enhances the usability (quality and speed) of SmoothGrad -- a popular workhorse of XAI.

paragraphs: Gradient-based explanations can suffer from shattered gradients, making the resulting explanation difficult to use. SmoothGrad addresses this by smoothing gradients through a convolution, but estimates that high-dimensional calculation using samples. More samples improve approximation precision while increasing computation, leaving a practical tension between speed and quality.

SmoothDiff changes how the smoothing computation is handled. It uses automatic differentiation to decompose expected Jacobians across the network and targets the nonlinear components responsible for shattered gradients. This moves the treatment of the problem into the network’s differentiation structure rather than relying on increasing the number of samples used by SmoothGrad.

The paper reports a speedup exceeding two orders of magnitude, together with strong performance across experiments and benchmarks. It also describes the method as easy to implement. The contribution concerns the usability of smoothed gradient explanations: reducing the computational burden of obtaining smoother results while improving the quality–speed trade-off. The reported gains support an alternative computational route for a widely used explanation technique.
summary.tldr: SmoothDiff targets gradient-shattering nonlinearities through automatic differentiation, reporting over 100-fold speedup for smoothed gradient explanations.

title: Smoothed Differentiation Efficiently Mitigates Shattered Gradients in Explanations

abstract: Differentially private (DP) machine learning often relies on the availability of public data for tasks like privacy-utility trade-off estimation, hyperparameter tuning, and pretraining. While public data assumptions may be reasonable in text and image data, they are less likely to hold for tabular data due to tabular data heterogeneity across domains. We propose leveraging powerful priors to address this limitation; specifically, we synthesize realistic tabular data directly from schema-level specifications -- such as variable names, types, and permissible ranges -- without ever accessing sensitive records. To that end, this work introduces the notion of ``surrogate'' public data -- datasets generated independently of sensitive data, which consume no privacy loss budget and are constructed solely from publicly available schema or metadata. Surrogate public data are intended to encode plausible statistical assumptions (informed by publicly available information) into a dataset with many downstream uses in private mechanisms. We automate the process of generating surrogate public data with large language models (LLMs); in particular, we propose two methods: direct record generation as CSV files, and automated structural causal model (SCM) construction for sampling records. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that surrogate public tabular data can effectively replace traditional public data when pretraining differentially private tabular classifiers. To a lesser extent, surrogate public data are also useful for hyperparameter tuning of DP synthetic data generators, and for estimating the privacy-utility tradeoff.

paragraphs: Differentially private learning often uses public data for pretraining, tuning, or estimating the balance between privacy and utility. Suitable public tabular data can be difficult to find because tables vary substantially across domains. This paper proposes generating surrogate public data from publicly available descriptions of a table, without accessing sensitive records.

The inputs include column names, variable types, and permitted ranges. Language models turn this information into plausible records through either direct CSV generation or construction of a structural causal model from which records can be sampled. Because generation is independent of sensitive records and uses only public metadata, the surrogate dataset itself consumes no privacy budget.

Experiments show that these datasets can effectively replace conventional public data for pretraining differentially private tabular classifiers. Benefits are more limited for tuning private synthetic-data generators and estimating privacy–utility tradeoffs. The findings support encoding publicly informed statistical assumptions into reusable datasets, while showing that their usefulness depends on the downstream task.
summary.tldr: LLM-generated tabular data based solely on public metadata can support private learning, with the strongest reported benefits in classifier pretraining.

title: Do You Really Need Public Data? Surrogate Public Data for Differential Privacy on Tabular Data

abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D segmentation is a fundamental yet challenging task, requiring a mutual understanding of both segmentation and language. However, existing Gaussian-splatting-based methods rely either on a single 3D language field, leading to inferior segmentation, or on pre-computed class-agnostic segmentations, suffering from error accumulation. To address these limitations, we present COS3D, a new collaborative prompt-segmentation framework that contributes to effectively integrating complementary language and segmentation cues throughout its entire pipeline. We first introduce the new concept of collaborative field, comprising an instance field and a language field, as the cornerstone for collaboration. During training, to effectively construct the collaborative field, our key idea is to capture the intrinsic relationship between the instance field and language field, through a novel instance-to-language feature mapping and designing an efficient two-stage training strategy. During inference, to bridge distinct characteristics of the two fields, we further design an adaptive language-to-instance prompt refinement, promoting high-quality prompt-segmentation inference. Extensive experiments not only demonstrate COS3D's leading performance over existing methods on two widely-used benchmarks but also show its high potential to various applications,~\ie, novel image-based 3D segmentation, hierarchical segmentation, and robotics.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary 3D segmentation connects language descriptions with regions in a three-dimensional scene. It requires both identifying the intended object and separating its extent from surrounding content. The paper argues that existing Gaussian-splatting approaches lose quality when they rely on language features alone or inherit errors from segmentations computed in advance.

COS3D combines an instance field and a language field into a collaborative representation. The instance field supplies segmentation information, while the language field supports interpretation of descriptions. During training, a mapping from instance features to language features captures their relationship, and a two-stage procedure builds the combined representation. The design makes cooperation between these sources part of learning.

During inference, the method adaptively refines language prompts into prompts suited to the instance field. This addresses differences between how the two fields represent information when producing a segmentation. Experiments report leading performance on two widely used benchmarks. The authors also demonstrate potential for image-based 3D segmentation, hierarchical segmentation, and robotics, extending the relevance of the collaboration mechanism beyond the main benchmark task.
summary.tldr: COS3D improves language-driven 3D segmentation by coordinating instance and language representations during both training and inference.

title: COS3D: Collaborative Open-Vocabulary 3D Segmentation

abstract: We propose the Multi-modal Untrimmed Video Retrieval task, along with a new benchmark (MUVR) to advance video retrieval for long-video platforms. MUVR aims to retrieve untrimmed videos containing relevant segments using multi-modal queries. It has the following features: **1) Practical retrieval paradigm:** MUVR supports video-centric multi-modal queries, expressing fine-grained retrieval needs through long text descriptions, video tag prompts, and mask prompts. It adopts a one-to-many retrieval paradigm and focuses on untrimmed videos, tailored for long-video platform applications. **2) Multi-level visual correspondence:** To cover common video categories (e.g., news, travel, dance) and precisely define retrieval matching criteria, we construct multi-level visual correspondence based on core video content (e.g., news events, travel locations, dance moves) which users are interested in and want to retrieve. It covers six levels: copy, event, scene, instance, action, and others. **3) Comprehensive evaluation criteria:** We develop 3 versions of MUVR (i.e., Base, Filter, QA). MUVR-Base/Filter evaluates retrieval models, while MUVR-QA assesses MLLMs in a question-answering format. We also propose a Reranking Score to evaluate the reranking ability of MLLMs. MUVR consists of 53K untrimmed videos from the video platform Bilibili, with 1,050 multi-modal queries and 84K matches. Extensive evaluations of 3 state-of-the-art video retrieval models, 6 image-based VLMs, and 10 MLLMs are conducted. MUVR reveals the limitations of retrieval methods in processing untrimmed videos and multi-modal queries, as well as MLLMs in multi-video understanding and reranking. Our code and benchmark is available at https://github.com/debby-0527/MUVR.

paragraphs: MUVR studies retrieving long, untrimmed videos that contain relevant segments. Queries can combine video with long text descriptions, tags, and mask prompts, allowing more specific requests than a single text description. One query can match several videos, reflecting a retrieval setting designed for long-video platforms.

The benchmark defines matches through six levels of visual correspondence: copy, event, scene, instance, action, and an additional category. These levels distinguish different reasons that videos may match a request. Its Base and Filter versions evaluate retrieval models, while a question-answering version evaluates multimodal language models. A separate Reranking Score measures their ability to reorder candidate results.

MUVR contains 53,000 Bilibili videos, 1,050 multimodal queries, and 84,000 matches. Evaluations span three video-retrieval models, six image-based vision-language models, and ten multimodal language models. The results expose difficulties handling untrimmed footage and multimodal requests, as well as comparing and reranking multiple videos. The benchmark makes these connected retrieval and understanding problems available for systematic evaluation.
summary.tldr: MUVR evaluates multimodal retrieval of untrimmed videos and exposes weaknesses in matching, multi-video understanding, and reranking.

title: MUVR: A Multi-Modal Untrimmed Video Retrieval Benchmark with Multi-Level Visual Correspondence

abstract: Training high-performing Small Language Models (SLMs) remains computationally expensive, even with knowledge distillation and pruning from larger teacher models. Existing approaches often face three key challenges: (1) information loss from hard pruning, (2) inefficient alignment of representations, and (3) underutilization of informative activations, particularly from Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs). To address these challenges, we introduce \textbf{Low-Rank Clone (LRC)}, an efficient pre-training method that constructs SLMs aspiring to behavioral equivalence with strong teacher models. LRC trains a set of low-rank projection matrices that jointly enable soft pruning by compressing teacher weights, and activation clone by aligning student activations, including FFN signals, with those of the teacher. This unified design maximizes knowledge transfer while removing the need for explicit alignment modules. Extensive experiments with open-source teachers such as Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B/7B-Instruct show that LRC matches or surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art models trained on trillions of tokens--using only 20B tokens, achieving over \textbf{1,000$\times$} greater training efficiency. Our codes and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/CURRENTF/LowRankClone and https://huggingface.co/JitaiHao/LRC-4B-Base.

paragraphs: Building a smaller language model from a larger teacher can lose information when weights are removed outright. It can also require inefficient matching between internal representations, while leaving useful feed-forward activations underused. Low-Rank Clone addresses these problems together, aiming to preserve more of a teacher's behavior during efficient student pretraining.

The method learns low-rank projection matrices that serve two purposes. They compress the teacher's weights through soft pruning and align the student's activations with the teacher's, including signals from feed-forward networks. Using the same learned projections for compression and activation matching removes the need for separate alignment modules.

Experiments use teachers from the Llama and Qwen families. With 20 billion training tokens, the resulting models match or exceed the reported performance of leading models trained on trillions of tokens, and the authors report over 1,000-fold greater training efficiency. These findings support the value of coordinating weight compression with internal signal transfer; behavioral equivalence remains the method's aspiration rather than a demonstrated universal guarantee.
summary.tldr: Low-Rank Clone jointly compresses teacher weights and matches internal activations, achieving strong small-model performance with 20 billion training tokens.

title: A Token is Worth over 1,000 Tokens: Efficient Knowledge Distillation through Low-Rank Clone

abstract: Source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) aims to adapt a pre-trained source model to an unlabeled target domain without requiring labeled source data. In a self supervised setting, relying on pseudo labels on target domain samples facilitates the domain adaptation performance providing strong supervision. However, a critical problem of this approach is the inherent instability of the pre-trained source model in the target domain, leading to unreliable pseudo labels for the target domain data. To tackle this, we propose a novel Dual-perspective pseudo labeling strategy that jointly leverages a task-specific perspective and a domain-invariant perspective, assigning pseudo labels only to target samples on which the target model’s predictions and CLIP’s predictions agree. To further enhance representation learning without introducing noisy supervision, we apply consistency training to uncertain samples. Additionally, we introduce a Tsallis mutual information(TMI)-based vision optimization strategy guided by an Uncertainty-based adaptation index (UAI), which dynamically modulates entropy sensitivity based on the model’s adaptation uncertainty. The UAI-based training paradigm enables stable and adaptive domain alignment by effectively balancing exploration and exploitation processes during the optimization process. Our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on domain adaptation benchmark datasets, improving adaptation accuracy by 1.6% on Office-Home, 1.4% on VisDA-C, and 2.9% on DomainNet-126, demonstrating its effectiveness in SFDA. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/l3umblee/duet-sfda.

paragraphs: Source-free domain adaptation updates a pretrained model for an unlabeled target domain without access to labeled source data. A common approach uses the model’s predictions as training labels, but those predictions can be unreliable after a domain change. DUET addresses this problem by controlling which predictions become supervision and how uncertainty influences adaptation.

Its pseudo-labeling rule combines two perspectives: the target model’s task-specific predictions and CLIP’s predictions as a domain-invariant perspective. Only samples on which they agree receive pseudo labels. Uncertain samples still contribute through consistency training, allowing representation learning without assigning them potentially noisy labels. Agreement therefore determines the form of learning applied to each sample.

DUET also uses a Tsallis mutual-information objective whose sensitivity to entropy changes according to an uncertainty-based adaptation index. This dynamically balances exploration and exploitation during training. The authors report state-of-the-art benchmark performance, with adaptation accuracy improvements of 1.6% on Office-Home, 1.4% on VisDA-C, and 2.9% on DomainNet-126. These results support combining selective supervision with uncertainty-responsive optimization.
summary.tldr: DUET adapts models to unlabeled domains using agreement-based pseudo labels, consistency training, and uncertainty-guided optimization.

title: DUET: Dual-Perspective Pseudo Labeling and Uncertainty-aware Exploration & Exploitation Training for Source-Free Domain Adaptation

abstract: This paper proposes a new algorithm for learning gradient boosted decision trees while ensuring the existence of recourse actions. Algorithmic recourse aims to provide a recourse action for altering the undesired prediction result given by a model. While existing studies often focus on extracting valid and executable actions from a given learned model, such reasonable actions do not always exist for models optimized solely for predictive accuracy. To address this issue, recent studies proposed a framework for learning a model while guaranteeing the existence of reasonable actions with high probability. However, these methods can not be applied to gradient boosted decision trees, which are renowned as one of the most popular models for tabular datasets. We propose an efficient gradient boosting algorithm that takes recourse guarantee into account, while maintaining the same time complexity as the standard ones. We also propose a post-processing method for refining a learned model under the constraint of a recourse guarantee and provide a PAC-style analysis of the refined model. Experimental results demonstrated that our method successfully provided reasonable actions to more instances than the baselines without significantly degrading accuracy and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Algorithmic recourse asks what feasible changes could turn an unfavorable model prediction into a favorable one. Searching for such changes after training can fail because a model optimized only for accuracy may offer no reasonable action. This paper builds recourse considerations into the learning of gradient boosted decision trees, a widely used model family for tabular data.

The proposed boosting algorithm accounts for a recourse guarantee while retaining the same time complexity as standard boosting algorithms. The authors also introduce a post-processing procedure that refines a trained model while respecting a recourse constraint. A PAC-style analysis provides a probabilistic theoretical treatment of the refined model's guarantee.

Experiments show that the method supplies reasonable actions for more instances than the baselines, without significantly harming predictive accuracy or computational efficiency. This makes recourse availability part of model construction rather than solely a question asked afterward. The combination of training and constrained refinement extends work on probabilistic recourse guarantees to boosted trees, connecting useful predictions with the availability of actions that can change them.
summary.tldr: A recourse-aware boosting algorithm makes reasonable prediction-changing actions available for more instances while preserving accuracy and computational efficiency in experiments.

title: Learning Gradient Boosted Decision Trees with Algorithmic Recourse

abstract: Learning generalizable robotic manipulation policies remains a key challenge due to the scarcity of diverse real-world training data. While recent approaches have attempted to mitigate this through self-supervised representation learning, most either rely on 2D vision pretraining paradigms such as masked image modeling, which primarily focus on static semantics or scene geometry, or utilize large-scale video prediction models that emphasize 2D dynamics, thus failing to jointly learn the geometry, semantics, and dynamics required for effective manipulation. In this paper, we present DynaRend, a representation learning framework that learns 3D-aware and dynamics-informed triplane features via masked reconstruction and future prediction using differentiable volumetric rendering. By pretraining on multi-view RGB-D video data, DynaRend jointly captures spatial geometry, future dynamics, and task semantics in a unified triplane representation. The learned representations can be effectively transferred to downstream robotic manipulation tasks via action value map prediction. We evaluate DynaRend on two challenging benchmarks, RLBench and Colosseum, as well as in real-world robotic experiments, demonstrating substantial improvements in policy success rate, generalization to environmental perturbations, and real-world applicability across diverse manipulation tasks.

paragraphs: Robotic manipulation requires understanding a scene's geometry, its task-relevant meaning, and how it will change. The paper argues that common representation-learning approaches do not learn all three together: static image objectives emphasize appearance or geometry, while video models often emphasize two-dimensional motion. DynaRend aims to build a representation that combines these requirements.

The framework pretrains on multi-view RGB-D videos using masked reconstruction and future prediction. Differentiable volumetric rendering connects these learning objectives to a unified triplane representation. By learning to reconstruct missing information and predict later observations, the model develops features informed by both three-dimensional structure and dynamics.

These representations are transferred to robotic manipulation through action value map prediction, connecting the learned scene information to action selection. Evaluations on RLBench, Colosseum, and real robots report substantial gains in policy success, resilience to environmental perturbations, and practical applicability across manipulation tasks. The findings support learning spatial structure and future change together as a useful preparation for robot control when diverse real-world training data is scarce.
summary.tldr: DynaRend jointly learns three-dimensional scene structure and future dynamics from RGB-D videos to improve robotic manipulation.

title: DynaRend: Learning 3D Dynamics via Masked Future Rendering for Robotic Manipulation

abstract: Cross-view geo-localization (CVGL) aims to estimate the geographic location of a street image by matching it with a corresponding aerial image. This is critical for autonomous navigation and mapping in complex real-world scenarios. However, the task remains challenging due to significant viewpoint differences and the influence of confounding factors. To tackle these issues, we propose the Causal Learning and Geometric Topology (CLGT) framework, which integrates two key components: a Causal Feature Extractor (CFE) that mitigates the influence of confounding factors by leveraging causal intervention to encourage the model to focus on stable, task-relevant semantics; and a Geometric Topology Fusion (GT Fusion) module that injects Bird’s Eye View (BEV) road topology into street features to alleviate cross-view inconsistencies caused by extreme perspective changes. Additionally, we introduce a Data-Adaptive Pooling (DA Pooling) module to enhance the representation of semantically rich regions. Extensive experiments on CVUSA, CVACT, and their robustness-enhanced variants (CVUSA-C-ALL and CVACT-C-ALL) demonstrate that CLGT achieves state-of-the-art performance, particularly under challenging real-world corruptions.

paragraphs: Cross-view geo-localization finds the location of a street photograph by matching it to an aerial image. The same place can look very different from those viewpoints, and unrelated visual factors can distract the model. The proposed CLGT framework addresses both problems by combining causal feature learning with information about road structure.

Its Causal Feature Extractor uses causal intervention to encourage representations based on stable, relevant meaning while reducing the influence of confounding factors. A separate Geometric Topology Fusion module adds bird's-eye-view road topology to the street-image features. This gives the matching process structural information that helps bridge extreme perspective changes. A data-adaptive pooling module further emphasizes regions with rich semantic information.

The authors evaluate CLGT on CVUSA and CVACT, together with robustness-focused variants containing challenging corruptions. They report state-of-the-art performance, particularly under those corruptions. The results support combining stable visual semantics with road topology: one component addresses misleading associations, while the other makes the two viewpoints easier to reconcile. Together, they improve the tested system's ability to match street and aerial observations.
summary.tldr: CLGT combines causal feature learning and road topology to improve street-to-aerial image matching, especially under visual corruptions.

title: CVGL: Causal Learning and Geometric Topology

abstract: Despite rapid progress on AI benchmarks, the real-world meaning of benchmark performance remains unclear. To quantify the capabilities of AI systems in terms of human capabilities, we propose a new metric: 50%-task-completion time horizon. This is the time humans typically take to complete tasks that AI models can complete with 50% success rate. We first timed humans with relevant domain expertise on a combination of RE-Bench, HCAST, and 66 novel shorter tasks. On these tasks, current frontier AI models such as o3 have a 50% time horizon of around 110 minutes. Furthermore, frontier AI time horizon has been doubling approximately every seven months since 2019, though the trend may have accelerated since 2024. The increase in AI models’ time horizons seems to be primarily driven by greater reliability and ability to adapt to mistakes, combined with better logical reasoning and tool use capabilities. We discuss the limitations of our results—including their degree of external validity—and the implications of increased autonomy for dangerous capabilities. If these results generalize to real-world software tasks, extrapolation of this trend predicts that within 5 years, AI systems will be capable of automating many software tasks that currently take humans a month.

paragraphs: Benchmark scores can be difficult to translate into the scale of work an AI system can handle. This paper proposes the 50%-task-completion time horizon: the typical human duration of tasks that a model completes successfully half the time. It anchors capability to expert human effort, rather than the model’s own runtime.

The researchers timed people with relevant expertise on tasks from RE-Bench, HCAST, and 66 new shorter tasks. Within this evaluation, frontier models such as o3 reached a horizon of about 110 minutes. The authors report that frontier horizons approximately doubled every seven months from 2019, with possible acceleration after 2024. They suggest reliability, recovery from mistakes, reasoning, and tool use as primary contributors.

The extrapolation is explicitly conditional. If the findings generalize to real-world software work, continuing the trend predicts automation of many month-long human tasks within five years of the study. The paper discusses external-validity limits and implications for dangerous capabilities. Its measured horizon and its longer-term forecast therefore carry different evidential strength.
summary.tldr: The paper measures AI task capability in expert-human completion time and finds rising horizons, with longer-term automation forecasts conditional on generalization.

title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks

abstract: Visual processing starts in the outer retina where photoreceptors transform light into electrochemical signals. These signals are modulated by inhibition from horizontal cells and sent to the inner retina via excitatory bipolar cells. The outer retina is thought to play an important role in contrast invariant coding of visual information, but how the different cell types implement this computation together remains incompletely understood. To understand the role of each cell type, we developed a fully-differentiable biophysical model of a circular patch of mouse outer retina. The model includes 200 cone photoreceptors with a realistic phototransduction cascade and ribbon synapses as well as horizontal and bipolar cells, all with cell-type specific ion channels. Going beyond decades of work constraining biophysical models of neurons only by experimental data, we used a dual approach, constraining some parameters of the model with available measurements and others by a visual task: (1) We fit the parameters of the cone models to whole cell patch-clamp measurements of photocurrents and two-photon glutamate imaging measurements of synaptic release. (2) We then trained the spatiotemporal outer retina model with photoreceptors and the other cell types to perform a visual classification task with varying contrast and luminance levels. We found that our outer retina model could learn to solve the classification task despite contrast and luminance variance in the stimuli. Testing different cell type compositions and connectivity patterns, we found that feedback from horizontal cells did not further improve task performance beyond that of excitatory photoreceptors and bipolar cells. This is surprising given that horizontal cells are positioned to mediate communication across cones and that they add to the model's number of trainable parameters. Finally, we found that our model generalized better to out of distribution contrast levels than a linear classifier. Our work shows how the nonlinearities found in the outer retina can accomplish contrast invariant classification and teases apart the contributions of different cell types.

paragraphs: This paper asks how the first stages of mouse vision can support recognition when contrast and brightness change. The researchers build a differentiable biophysical model containing 200 cone photoreceptors, horizontal cells, and bipolar cells. Its components include mechanisms for converting light into electrical signals, releasing neurotransmitters, and controlling cell activity through cell-specific ion channels.

The model combines two sources of constraint. Cone parameters are fitted to measurements of electrical responses and synaptic release. The larger retinal circuit is then trained on visual classification with changing contrast and luminance. This connects measured cellular behavior with a functional task, allowing the researchers to examine how different cell populations contribute.

The model learns classification despite those variations and generalizes to unseen contrast levels better than a linear classifier. In the tested configurations, adding horizontal-cell feedback does not improve performance beyond photoreceptors and bipolar cells. These findings show how modeled retinal nonlinearities can support contrast-tolerant classification, while locating the horizontal-cell result within this particular model and task.
summary.tldr: A biologically grounded mouse-retina model learns contrast-tolerant classification, with no additional task benefit from horizontal-cell feedback in the tested configurations.

title: A data and task-constrained mechanistic model of the mouse outer retina shows robustness to contrast variations

abstract: This paper studies how to integrate historical control data with experimental data to enhance A/B testing, while addressing the distributional shift between historical and experimental datasets. We propose a pessimistic data integration method that combines two causal effect estimators constructed based on experimental and historical datasets. Our main idea is to conceptualize the weight function for this combination as a policy so that existing pessimistic policy learning algorithms are applicable to learn the optimal weight that minimizes the resulting weighted estimator's mean squared error. Additionally, we conduct comprehensive theoretical and empirical analyses to compare our method against various baseline estimators across five scenarios. Both our theoretical and numerical findings demonstrate that the proposed estimator achieves near-optimal performance across all scenarios.

paragraphs: Historical control data could make an A/B test more informative, but the historical and experimental populations may differ. Combining them therefore requires deciding how much to trust each source. This paper studies that decision through an estimator that combines two causal-effect estimates constructed using experimental and historical datasets.

The central move is to treat the combination’s weighting function as a policy. That reformulation makes existing pessimistic policy-learning algorithms available for choosing the weights. The goal is to minimize the combined estimator’s mean squared error, so the integration decision is tied directly to the accuracy of the resulting effect estimate rather than to a fixed mixing rule.

The authors compare their method with baseline estimators through theoretical and empirical analyses spanning five scenarios. Both forms of analysis find near-optimal performance across those scenarios. The result supports learning how to combine the sources while accounting for their distributional differences. The near-optimality claim applies to the scenarios analyzed, preserving the importance of the setting in which historical information is reused.
summary.tldr: The method learns how to weight historical and experimental causal estimates using pessimistic policy learning, achieving near-optimal performance in five analyzed scenarios.

title: Pessimistic Data Integration for Policy Evaluation

abstract: Density estimation is essential for generative modeling, particularly with the rise of modern neural networks. While existing methods capture complex data distributions, they often lack interpretability and uncertainty quantification. Bayesian nonparametric methods, especially the Pólya tree, offer a robust framework that addresses these issues by accurately capturing function behavior over small intervals. Traditional techniques like Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) face high computational complexity and scalability limitations, hindering the use of Bayesian nonparametric methods in deep learning. To tackle this, we introduce the variational Pólya tree (VPT) model, which employs stochastic variational inference to compute posterior distributions. This model provides a flexible, nonparametric Bayesian prior that captures latent densities and works well with stochastic gradient optimization. We also leverage the joint distribution likelihood for a more precise variational posterior approximation than traditional mean-field methods. We evaluate the model performance on both real data and images, and demonstrate its competitiveness with other state-of-the-art deep density estimation methods. We also explore its ability in enhancing interpretability and uncertainty quantification. Code is available at https://github.com/howardchanth/var-polya-tree.

paragraphs: Density estimation describes how probability is distributed across possible data values, making it central to generative modeling. Flexible neural methods can capture complex distributions but often provide limited interpretability and uncertainty quantification. Pólya trees offer a Bayesian nonparametric approach that represents distributional behavior over small intervals, although traditional inference can be computationally costly.

The variational Pólya tree replaces reliance on expensive sampling-based inference with stochastic variational inference for posterior computation. Its flexible Bayesian prior models latent densities and works with stochastic gradient optimization. This connects the Pólya tree framework to the optimization machinery used in deep learning, addressing a practical barrier to combining the two.

The model also uses the joint distribution likelihood to obtain a more precise variational posterior approximation than traditional mean-field methods. Evaluations on real data and images show competitive performance against state-of-the-art deep density estimators. The authors additionally explore interpretability and uncertainty quantification, positioning the method as a way to retain useful Bayesian structure while supporting scalable neural density modeling.
summary.tldr: Variational Pólya trees bring Bayesian nonparametric density modeling into stochastic-gradient training while exploring interpretability and uncertainty benefits.

title: Variational Pólya Tree

abstract: Despite progress, deep neural networks still suffer performance declines under distribution shifts between training and test domains, leading to a substantial decrease in Quality of Experience (QoE) for applications. Existing test-time adaptation (TTA) methods are challenged by dynamic, multiple test distributions within batches. We observe that feature distributions across different domains inherently cluster into distinct groups with varying means and variances. This divergence reveals a critical limitation of previous global normalization strategies in TTA, which inevitably distort the original data characteristics. Based on this insight, we propose Feature-based Instance Neighbor Discovery (FIND), which comprises three key components: Layer-Wise Feature Disentanglement (LFD), Feature-Aware Batch Normalization (FABN) and Selective FABN (S-FABN). LFD stably captures features with similar distributions at each layer by constructing graph structures; while FABN optimally combines source statistics with test-time distribution-specific statistics for robust feature representation. Finally, S-FABN determines which layers require feature partitioning and which can remain unified, thus enhancing the efficiency of inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FIND significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving up to approximately 30\% accuracy improvement in dynamic scenarios while maintaining computational efficiency. The source code is available at https://github.com/Peanut-255/FIND.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation adjusts a model when deployment data differ from its training data. FIND targets the harder situation where a single batch contains examples from multiple changing distributions. The authors observe that features from different domains form groups with different means and variances, making global normalization distort the original feature characteristics.

FIND first builds graph structures at individual layers to identify features with similar distributions. Its feature-aware batch normalization then combines source statistics with statistics specific to the test-time distributions. Together, these steps allow normalization to reflect groups within a batch instead of treating the whole batch as one homogeneous population.

A selective component decides which layers need this partitioning and which can remain unified, improving inference efficiency. Experiments report gains of up to approximately 30% in accuracy in dynamic scenarios while maintaining computational efficiency. The stated maximum is an observed result, and the broader contribution is an adaptation framework that explicitly handles distribution differences within the same incoming batch.
summary.tldr: FIND adapts normalization to distribution-specific feature groups within test batches, reporting accuracy improvements of up to approximately 30% in dynamic scenarios.

title: Feature-Based Instance Neighbor Discovery: Advanced Stable Test-Time Adaptation in Dynamic World

abstract: Instruction-based image editing enables precise modifications via natural language prompts, but existing methods face a precision-efficiency tradeoff: fine-tuning demands massive datasets (>10M) and computational resources, while training-free approaches suffer from weak instruction comprehension. We address this by proposing \textbf{ICEdit}, which leverages the inherent comprehension and generation abilities of large-scale Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) through three key innovations: (1) An in-context editing paradigm without architectural modifications; (2) Minimal parameter-efficient fine-tuning for quality improvement; (3) Early Filter Inference-Time Scaling, which uses VLMs to select high-quality noise samples for efficiency. Experiments show that ICEdit achieves state-of-the-art editing performance with only 0.1\% of the training data and 1\% trainable parameters compared to previous methods. Our approach establishes a new paradigm for balancing precision and efficiency in instructional image editing.

paragraphs: Instruction-based image editing asks a model to modify an image according to a natural-language request. The paper identifies a precision–efficiency tradeoff: existing fine-tuning approaches can require more than ten million training examples and substantial computation, while training-free approaches struggle to understand instructions. ICEdit seeks to make better use of abilities already present in large diffusion transformers.

Its central contribution is an in-context editing approach that requires no architectural changes. A small amount of parameter-efficient fine-tuning improves quality. The framework also introduces Early Filter Inference-Time Scaling, which uses vision-language models to select high-quality noise samples, making sample selection part of its efficiency strategy during inference.

The authors report state-of-the-art editing performance using only 0.1% of the training data and 1% of the trainable parameters compared with previous methods. These findings support combining an existing model's comprehension and generation abilities with limited adaptation and inference-time selection. The reported resource reductions concern training data and trainable parameters, alongside the demonstrated editing performance.
summary.tldr: ICEdit combines in-context diffusion editing, limited fine-tuning, and noise-sample selection to achieve strong editing performance with far fewer training resources.

title: Enabling Instructional Image Editing with In-Context Generation in Large Scale Diffusion Transformer

abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) provide a powerful approach in neuroscience to infer latent dynamics in neural populations and to generate hypotheses about the neural computations underlying behavior. However, past work has focused on relatively simple, input-driven, and largely deterministic behaviors - little is known about the mechanisms that would allow RNNs to generate the richer, spontaneous, and potentially stochastic behaviors observed in natural settings. Modeling with Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) has revealed a segmentation of natural behaviors into discrete latent states with stochastic transitions between them, a type of dynamics that may appear at odds with the continuous state spaces implemented by RNNs. Here we first show that RNNs can replicate HMM emission statistics and then reverse-engineer the trained networks to uncover the mechanisms they implement. In the absence of inputs, the activity of trained RNNs collapses towards a single fixed point. When driven by stochastic input, trajectories instead exhibit noise-sustained dynamics along closed orbits. Rotation along these orbits modulates the emission probabilities and is governed by transitions between regions of slow, noise-driven dynamics connected by fast, deterministic transitions. The trained RNNs develop highly structured connectivity, with a small set of “kick neurons” initiating transitions between these regions. This mechanism emerges during training as the network shifts into a regime of stochastic resonance, enabling it to perform probabilistic computations. Analyses across multiple HMM architectures — fully connected, cyclic, and linear-chain — reveal that this solution generalizes through the modular reuse of the same dynamical motif, suggesting a compositional principle by which RNNs can emulate complex discrete latent dynamics.

paragraphs: Hidden Markov models describe behavior through discrete hidden states with random transitions, whereas recurrent neural networks maintain continuous internal states. This paper investigates how an RNN can reproduce HMM emission statistics despite that difference. The researchers train networks to emulate these statistics and then analyze their internal dynamics to uncover the mechanism.

Without input, trained network activity approaches a single fixed point. With stochastic input, activity instead follows noise-sustained closed orbits. Movement around those orbits changes emission probabilities. The trajectories alternate between regions with slow, noise-driven motion and rapid, deterministic transitions connecting them. These findings suggest a compositional way for continuous recurrent networks to emulate more complex discrete latent dynamics, while grounding that suggestion in the trained networks and HMM architectures examined.
summary.tldr: Trained RNNs emulate HMM statistics through noise-sustained orbits and specialized neurons that trigger transitions between slow dynamical regions.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability of RNNs emulating Hidden Markov Models

abstract: Neural video compression (NVC) has made significant progress in recent years, while neural B-frame video compression (NBVC) remains underexplored compared to P-frame compression. NBVC can adopt bi-directional reference frames for better compression performance. However, NBVC's hierarchical coding may complicate continuous temporal prediction, especially at some hierarchical levels with a large frame span, which could cause the contribution of the two reference frames to be unbalanced. To optimize reference information utilization, we propose a novel NBVC method, termed Bi-directional Reference Harmonization Video Compression (BRHVC), with the proposed Bi-directional Motion Converge (BMC) and Bi-directional Contextual Fusion (BCF). BMC converges multiple optical flows in motion compression, leading to more accurate motion compensation on a larger scale. Then BCF explicitly models the weights of reference contexts under the guidance of motion compensation accuracy. With more efficient motions and contexts, BRHVC can effectively harmonize bi-directional references. Experimental results indicate that our BRHVC outperforms previous state-of-the-art NVC methods, even surpassing the traditional coding, VTM-RA (under random access configuration), on the HEVC datasets. The source code will be released. The source code is released at https://github.com/kwai/NVC.

paragraphs: Neural B-frame compression predicts a frame using references in both temporal directions. Hierarchical coding can place those references far apart, making continuous motion prediction harder and leaving the two references unevenly useful. BRHVC addresses how a compressor combines this bidirectional information, aiming to extract better motion and contextual guidance from both sides.

The method introduces two components. Bi-directional Motion Converge combines multiple optical flows during motion compression to improve motion compensation over larger scales. Bi-directional Contextual Fusion then assigns weights to reference contexts using the accuracy of that compensation. The weighting explicitly accounts for how well each reference helps predict the current content.

By improving motion estimation and adapting contextual contributions, BRHVC harmonizes the information supplied by its two references. Experiments report better compression performance than previous state-of-the-art neural methods and results exceeding VTM in its random-access configuration on HEVC datasets. These findings support reference coordination as an effective way to improve neural B-frame compression in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: BRHVC improves neural B-frame compression by combining motion estimates and weighting bidirectional reference information according to prediction accuracy.

title: Neural B-frame Video Compression with Bi-directional Reference Harmonization

abstract: This paper proposes a novel matrix quantization method, Binary Quadratic Quan- tization (BQQ). In contrast to conventional first-order quantization approaches— such as uniform quantization and binary coding quantization—that approximate real-valued matrices via linear combinations of binary bases, BQQ leverages the expressive power of binary quadratic expressions while maintaining an extremely compact data format. We validate our approach with two experiments: a matrix compression benchmark and post-training quantization (PTQ) on pretrained Vision Transformer-based models. Experimental results demonstrate that BQQ consistently achieves a superior trade-off between memory efficiency and reconstruction error than conventional methods for compressing diverse matrix data. It also delivers strong PTQ performance, even though we neither target state-of-the-art PTQ accuracy under tight memory constraints nor rely on PTQ-specific binary matrix optimization. For example, our proposed method outperforms the state-of- the-art PTQ method by up to 2.2% and 59.1% on the ImageNet dataset under the calibration-based and data-free scenarios, respectively, with quantization equivalent to 2 bits. These findings highlight the surprising effectiveness of binary quadratic expressions for efficient matrix approximation and neural network compression.

paragraphs: Matrix quantization reduces storage by representing real-valued entries in a compact format. Conventional approaches considered here reconstruct matrices through linear combinations of binary components. Binary Quadratic Quantization, or BQQ, instead uses quadratic expressions in binary variables, giving the representation additional expressive capacity while retaining a very compact data format.

The authors test this idea on general matrix compression and on post-training quantization of pretrained Vision Transformer models. Across the matrix data examined, BQQ offers a better balance between memory use and reconstruction error than conventional methods. This evaluates whether the richer binary representation can preserve more information for a given storage budget.

The neural-network results also show strong performance without PTQ-specific binary matrix optimization. At an equivalent two-bit setting on ImageNet, the authors report improvements over a state-of-the-art PTQ method of up to 2.2% with calibration and 59.1% without data. They explicitly do not position tight-memory PTQ accuracy as their main optimization target; the broader finding concerns the effectiveness of quadratic binary representations.
summary.tldr: BQQ uses quadratic binary expressions to improve matrix compression and delivers strong reported results when quantizing Vision Transformers.

title: Binary Quadratic Quantization: Beyond First-Order Quantization for Real-Valued Matrix Compression

abstract: Multimodal contrastive learning models (e.g., CLIP) can learn high-quality representations from large-scale image-text datasets, while they exhibit significant vulnerabilities to backdoor attacks, raising serious safety concerns. In this paper, we reveal that CLIP's vulnerabilities primarily stem from its tendency to encode features beyond in-dataset predictive patterns, compromising its visual feature resistivity to input perturbations. This makes its encoded features highly susceptible to being reshaped by backdoor triggers. To address this challenge, we propose Repulsive Visual Prompt Tuning (RVPT), a novel defense approach that employs deep visual prompt tuning with a specially designed feature-repelling loss. Specifically, RVPT adversarially repels the encoded features from deeper layers while optimizing the standard cross-entropy loss, ensuring that only predictive features in downstream tasks are encoded, thereby enhancing CLIP’s visual feature resistivity against input perturbations and mitigating its susceptibility to backdoor attacks. Unlike existing multimodal backdoor defense methods that typically require the availability of poisoned data or involve fine-tuning the entire model, RVPT leverages few-shot downstream clean samples and only tunes a small number of parameters. Empirical results demonstrate that RVPT tunes only 0.27\% of the parameters in CLIP, yet it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art defense methods, reducing the attack success rate from 89.70\% to 2.76\% against the most advanced multimodal attacks on ImageNet and effectively generalizes its defensive capabilities across multiple datasets. Our code is available on https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rvpt-anonymous.

Our code is available on https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rvpt-anonymous.
