This paper attributes much of that vulnerability to features extending beyond patterns that predict the task within the dataset. Those additional features make visual representations easier for a trigger to reshape, allowing an input perturbation to redirect model behavior.

Repulsive Visual Prompt Tuning, or RVPT, combines deep visual prompts with a feature-repelling objective. During adaptation, it repels encoded features from deeper layers while also optimizing the usual classification loss. The intended effect is to retain task-predictive information and strengthen resistance to perturbations. The method uses a few clean downstream examples and adjusts only a small portion of the model.

In the reported experiments, RVPT updates 0.27% of CLIP's parameters. Against the evaluated advanced multimodal attacks on ImageNet, attack success falls from 89.70% to 2.76%, outperforming the compared defenses. Results across multiple datasets also indicate defensive generalization. These findings support a compact adaptation approach that does not require access to poisoned training examples.
summary.tldr: RVPT uses a few clean examples and lightweight visual prompt tuning to substantially reduce backdoor attack success in CLIP.

title: Defending Multimodal Backdoored Models by Repulsive Visual Prompt Tuning

abstract: In recent years, large language models with Transformer architecture as the core have made breakthrough progress in many fields. At the same time, there are also some weaknesses in the large language model that have prompted people to reflect, among which the most fundamental one is the reflection on the Transformer architecture. The Transformer architecture has high parallelism and can fully utilize the computing power of GPUs, thus replacing models such as LSTM in the past few years. However, high parallelism is not a free lunch, as it fundamentally limits the performance of models. Especially, the problems that logarithmic precision Transformer architecture can solve are strictly limited to the $TC^0$. And there are many important issues that are usually considered out of $TC^0$, such as Python code evaluation, entity tracking, chess, and other state tracking tasks. Meanwhile, some recent state space methods based on Delta Rule have been able to break through the $TC^0$ architecture, but they are limited by fixed size state spaces and perform poorly on many tasks. To this end, we have re-examined the Transformer from the perspective of a state space with kernel functions and propose an improved Transformer called DeltaFormer. We have theoretically and practically demonstrated that the proposed new architecture can break through the limitation of the inherent $TC^0$ expressivity of Transformers and verified that it is not weaker than standard Transformer in language modeling tasks. We hope our work can provide inspiration for designing more expressive models.

It revisits the Transformer as a state-space model expressed through kernel functions and uses that interpretation to develop an improved architecture.

The authors report theoretical and practical evidence that DeltaFormer exceeds the stated TC⁰ restriction of standard Transformers. They also verify that it is no weaker than the standard Transformer on the language-modeling tasks considered. The result connects architectural expressivity with practical modeling performance: expanding the kinds of computation an architecture can represent need not come at the expense of the reported language-modeling capability.
summary.tldr: DeltaFormer uses a kernel-based state-space perspective to exceed a stated Transformer expressivity bound while retaining tested language-modeling performance.

title: DeltaFormer: Unlock the state space of Transformer

abstract: To reduce risk, investors seek assets that have high expected return and are unlikely to move in tandem. Correlation measures are generally used to quantify the connections between equities. The 2008 financial crisis, and its aftermath, demonstrated the need for a better way to quantify these connections. We present a machine learning-based method to build a connectedness matrix to address the shortcomings of correlation in capturing events such as large losses. Our method uses an unconstrained optimization to learn this matrix, while ensuring that the resulting matrix is positive semi-definite. We show that this matrix can be used to build portfolios that not only “beat the market,” but also outperform optimal (i.e., minimum variance) portfolios.

paragraphs: Portfolio construction depends partly on understanding which assets tend to move together. Investors seek attractive expected returns while avoiding combinations that expose them to shared losses. The paper argues that ordinary correlation can miss important aspects of these connections, particularly events involving large losses, motivating a different measure of connectedness.

The authors introduce a machine-learning method that learns a connectedness matrix through unconstrained optimization. Despite using an unconstrained optimization procedure, the method ensures that the resulting matrix is positive semidefinite. This combines flexibility in learning the connections with a specific mathematical property of the final representation.

The learned matrix is then used to construct investment portfolios. The paper reports portfolios that outperform both the market and portfolios optimized for minimum variance. These findings suggest that the learned connections contain useful information for the portfolio-construction setting studied. The result concerns the demonstrated use of this matrix; it does not turn that reported outperformance into a promise about every future portfolio or market condition.
summary.tldr: A learned asset-connectedness matrix supports portfolios reported to outperform the market and minimum-variance portfolios.

title: Learning Connections in Financial Time Series

abstract: The multi-armed bandit problem has attracted remarkable attention in the machine learning community and many efficient algorithms have been proposed to handle the so-called exploitation-exploration dilemma in various bandit setups. At the same time, significantly less effort has been devoted to adapting bandit algorithms to particular architectures, such as sensor networks, multi-core machines, or peer-to-peer (P2P) environments, which could potentially speed up their convergence. Our goal is to adapt stochastic bandit algorithms to P2P networks. In our setup, the same set of arms is available in each peer. In every iteration each peer can pull one arm independently of the other peers, and then some limited communication is possible with a few random other peers. As our main result, we show that our adaptation achieves a linear speedup in terms of the number of peers participating in the network. More precisely, we show that the probability of playing a suboptimal arm at a peer in iteration t = Ω( \log N ) is proportional to 1/(Nt) where N denotes the number of peers. The theoretical results are supported by simulation experiments showing that our algorithm scales gracefully with the size of network.

paragraphs: A stochastic bandit learner repeatedly chooses among actions with uncertain rewards, balancing exploration with use of the best options found so far. This paper adapts that problem to a peer-to-peer network. Every peer has the same available actions and can independently choose one action during each iteration.

After acting, peers communicate with a few randomly selected peers. This limited, gossip-style communication provides a way to share information gathered across the network. The central question is whether decentralized learners can turn their collective observations into faster learning despite communicating with only a small part of the network at each step.

The authors prove a linear speedup with the number of participating peers. More precisely, after an iteration threshold on the order of log N, the probability that a peer selects a suboptimal action is proportional to 1/(Nt), where N is the number of peers and t is the iteration. Simulations support the theoretical result and show graceful scaling with network size in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Limited random communication lets peer-to-peer bandit learners achieve a provable linear learning speedup with network size.

title: Gossip-based distributed stochastic bandit algorithms

abstract: \citettaddy13mnir proposed multinomial inverse regression (MNIR) as a new model of annotated text based on the influence of metadata and response variables on the distribution of words in a document. While effective, MNIR has no way to exploit structure in the corpus to improve its predictions or facilitate exploratory data analysis. On the other hand, traditional probabilistic topic models (like latent Dirichlet allocation) capture natural heterogeneity in a collection but do not account for external variables. In this paper, we introduce the inverse regression topic model (IRTM), a mixed-membership extension of MNIR that combines the strengths of both methodologies. We present two inference algorithms for the IRTM: an efficient batch estimation algorithm and an online variant, which is suitable for large corpora. We apply these methods to a corpus of 73K Congressional press releases and another of 150K Yelp reviews, demonstrating that the IRTM outperforms both MNIR and supervised topic models on the prediction task. Further, we give examples showing that the IRTM enables systematic discovery of in-topic lexical variation, which is not possible with previous supervised topic models.

paragraphs: The paper combines two ways of modeling annotated text. Multinomial inverse regression relates word distributions to metadata and response variables, but does not exploit corpus structure. Traditional topic models capture variation within a document collection but do not account for external variables. The goal is to bring these complementary sources of information together.

The inverse regression topic model is a mixed-membership extension of multinomial inverse regression. It incorporates topic structure while retaining the connection between word use and external variables. The authors provide an efficient batch estimation algorithm and an online version suitable for large corpora, giving the model two routes to practical inference.

Applications use 73,000 Congressional press releases and 150,000 Yelp reviews. The model outperforms both multinomial inverse regression and supervised topic models on prediction in these evaluations. Examples also demonstrate systematic discovery of lexical variation within topics, a capability the authors distinguish from previous supervised topic models. This adds an exploratory use alongside the predictive benefit.
summary.tldr: The inverse regression topic model combines corpus structure with external variables to improve prediction and reveal word-use variation within topics.

title: The Inverse Regression Topic Model

abstract: Fully observed large binary matrices appear in a wide variety of contexts. To model them, probabilistic matrix factorization (PMF) methods are an attractive solution. However, current batch algorithms for PMF can be inefficient because they need to analyze the entire data matrix before producing any parameter updates. We derive an efficient stochastic inference algorithm for PMF models of fully observed binary matrices. Our method exhibits faster convergence rates than more expensive batch approaches and has better predictive performance than scalable alternatives. The proposed method includes new data subsampling strategies which produce large gains over standard uniform subsampling. We also address the task of automatically selecting the size of the minibatches of data used by our method. For this, we derive an algorithm that adjusts this hyper-parameter online.

paragraphs: Large, fully observed binary matrices occur in many applications, and probabilistic matrix factorization offers a way to model them. Batch inference can be costly because it processes the entire matrix before updating model parameters. The paper develops stochastic inference to make useful progress without waiting for each complete pass.

The proposed algorithm includes new strategies for subsampling the data, which produce substantial gains over standard uniform sampling. This makes the choice of observations within an update an important part of the method. The authors also derive an algorithm that adjusts minibatch size online, automatically controlling how much data each update uses.

The method exhibits faster convergence rates than more expensive batch approaches and better predictive performance than scalable alternatives. These findings connect computational efficiency with the quality of the resulting model. The contribution combines stochastic updates, improved sampling, and adaptive minibatch selection for the specific setting of fully observed binary matrices, addressing several decisions that determine the effectiveness of scalable inference.
summary.tldr: Stochastic matrix-factorization inference combines improved subsampling with adaptive minibatch sizes to model fully observed binary matrices more efficiently.

title: Stochastic Inference for Scalable Probabilistic Modeling of Binary Matrices

abstract: We revisit the classic problem of estimating the population mean of an unknown single-dimensional distribution from samples, taking a game-theoretic viewpoint. In our setting, samples are supplied by strategic agents, who wish to pull the estimate as close as possible to their own value. In this setting, the sample mean gives rise to manipulation opportunities, whereas the sample median does not. Our key question is whether the sample median is the best (in terms of mean squared error) truthful estimator of the population mean. We show that when the underlying distribution is symmetric, there are truthful estimators that dominate the median. Our main result is a characterization of worst-case optimal truthful estimators, which provably outperform the median, for possibly asymmetric distributions with bounded support.

Our key question is whether the sample median is the best (in terms of mean squared error) truthful estimator of the population mean. Our main result is a characterization of worst-case optimal truthful estimators, which provably outperform the median, for possibly asymmetric distributions with bounded support.

paragraphs: Estimating a population mean usually treats samples as observations rather than strategic choices. This paper considers a different setting: each sample is supplied by an agent who wants the final estimate to be close to their own value. An estimator must therefore be judged both by statistical accuracy and by the incentives it creates for reporting.

The sample mean can be manipulated in this setting, while the sample median is truthful. The authors ask whether that incentive advantage makes the median the most accurate truthful estimator of the population mean, measured by mean squared error. They show that for symmetric underlying distributions, other truthful estimators can dominate the median.

The main result characterizes worst-case optimal truthful estimators for distributions with bounded support, including distributions that may be asymmetric. These estimators provably outperform the median under the stated criterion. The findings show that truthful reporting and improved mean estimation can coexist within these distributional settings. They also make the statistical objective explicit: estimating the mean remains the goal even when the median supplies the familiar truthful baseline.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies truthful estimators of a population mean that outperform the median under stated distributional and worst-case criteria.

title: Truthful Univariate Estimators

abstract: Can we summarize multi-category data based on user preferences in a scalable manner? Many utility functions used for data summarization satisfy submodularity, a natural diminishing returns property. We cast personalized data summarization as an instance of a general submodular maximization problem subject to multiple constraints. We develop the first practical and FAst coNsTrained submOdular Maximization algorithm, FANTOM, with strong theoretical guarantees. FANTOM maximizes a submodular function (not necessarily monotone) subject to intersection of a p-system and l knapsacks constrains. It achieves a (1 + ε)(p + 1)(2p + 2l + 1)/p approximation guarantee with only O(nrp log(n)/ε) query complexity (n and r indicate the size of the ground set and the size of the largest feasible solution, respectively). We then show how we can use FANTOM for personalized data summarization. In particular, a p-system can model different aspects of data, such as categories or time stamps, from which the users choose. In addition, knapsacks encode users’ constraints including budget or time. In our set of experiments, we consider several concrete applications: movie recommendation over 11K movies, personalized image summarization with 10K images, and revenue maximization on the YouTube social networks with 5000 communities. We observe that FANTOM constantly provides the highest utility against all the baselines.

Its utility functions satisfy diminishing returns: an item can add less value when much relevant material is already selected. The formulation also permits nonmonotone utility, so adding an item need not always improve the summary.

The proposed FANTOM algorithm handles the intersection of a p-system and multiple knapsack constraints. In the summarization application, the p-system can represent selection rules involving categories or timestamps, while knapsacks express limits such as budget or time. The algorithm comes with an approximation guarantee and a bound on the number of utility queries, making both solution quality and computational effort part of the analysis.

FANTOM consistently achieves the highest utility among the baselines in those experiments. These results support its practical use for constrained selection across several applications, while the theoretical formulation explains how diverse user requirements can fit into one optimization problem.
summary.tldr: FANTOM efficiently selects high-utility summaries while accommodating category rules, budgets, and other simultaneous constraints.

title: Fast Constrained Submodular Maximization: Personalized Data Summarization

abstract: We propose a probabilistic video model, the Video Pixel Network (VPN), that estimates the discrete joint distribution of the raw pixel values in a video. The model and the neural architecture reflect the time, space and color structure of video tensors and encode it as a four-dimensional dependency chain. The VPN approaches the best possible performance on the Moving MNIST benchmark, a leap over the previous state of the art, and the generated videos show only minor deviations from the ground truth. The VPN also produces detailed samples on the action-conditional Robotic Pushing benchmark and generalizes to the motion of novel objects.

The VPN also produces detailed samples on the action-conditional Robotic Pushing benchmark and generalizes to the motion of novel objects.

paragraphs: Modeling video requires accounting for how visual information is related across both space and time. This paper introduces the Video Pixel Network, or VPN, a probabilistic model of the discrete raw pixel values in a video. Its target is their joint distribution, allowing the model to represent dependencies across the video rather than treating its pixel values independently.

The neural architecture reflects the structure of a video tensor: time, two spatial dimensions, and color. It encodes these relationships as a four-dimensional dependency chain. This design connects the probability model to the organization of the data, so temporal development and within-frame visual structure are represented within the same modeling framework.

On Moving MNIST, the authors report performance approaching the best possible level, a large improvement over prior results, with generated videos differing only slightly from ground truth. On action-conditional Robotic Pushing, VPN produces detailed samples and generalizes to motion involving novel objects. These findings support its ability to capture both image detail and motion in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Video Pixel Networks model joint pixel probabilities across time, space, and color, producing strong results on two video benchmarks.

title: Video Pixel Networks

abstract: The search space for the feature selection problem in decision tree learning is the lattice of subsets of the available features. We provide an exact enumeration procedure of the subsets that lead to all and only the distinct decision trees. The procedure can be adopted to prune the search space of complete and heuristics search methods in wrapper models for feature selection. Based on this, we design a computational optimization of the sequential backward elimination heuristics with a performance improvement of up to 100X.
originalAbstract: The search space for the feature selection problem in decision tree learning is the lattice of subsets of the available features. We provide an exact enumeration procedure of the subsets that lead to all and only the distinct decision trees. The procedure can be adopted to prune the search space of complete and heuristics search methods in wrapper models for feature selection. Based on this, we design a computational optimization of the sequential backward elimination heuristics with a performance improvement of up to 100X.

paragraphs: Selecting features for a decision tree involves searching among subsets of the available inputs. The paper examines that search space through the trees those subsets produce. Its central contribution is an exact enumeration procedure that identifies subsets leading to every distinct decision tree, while avoiding redundant coverage of the same tree.

This matters for wrapper feature-selection methods, where feature subsets are assessed through the learning procedure. Searching different subsets can repeat work when those subsets lead to the same decision tree. The proposed enumeration can prune that search space while retaining coverage of the distinct trees. The authors describe its use with both complete search methods and heuristic searches.

They then use the enumeration result to optimize the computation performed by sequential backward elimination, a feature-selection heuristic. The reported performance improvement reaches up to a factor of 100. That figure describes the achieved computational improvement, rather than a guaranteed speedup on every problem. The contribution connects an exact description of distinct outcomes to a practical reduction in feature-search effort.
summary.tldr: An exact enumeration of feature subsets producing distinct decision trees reduces redundant search and speeds up sequential backward elimination by up to 100 times.

title: Enumerating Distinct Decision Trees

abstract: We show that Entropy-SGD (Chaudhari et al., 2017), when viewed as a learning algorithm, optimizes a PAC-Bayes bound on the risk of a Gibbs (posterior) classifier, i.e., a randomized classifier obtained by a risk-sensitive perturbation of the weights of a learned classifier. Entropy-SGD works by optimizing the bound’s prior, violating the hypothesis of the PAC-Bayes theorem that the prior is chosen independently of the data. Indeed, available implementations of Entropy-SGD rapidly obtain zero training error on random labels and the same holds of the Gibbs posterior. In order to obtain a valid generalization bound, we rely on a result showing that data-dependent priors obtained by stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD) yield valid PAC-Bayes bounds provided the target distribution of SGLD is eps-differentially private. We observe that test error on MNIST and CIFAR10 falls within the (empirically nonvacuous) risk bounds computed under the assumption that SGLD reaches stationarity. In particular, Entropy-SGLD can be configured to yield relatively tight generalization bounds and still fit real labels, although these same settings do not obtain state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: This paper interprets Entropy-SGD as optimizing a PAC-Bayes risk bound for a randomized classifier formed by perturbing learned weights. The problem is that it optimizes the bound's prior using training data, violating the theorem's requirement that the prior be chosen independently. Available implementations can rapidly fit random labels, including through the associated randomized classifier.

The authors pursue valid bounds through stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, or SGLD. They rely on a result allowing data-dependent priors when SGLD's target distribution satisfies epsilon-differential privacy. This supplies a conditional route to justifying a learned prior, rather than treating dependence on training data as automatically acceptable.

On MNIST and CIFAR10, observed test errors lie within empirically informative risk bounds calculated under the assumption that SGLD reaches stationarity. Entropy-SGLD can produce relatively tight bounds while still fitting real labels. However, the settings that yield these bounds do not achieve state-of-the-art performance. The findings connect generalization guarantees to explicit privacy and stationarity requirements, alongside an observed performance tradeoff.
summary.tldr: The paper exposes an invalid prior choice in Entropy-SGD's PAC-Bayes interpretation and develops conditional generalization bounds using SGLD.

title: Entropy-SGD optimizes the prior of a PAC-Bayes bound: Generalization properties of Entropy-SGD and data-dependent priors

abstract: Differential privacy (DP) is a formal notion for quantifying the privacy loss of algorithms. Algorithms in the central model of DP achieve high accuracy but make the strongest trust assumptions whereas those in the local DP model make the weakest trust assumptions but incur substantial accuracy loss. The shuffled DP model [Bittau et al 2017, Erlingsson et al 2019, Cheu et al 19] has recently emerged as a feasible middle ground between the central and local models, providing stronger trust assumptions than the former while promising higher accuracies than the latter. In this paper, we obtain practical communication-efficient algorithms in the shuffled DP model for two basic aggregation primitives used in machine learning: 1) binary summation, and 2) histograms over a moderate number of buckets. Our algorithms achieve accuracy that is arbitrarily close to that of central DP algorithms with an expected communication per user essentially matching what is needed without any privacy constraints! We demonstrate the practicality of our algorithms by experimentally evaluating them and comparing their performance to several widely-used protocols such as Randomized Response [Warner 1965] and RAPPOR [Erlingsson et al. 2014].

Algorithms in the central model of DP achieve high accuracy but make the strongest trust assumptions whereas those in the local DP model make the weakest trust assumptions but incur substantial accuracy loss. The shuffled DP model [Bittau et al 2017, Erlingsson et al 2019, Cheu et al 19] has recently emerged as a feasible middle ground between the central and local models, providing stronger trust assumptions than the former while promising higher accuracies than the latter. In this paper, we obtain practical communication-efficient algorithms in the shuffled DP model for two basic aggregation primitives used in machine learning: 1) binary summation, and 2) histograms over a moderate number of buckets. Our algorithms achieve accuracy that is arbitrarily close to that of central DP algorithms with an expected communication per user essentially matching what is needed without any privacy constraints! We demonstrate the practicality of our algorithms by experimentally evaluating them and comparing their performance to several widely-used protocols such as Randomized Response [Warner 1965] and RAPPOR [Erlingsson et al. 2014].

paragraphs: Private aggregation must balance accuracy, communication, and assumptions about whom users trust. Central differential privacy offers high accuracy, whereas local differential privacy incurs substantial accuracy costs under weaker trust assumptions. This paper works in the shuffled model, where anonymous messages provide another setting for designing private aggregation algorithms.

The authors develop communication-efficient algorithms for two basic tasks: summing binary values and constructing histograms with a moderate number of buckets. They achieve accuracy arbitrarily close to central differential privacy algorithms. At the same time, the expected communication per user essentially matches the communication needed without privacy constraints.

The combination matters because privacy mechanisms can otherwise impose costs on both the quality of aggregate statistics and the volume of messages users send. Here, the stated accuracy result is paired with a particularly small expected communication burden. Experimental evaluations, including comparisons with Randomized Response and RAPPOR, demonstrate the practicality of the proposed algorithms for these aggregation tasks.
summary.tldr: Shuffled private counting achieves accuracy arbitrarily close to central privacy methods with nearly nonprivate expected communication per user.

title: Private Counting from Anonymous Messages: Near-Optimal Accuracy with Vanishing Communication Overhead

abstract: Due to the wider availability of modern electronic health records, patient care data is often being stored in the form of time-series. Clustering such time-series data is crucial for patient phenotyping, anticipating patients’ prognoses by identifying “similar” patients, and designing treatment guidelines that are tailored to homogeneous patient subgroups. In this paper, we develop a deep learning approach for clustering time-series data, where each cluster comprises patients who share similar future outcomes of interest (e.g., adverse events, the onset of comorbidities). To encourage each cluster to have homogeneous future outcomes, the clustering is carried out by learning discrete representations that best describe the future outcome distribution based on novel loss functions. Experiments on two real-world datasets show that our model achieves superior clustering performance over state-of-the-art benchmarks and identifies meaningful clusters that can be translated into actionable information for clinical decision-making.

Grouping these histories can help identify patient subgroups and anticipate their prognoses. This paper develops a clustering approach in which similarity is defined through future outcomes of interest, such as adverse events or the onset of additional conditions.

The method learns discrete representations of patient time series using deep learning. Its loss functions encourage those representations to describe the distribution of future outcomes, so patients assigned to the same cluster have more homogeneous expected outcomes. This ties the clustering objective directly to the prognostic information the groups are intended to convey.

The findings support outcome-oriented clustering as a way to turn longitudinal patient records into interpretable subgroups; the stated evidence concerns clustering performance and the clinical relevance of the resulting groups.
summary.tldr: Deep predictive clustering groups patient histories by similar future outcome distributions, producing meaningful subgroups in two real-world datasets.

title: Temporal Phenotyping using Deep Predictive Clustering of Disease Progression

abstract: Riemannian manifolds provide a principled way to model nonlinear geometric structure inherent in data. A Riemannian metric on said manifolds determines geometry-aware shortest paths and provides the means to define statistical models accordingly. However, these operations are typically computationally demanding. To ease this computational burden, we advocate probabilistic numerical methods for Riemannian statistics. In particular, we focus on Bayesian quadrature (BQ) to numerically compute integrals over normal laws on Riemannian manifolds learned from data. In this task, each function evaluation relies on the solution of an expensive initial value problem. We show that by leveraging both prior knowledge and an active exploration scheme, BQ significantly reduces the number of required evaluations and thus outperforms Monte Carlo methods on a wide range of integration problems. As a concrete application, we highlight the merits of adopting Riemannian geometry with our proposed framework on a nonlinear dataset from molecular dynamics.

paragraphs: Data can have nonlinear geometric structure that is better described by a curved manifold than by ordinary flat space. A Riemannian metric makes it possible to define geometry-aware paths and statistical models on that manifold. The paper addresses the computational expense of using those models, focusing on numerical integration over normal distributions on manifolds learned from data.

In this setting, evaluating the function being integrated requires solving an expensive initial-value problem. Consequently, the number of evaluations matters directly to computational cost. The authors use Bayesian quadrature, a probabilistic numerical method, together with prior knowledge and an active exploration strategy to choose informative evaluations.

The reported results show that this approach substantially reduces the required evaluations and outperforms Monte Carlo methods across a wide range of integration problems. An application to a nonlinear molecular-dynamics dataset illustrates the value of combining Riemannian modeling with this computational framework. The contribution makes geometry-aware statistical calculations less burdensome by improving how their expensive numerical information is gathered.
summary.tldr: Bayesian quadrature reduces expensive function evaluations when computing integrals on learned Riemannian data manifolds.

title: Bayesian Quadrature on Riemannian Data Manifolds

abstract: In this paper, sample-aware policy entropy regularization is proposed to enhance the conventional policy entropy regularization for better exploration. Exploiting the sample distribution obtainable from the replay buffer, the proposed sample-aware entropy regularization maximizes the entropy of the weighted sum of the policy action distribution and the sample action distribution from the replay buffer for sample-efficient exploration. A practical algorithm named diversity actor-critic (DAC) is developed by applying policy iteration to the objective function with the proposed sample-aware entropy regularization. Numerical results show that DAC significantly outperforms existing recent algorithms for reinforcement learning.

A practical algorithm named diversity actor-critic (DAC) is developed by applying policy iteration to the objective function with the proposed sample-aware entropy regularization. paragraphs: Entropy regularization encourages a reinforcement learning policy to keep its action choices varied. This paper extends that idea by incorporating information about actions already represented in the replay buffer. Its aim is more sample-efficient exploration: exploration shaped by the learner’s collected experience as well as its current policy.

The proposed objective maximizes the entropy of a weighted mixture of two distributions. One is the policy’s action distribution, and the other is the sample action distribution obtained from replayed experience. Consequently, the exploration objective depends on both current action choices and the actions present in stored data. This is the central meaning of making entropy regularization sample-aware.

The authors apply policy iteration to this objective to obtain a practical algorithm called diversity actor-critic, or DAC. Numerical results show significant improvements over recent reinforcement learning algorithms. The contribution connects a specific change in the exploration objective with an implementable actor-critic method and reported performance gains, using the replay buffer as a source of information for exploration.
summary.tldr: Diversity actor-critic combines policy and replay-buffer action distributions in an entropy objective to improve exploration efficiency.

title: Diversity Actor-Critic: Sample-Aware Entropy Regularization for Sample-Efficient Exploration

abstract: Collecting more diverse and representative training data is often touted as a remedy for the disparate performance of machine learning predictors across subpopulations. However, a precise framework for understanding how dataset properties like diversity affect learning outcomes is largely lacking. By casting data collection as part of the learning process, we demonstrate that diverse representation in training data is key not only to increasing subgroup performances, but also to achieving population-level objectives. Our analysis and experiments describe how dataset compositions influence performance and provide constructive results for using trends in existing data, alongside domain knowledge, to help guide intentional, objective-aware dataset design

paragraphs: Calls for more representative training data often aim to reduce performance differences between subpopulations. This paper asks how dataset composition actually shapes learning outcomes. It treats data collection as part of the learning process, making the allocation of training examples across groups an explicit subject of analysis and design.

The authors show that diverse representation matters for subgroup performance and for objectives measured across the population. Their analysis and experiments describe how changing the composition of a dataset influences performance. This connects decisions about whose examples are collected with the goals used to assess the resulting predictor.

The paper also provides constructive results for guiding dataset design using trends visible in existing data together with domain knowledge. The intended allocation is therefore informed by the learning objective and available evidence about performance. Its contribution is a framework for intentional data collection: subgroup representation becomes a decision linked to desired outcomes, helping make a broad call for diversity more concrete and operational.
summary.tldr: Treating subgroup allocation as part of learning helps connect representative data collection with subgroup and population-level performance objectives.

title: Representation Matters: Assessing the Importance of Subgroup Allocations in Training Data

abstract: We consider a price-based revenue management problem with reusable resources over a finite time horizon $T$. The problem finds important applications in car/bicycle rental, ridesharing, cloud computing, and hospitality management. Customers arrive following a price-dependent Poisson process and each customer requests one unit of $c$ homogeneous reusable resources. If there is an available unit, the customer gets served within a price-dependent exponentially distributed service time; otherwise, she waits in a queue until the next available unit. The decision maker assumes that the inter-arrival and service intervals have an unknown linear dependence on a $d_f$-dimensional feature vector associated with the posted price. We propose a rate-optimal online learning and pricing algorithm, termed Batch Linear Confidence Bound (BLinUCB), and prove that the cumulative regret is $\tilde{O}( d_f \sqrt{T } )$. In establishing the regret, we bound the transient system performance upon price changes via a coupling argument, and also generalize linear bandits to accommodate sub-exponential rewards.

paragraphs: Pricing reusable resources requires accounting for both demand and how long each resource remains occupied. This paper studies a finite-horizon setting with a fixed number of interchangeable units. Customers arrive according to a price-dependent Poisson process, receive exponentially distributed service with a price-dependent duration, and wait in a queue when no unit is available.

The decision maker does not know how pricing affects arrival and service intervals. The model assumes those intervals depend linearly on a feature vector associated with the posted price. The proposed Batch Linear Confidence Bound algorithm, BLinUCB, learns these relationships while choosing prices, bringing online learning into a system where earlier customers can continue occupying resources.

Under this model, the authors prove a rate-optimal cumulative regret bound proportional to the feature dimension times the square root of the horizon, up to logarithmic factors. Their analysis uses a coupling argument to control temporary system behavior after price changes. It also extends linear-bandit analysis to sub-exponential rewards, providing tools for handling the reward behavior arising in this reusable-resource problem.
summary.tldr: BLinUCB learns prices for a specified reusable-resource queueing model with rate-optimal regret, accounting for temporary effects after price changes.

title: Online Learning and Pricing with Reusable Resources: Linear Bandits with Sub-Exponential Rewards

abstract: Visual attention helps achieve robust perception under noise, corruption, and distribution shifts in human vision, which are areas where modern neural networks still fall short. We present VARS, Visual Attention from Recurrent Sparse reconstruction, a new attention formulation built on two prominent features of the human visual attention mechanism: recurrency and sparsity. Related features are grouped together via recurrent connections between neurons, with salient objects emerging via sparse regularization. VARS adopts an attractor network with recurrent connections that converges toward a stable pattern over time. Network layers are represented as ordinary differential equations (ODEs), formulating attention as a recurrent attractor network that equivalently optimizes the sparse reconstruction of input using a dictionary of “templates” encoding underlying patterns of data. We show that self-attention is a special case of VARS with a single-step optimization and no sparsity constraint. VARS can be readily used as a replacement for self-attention in popular vision transformers, consistently improving their robustness across various benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper develops an attention mechanism inspired by recurrence and sparsity in human visual attention. Called VARS, it uses recurrent connections to group related features and sparse regularization to make salient objects emerge. The mechanism is an attractor network whose activity evolves toward a stable pattern over time.

The authors express its layers as ordinary differential equations and connect the recurrent dynamics to an optimization problem. In that interpretation, attention reconstructs the input sparsely using a dictionary of templates that encode underlying data patterns. The formulation gives the attention mechanism both a dynamical description and an equivalent reconstruction-based objective.

Within this framework, self-attention appears as a special case using a single optimization step and no sparsity constraint. VARS can replace self-attention in popular vision transformers, and the authors report consistent robustness improvements across multiple benchmarks. The results support recurrent sparse reconstruction as a practical attention design while also explaining how it relates mathematically to an established mechanism.
summary.tldr: VARS formulates attention as recurrent sparse reconstruction, generalizes self-attention, and improves reported vision-transformer robustness.

title: Visual Attention Emerges from Recurrent Sparse Reconstruction

abstract: The hierarchical variational autoencoder (HVAE) is a popular generative model used for many representation learning tasks. However, its application to image synthesis often yields models with poor sample quality. In this work, we treat image synthesis itself as a hierarchical representation learning problem and regularize an HVAE toward representations that improve the model’s image synthesis performance. We do so by leveraging the progressive coding hypothesis, which claims hierarchical latent variable models that are good at progressive lossy compression will generate high-quality samples. To test this hypothesis, we first show empirically that conventionally-trained HVAEs are not good progressive coders. We then propose a simple method that constrains the hierarchical representations to prioritize the encoding of information beneficial for lossy compression, and show that this modification leads to improved sample quality. Our work lends further support to the progressive coding hypothesis and demonstrates that this hypothesis should be exploited when designing variational autoencoders.

We do so by leveraging the progressive coding hypothesis, which claims hierarchical latent variable models that are good at progressive lossy compression will generate high-quality samples. paragraphs: Hierarchical variational autoencoders learn representations at multiple latent levels, but their generated images can have poor quality. This paper treats image generation as a problem of organizing information across that hierarchy. Its guiding idea is the progressive coding hypothesis: hierarchical models that perform well at progressive lossy compression should also generate high-quality samples.

The authors first examine whether conventionally trained hierarchical autoencoders already behave as effective progressive coders. Their empirical findings indicate that they do not. Having a hierarchy of latent variables therefore does not, by itself, establish that the model prioritizes information in a way that is useful for progressively reconstructing an image.

The proposed method constrains the learned representations to prioritize information beneficial for lossy compression. Applying this constraint improves the quality of generated samples in the reported experiments. The results offer further support for the progressive coding hypothesis and suggest a concrete design principle: how information is allocated within a latent hierarchy can matter for image synthesis.
summary.tldr: Prioritizing compression-useful information within hierarchical variational autoencoders improves generated image quality and supports the progressive coding hypothesis.

title: Bit Prioritization in Variational Autoencoders via Progressive Coding

abstract: Deep topic models have shown an impressive ability to extract multi-layer document latent representations and discover hierarchical semantically meaningful topics.However, most deep topic models are limited to the single-step generative process, despite the fact that the progressive generative process has achieved impressive performance in modeling image data. To this end, in this paper, we propose a novel progressive deep topic model that consists of a knowledge-informed textural data coarsening process and a corresponding progressive generative model. The former is used to build multi-level observations ranging from concrete to abstract, while the latter is used to generate more concrete observations gradually. Additionally, we incorporate a graph-enhanced decoder to capture the semantic relationships among words at different levels of observation. Furthermore, we perform a theoretical analysis of the proposed model based on the principle of information theory and show how it can alleviate the well-known "latent variable collapse" problem. Finally, extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed model effectively improves the ability of deep topic models, resulting in higher-quality latent document representations and topics.

paragraphs: Deep topic models learn layered document representations and hierarchies of meaningful topics. However, the authors identify a mismatch: these models commonly use a single-step generative process despite representing several levels of abstraction. They propose a progressive model that builds text observations through successive levels of detail.

The method first uses a knowledge-informed coarsening process to construct observations ranging from concrete to abstract. A corresponding generative model then moves in the opposite direction, gradually producing more concrete observations. A graph-enhanced decoder captures semantic relationships among words across the observation levels, incorporating those relationships into the progressive construction.

An information-theoretic analysis explains how the model can alleviate latent variable collapse, a problem in which latent variables fail to play their intended role. Experiments report improvements in the quality of both document representations and discovered topics. The significance is the alignment between a hierarchy of textual observations and a generative process that works through that hierarchy, supported by semantic relationships and a theoretical account of improved latent-variable use.
summary.tldr: A progressive topic model generates increasingly concrete text representations and can reduce latent variable collapse.

title: Bayesian Progressive Deep Topic Model with Knowledge Informed Textual Data Coarsening Process

abstract: Systematic under-counting effects are observed in data collected across many disciplines, e.g., epidemiology and ecology. Under-counted tensor completion (UC-TC) is well-motivated for many data analytics tasks, e.g., inferring the case numbers of infectious diseases at unobserved locations from under-counted case numbers in neighboring regions. However, existing methods for similar problems often lack supports in theory, making it hard to understand the underlying principles and conditions beyond empirical successes. In this work, a low-rank Poisson tensor model with an expressive unknown nonlinear side information extractor is proposed for under-counted multi-aspect data. A joint low-rank tensor completion and neural network learning algorithm is designed to recover the model. Moreover, the UC-TC formulation is supported by theoretical analysis showing that the fully counted entries of the tensor and each entry’s under-counting probability can be provably recovered from partial observations—under reasonable conditions. To our best knowledge, the result is the first to offer theoretical supports for under-counted multi-aspect data completion. Simulations and real-data experiments corroborate the theoretical claims.

paragraphs: Some datasets contain both missing entries and observed counts that systematically fall below the true totals. This paper studies that combination in multi-aspect data represented as tensors. The motivating problem includes estimating unobserved disease counts from neighboring regions whose recorded counts are themselves incomplete.

The proposed model combines a low-rank Poisson tensor with an unknown nonlinear extractor of side information. A joint algorithm learns the tensor structure and a neural network, using attributes alongside the observed counts. The modeling task includes both completing missing data and accounting for the process that causes under-counting.

The authors prove that, under stated reasonable conditions, partial observations can support recovery of fully counted tensor entries and each entry’s under-counting probability. The guarantee is conditional, rather than a claim that arbitrary incomplete counts reveal their true totals. Simulations and real-data experiments corroborate the theoretical claims. The authors identify this as the first theoretical support for under-counted multi-aspect completion, offering an explanation of when recovery is possible alongside an algorithm for performing it.
summary.tldr: A joint tensor and neural model can recover missing true counts and under-counting probabilities under the paper’s theoretical conditions.

title: Under-Counted Tensor Completion with Neural Incorporation of Attributes

abstract: Activity and property prediction models are the central workhorses in drug discovery and materials sciences, but currently, they have to be trained or fine-tuned for new tasks. Without training or fine-tuning, scientific language models could be used for such low-data tasks through their announced zero- and few-shot capabilities. However, their predictive quality at activity prediction is lacking. In this work, we envision a novel type of activity prediction model that is able to adapt to new prediction tasks at inference time, via understanding textual information describing the task. To this end, we propose a new architecture with separate modules for chemical and natural language inputs, and a contrastive pretraining objective on data from large biochemical databases. In extensive experiments, we show that our method CLAMP yields improved predictive performance on few-shot learning benchmarks and zero-shot problems in drug discovery. We attribute the advances of our method to the modularized architecture and to our pre-training objective.

paragraphs: Activity prediction models help estimate how chemicals behave in a particular task, but adapting them to new tasks typically requires training or fine-tuning. Scientific language models offer a possible route to prediction with little or no task-specific data, yet the paper identifies weak activity-prediction quality as a problem. CLAMP aims to connect chemical prediction with an understanding of task descriptions.

The architecture has separate modules for chemical inputs and natural-language inputs. It learns through a contrastive pretraining objective using large biochemical databases. This design lets the model use textual information describing a prediction task, supporting the goal of adapting at inference time rather than relying solely on task-specific parameter updates.

The authors report improved prediction on few-shot benchmarks and zero-shot drug-discovery problems. They attribute these gains to the modular architecture and the pretraining objective. The findings support combining specialized chemical and language representations for prediction when task data are scarce, with the reported evidence concerning predictive performance rather than downstream drug development outcomes.
summary.tldr: CLAMP combines chemical and language modules to improve activity prediction on few-shot and zero-shot drug-discovery tasks.

title: Enhancing Activity Prediction Models in Drug Discovery with the Ability to Understand Human Language

abstract: Real-world data contains a vast amount of multimodal information, among which vision and language are the two most representative modalities. Moreover, increasingly heavier models, e.g., Transformers, have attracted the attention of researchers to model compression. However, how to compress multimodal models, especially vison-language Transformers, is still under-explored. This paper proposes the Unified and Progressive Pruning (UPop) as a universal vison-language Transformer compression framework, which incorporates 1) unifiedly searching multimodal subnets in a continuous optimization space from the original model, which enables automatic assignment of pruning ratios among compressible modalities and structures; 2) progressively searching and retraining the subnet, which maintains convergence between the search and retrain to attain higher compression ratios. Experiments on various tasks, datasets, and model architectures demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of the proposed UPop framework. The code is available at https://github.com/sdc17/UPop.

paragraphs: Vision-language transformers process information across multiple modalities, making compression a question of how to distribute reductions across different model components. UPop introduces a unified framework for finding smaller subnetworks within these models. It addresses both where pruning should occur and how the resulting subnetwork should be searched for and retrained.

The unified search operates in a continuous optimization space and automatically assigns pruning ratios among compressible modalities and structures. This lets compression decisions be considered together across the model. The progressive component searches and retrains the subnetwork in stages, maintaining convergence between those activities to attain higher compression ratios.

Experiments across different tasks, datasets, and model architectures demonstrate the framework's effectiveness and versatility. The findings support the combination of coordinated pruning allocation and progressive retraining for vision-language compression. The method's significance lies in treating a multimodal model as a connected compression problem while providing a staged procedure for obtaining and training the smaller network.
summary.tldr: UPop compresses vision-language transformers by jointly allocating pruning across components and progressively searching and retraining subnetworks.

title: UPop: Unified and Progressive Pruning for Compressing Vision-Language Transformers

abstract: Pixel-wise regression tasks (e.g., monocular depth estimation (MDE) and optical flow estimation (OFE)) have been widely involved in our daily life in applications like autonomous driving, augmented reality and video composition. Although certain applications are security-critical or bear societal significance, the adversarial robustness of such models are not sufficiently studied, especially in the black-box scenario. In this work, we introduce the first unified black-box adversarial patch attack framework against pixel-wise regression tasks, aiming to identify the vulnerabilities of these models under query-based black-box attacks. We propose a novel square-based adversarial patch optimization framework and employ probabilistic square sampling and score-based gradient estimation techniques to generate the patch effectively and efficiently, overcoming the scalability problem of previous black-box patch attacks. Our attack prototype, named BadPart, is evaluated on both MDE and OFE tasks, utilizing a total of 7 models. BadPart surpasses 3 baseline methods in terms of both attack performance and efficiency. We also apply BadPart on the Google online service for portrait depth estimation, causing 43.5% relative distance error with 50K queries. State-of-the-art (SOTA) countermeasures cannot defend our attack effectively.

Although certain applications are security-critical or bear societal significance, the adversarial robustness of such models are not sufficiently studied, especially in the black-box scenario. Our attack prototype, named BadPart, is evaluated on both MDE and OFE tasks, utilizing a total of 7 models. BadPart surpasses 3 baseline methods in terms of both attack performance and efficiency. We also apply BadPart on the Google online service for portrait depth estimation, causing 43.5% relative distance error with 50K queries. State-of-the-art (SOTA) countermeasures cannot defend our attack effectively.

paragraphs: BadPart investigates vulnerabilities in models that predict a numerical value at every image pixel. Examples include estimating depth from a single image and estimating motion between images. The paper focuses on black-box attacks, where an attacker queries a model without accessing its internal workings, and changes a localized image patch to disrupt its predictions.

The method organizes patch optimization around squares. It combines probabilistic square sampling with gradient estimates derived from model scores to search for effective changes. This design addresses the scaling difficulties of earlier black-box patch attacks and provides one framework for both depth and optical-flow estimation.

Across seven models covering those two tasks, BadPart exceeds three baseline methods in attack effectiveness and efficiency. Against Google's online portrait-depth service, it produces a 43.5% relative distance error using 50,000 queries. The tested state-of-the-art countermeasures also fail to defend effectively. These results expose weaknesses in the evaluated systems, including an online service, under query-based patch attacks.
summary.tldr: BadPart efficiently finds adversarial image patches that disrupt depth and motion estimation through black-box model queries.

title: BadPart: Unified Black-box Adversarial Patch Attacks against Pixel-wise Regression Tasks

abstract: Learning Continuous-Time Dynamic Graphs (C-TDGs) requires accurately modeling spatio-temporal information on streams of irregularly sampled events. While many methods have been proposed recently, we find that most message passing-, recurrent- or self-attention-based methods perform poorly on long-range tasks. These tasks require correlating information that occurred "far" away from the current event, either spatially (higher-order node information) or along the time dimension (events occurred in the past). To address long-range dependencies, we introduce Continuous-Time Graph Anti-Symmetric Network (CTAN). Grounded within the ordinary differential equations framework, our method is designed for efficient propagation of information. In this paper, we show how CTAN’s (i) long-range modeling capabilities are substantiated by theoretical findings and how (ii) its empirical performance on synthetic long-range benchmarks and real-world benchmarks is superior to other methods. Our results motivate CTAN’s ability to propagate long-range information in C-TDGs as well as the inclusion of long-range tasks as part of temporal graph models evaluation.

The authors find that many existing message-passing, recurrent, and self-attention methods struggle with these long-range tasks.

They introduce the Continuous-Time Graph Anti-Symmetric Network, or CTAN, using an ordinary differential equation framework. Its design aims to propagate information efficiently so that distant events and higher-order node information can influence current predictions. The paper supplies theoretical findings supporting these long-range modeling capabilities.

Experiments on synthetic long-range tasks and real-world benchmarks report better performance than the compared methods. The results support CTAN's ability to carry relevant information across spatial and temporal distances in evolving graphs. They also motivate an evaluation change: temporal graph models should be tested explicitly on tasks requiring long-range dependencies, because those tasks expose weaknesses that are central to this modeling problem.
summary.tldr: CTAN uses a differential-equation framework to improve long-range information propagation in continuous-time dynamic graphs.

title: Long Range Propagation on Continuous-Time Dynamic Graphs

abstract: Since graph neural networks (GNNs) are often vulnerable to attack, we need to know when we can trust them. We develop a computationally effective approach towards providing robust certificates for message-passing neural networks (MPNNs) using a Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation function. Because our work builds on mixed-integer optimization, it encodes a wide variety of subproblems, for example it admits (i) both adding and removing edges, (ii) both global and local budgets, and (iii) both topological perturbations and feature modifications. Our key technology, topology-based bounds tightening, uses graph structure to tighten bounds. We also experiment with aggressive bounds tightening to dynamically change the optimization constraints by tightening variable bounds. To demonstrate the effectiveness of these strategies, we implement an extension to the open-source branch-and-cut solver SCIP. We test on both node and graph classification problems and consider topological attacks that both add and remove edges.

The method uses mixed-integer optimization to represent the network and the perturbations considered by the verification problem.

The formulation can accommodate added and removed edges, global and local perturbation budgets, and changes to both topology and features. Its central technique uses graph structure to tighten variable bounds within the optimization. The authors also investigate more aggressive tightening that dynamically updates constraints as variable bounds improve, aiming to make the verification computation more effective.

The approach is implemented as an extension to the open-source SCIP branch-and-cut solver. Experiments cover node classification and graph classification, with topological attacks that can both add and remove edges. The contribution combines a flexible representation of verification problems with graph-aware tightening strategies, and evaluates those strategies on both levels of graph prediction.
summary.tldr: Graph-structure-based bound tightening supports mixed-integer robustness verification of ReLU message-passing networks under specified perturbations.

title: Verifying message-passing neural networks via topology-based bounds tightening

abstract: Graph representation has gained widespread application across various machine learning domains, attributed to its ability to discern correlations among input nodes. In the realm of Multi- agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), agents are tasked with observing other entities within their environment to determine their behavior. Conventional MARL methodologies often suffer from training difficulties if Permutation Invariant (PI) and Permutation Equivariant (PE) properties are not considered during training. The adoption of graph representation offers a solution to these challenges by conceptualizing observed entities as a graph. In this context, we introduce the Hyper Graphical Attention Policy (HGAP) Network, which employs a graph attention mechanism to fulfill the PI and PE properties, while also understanding inter-entity interactions for decision-making. HGAP is assessed across various MARL benchmarks to confirm its effectiveness and efficiency. In addition, a series of ablation studies are provided to demonstrate its adaptability, transferability, and the capability to alleviate the complexities introduced by the POMDP constraint.

paragraphs: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, an agent chooses behavior from observations of other entities. The order in which those entities are represented should be handled consistently: some outputs should remain unchanged under reordering, while others should reorder correspondingly. The paper argues that overlooking these permutation properties can make conventional methods difficult to train.

The Hyper Graphical Attention Policy network, or HGAP, represents observed entities as a graph. Its graph attention mechanism fulfills permutation invariance and permutation equivariance while modeling interactions between entities for decision-making. These requirements are built into the policy representation, connecting the handling of entity order with the learning of relationships among entities.

Evaluations across multiple multi-agent benchmarks support HGAP’s effectiveness and efficiency. Ablation studies also demonstrate adaptability, transferability, and an ability to alleviate difficulties associated with partial observability. The contribution is a policy architecture that uses graph structure to address both ordering consistency and interaction modeling, with experiments examining its broader behavior across the studied settings.
summary.tldr: HGAP uses graph attention to respect entity-order symmetries and model interactions in multi-agent reinforcement learning.

title: HGAP: Boosting Permutation Invariant and Permutation Equivariant in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Graph Attention Network

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel approach called DIffusion-guided DIversity (DIDI) for offline behavioral generation. The goal of DIDI is to learn a diverse set of skills from a mixture of label-free offline data. We achieve this by leveraging diffusion probabilistic models as priors to guide the learning process and regularize the policy. By optimizing a joint objective that incorporates diversity and diffusion-guided regularization, we encourage the emergence of diverse behaviors while maintaining the similarity to the offline data. Experimental results in four decision-making domains (Push, Kitchen, Humanoid, and D4RL tasks) show that DIDI is effective in discovering diverse and discriminative skills. We also introduce skill stitching and skill interpolation, which highlight the generalist nature of the learned skill space. Further, by incorporating an extrinsic reward function, DIDI enables reward-guided behavior generation, facilitating the learning of diverse and optimal behaviors from sub-optimal data.

paragraphs: DIDI learns a collection of skills from an existing mixture of behavioral data without requiring skill labels. Its objective combines two demands: the learned behaviors should differ meaningfully from one another, and they should remain similar to behavior represented in the offline data. Diversity alone would not express both goals.

The method uses diffusion probabilistic models as priors that guide learning and regularize the policy. A joint objective combines this guidance with a diversity objective. The diffusion component supplies a connection to the observed behavioral distribution, while the diversity component encourages the policy to develop distinguishable skills within that learning process.

Experiments in Push, Kitchen, Humanoid, and D4RL tasks show effective discovery of diverse, discriminative skills. The authors also introduce skill stitching and interpolation to demonstrate flexibility in the learned skill space. Adding an external reward function enables reward-guided generation, which the paper presents as a way to learn diverse and optimal behaviors from suboptimal data. The approach therefore supports both unlabeled skill discovery and generation directed by a specified reward.
summary.tldr: DIDI combines diffusion-based guidance with a diversity objective to learn distinct skills from unlabeled offline behavior.

title: DIDI: Diffusion-Guided Diversity for Offline Behavioral Generation

abstract: Unsupervised and self-supervised objectives, such as next token prediction, have enabled pre-training generalist models from large amounts of unlabeled data. In reinforcement learning (RL), however, finding a truly general and scalable unsupervised pre-training objective for generalist policies from offline data remains a major open question. While a number of methods have been proposed to enable generic self-supervised RL, based on principles such as goal-conditioned RL, behavioral cloning, and unsupervised skill learning, such methods remain limited in terms of either the diversity of the discovered behaviors, the need for high-quality demonstration data, or the lack of a clear adaptation mechanism for downstream tasks. In this work, we propose a novel unsupervised framework to pre-train generalist policies that capture diverse, optimal, long-horizon behaviors from unlabeled offline data such that they can be quickly adapted to any arbitrary new tasks in a zero-shot manner. Our key insight is to learn a structured representation that preserves the temporal structure of the underlying environment, and then to span this learned latent space with directional movements, which enables various zero-shot policy “prompting” schemes for downstream tasks. Through our experiments on simulated robotic locomotion and manipulation benchmarks, we show that our unsupervised policies can solve goal-conditioned and general RL tasks in a zero-shot fashion, even often outperforming prior methods designed specifically for each setting. Our code and videos are available at https://seohong.me/projects/hilp/

paragraphs: This paper tackles how to pre-train general-purpose reinforcement-learning policies from unlabeled offline experience. Existing approaches can restrict behavioral diversity, depend on strong demonstrations, or leave downstream adaptation unclear. The proposed framework aims to capture diverse, optimal behaviors over long horizons and make them available for new tasks through zero-shot adaptation.

Its central idea is to learn a structured representation that preserves the environment’s temporal structure. Policies then learn directional movements spanning this representation space. Those directions provide a way to prompt the policy for downstream behavior, connecting the organization of the learned space to mechanisms for selecting actions appropriate to a task.

Experiments on simulated robotic locomotion and manipulation show that the pre-trained policies solve both goal-conditioned and general reinforcement-learning tasks without further task-specific training. They often outperform earlier methods tailored to the individual settings. These results support the usefulness of temporal representations and directional policy prompting for the evaluated tasks, while the broader framework is designed to enable adaptation to arbitrary new tasks.
summary.tldr: Hilbert representations organize offline experience into directional behaviors that can be prompted to solve downstream reinforcement-learning tasks without additional training.

title: Foundation Policies with Hilbert Representations

abstract: In the context of average-reward reinforcement learning, the requirement for oracle knowledge of the mixing time, a measure of the duration a Markov chain under a fixed policy needs to achieve its stationary distribution, poses a significant challenge for the global convergence of policy gradient methods. This requirement is particularly problematic due to the difficulty and expense of estimating mixing time in environments with large state spaces, leading to the necessity of impractically long trajectories for effective gradient estimation in practical applications. To address this limitation, we consider the Multi-level Actor-Critic (MAC) framework, which incorporates a Multi-level Monte-Carlo (MLMC) gradient estimator. With our approach, we effectively alleviate the dependency on mixing time knowledge, a first for average-reward MDPs global convergence. Furthermore, our approach exhibits the tightest available dependence of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\tau_{mix}})$ known from prior work. With a 2D grid world goal-reaching navigation experiment, we demonstrate that MAC outperforms the existing state-of-the-art policy gradient-based method for average reward settings.

paragraphs: Average-reward reinforcement learning evaluates performance over continued interaction. Global convergence results for policy-gradient methods can require advance knowledge of mixing time: how long a fixed policy’s Markov chain needs to approach its stationary distribution. Estimating this quantity is difficult in large state spaces and can lead to impractically long trajectories for gradient estimation.

The paper studies Multi-level Actor-Critic, or MAC, which uses a Multi-level Monte Carlo gradient estimator. The approach alleviates the need for oracle knowledge of mixing time in establishing global convergence for average-reward decision processes. This targets a gap between theoretical requirements and information realistically available during learning.

The analysis retains a dependence proportional to the square root of mixing time, matching the tightest dependence available from prior work. Thus, avoiding advance knowledge does not mean the process’s mixing behavior stops affecting the result. In a two-dimensional grid-world navigation experiment, MAC outperforms the existing state-of-the-art policy-gradient method for the average-reward setting, providing a concrete empirical demonstration alongside the convergence analysis.
summary.tldr: MAC uses multilevel gradient estimation to alleviate mixing-time oracle requirements while retaining strong mixing-time dependence in average-reward convergence analysis.

title: Towards Global Optimality for Practical Average Reward Reinforcement Learning without Mixing Time Oracles

abstract: We presents VoxBind, a new score-based generative model for 3D molecules conditioned on protein structures. Our approach represents molecules as 3D atomic density grids and leverages a 3D voxel-denoising network for learning and generation. We extend the neural empirical Bayes formalism (Saremi & Hyvärinen, 2019) to the conditional setting and generate structure-conditioned molecules with a two-step procedure: (i) sample noisy molecules from the Gaussian-smoothed conditional distribution with underdamped Langevin MCMC using the learned score function and (ii) estimate clean molecules from the noisy samples with single-step denoising. Compared to the current state of the art, our model is simpler to train, significantly faster to sample from, and achieves better results on extensive in silico benchmarks—the generated molecules are more diverse, exhibit fewer steric clashes, and bind with higher affinity to protein pockets.
