paragraphs: VoxBind generates three-dimensional molecules conditioned on protein structures. It represents molecules as grids of atomic density and learns with a three-dimensional voxel-denoising network. This connects the generation process directly to a spatial representation of molecules and the protein structures that guide their design.

The method extends neural empirical Bayes to conditional generation and separates generation into two steps. First, underdamped Langevin sampling uses a learned score function to draw noisy molecules from a Gaussian-smoothed conditional distribution. Second, a single denoising step estimates clean molecules from those noisy samples. Sampling and cleaning therefore operate as distinct parts of the procedure.

Compared with the stated current state of the art, the authors report simpler training, significantly faster sampling, and better results on extensive computational benchmarks. The generated molecules are more diverse, have fewer steric clashes, and show higher binding affinity to protein pockets in those evaluations. These are in silico findings, supporting the approach's promise for structure-conditioned molecular generation within the tested computational setting.
summary.tldr: VoxBind generates protein-conditioned molecules by sampling and denoising atomic-density grids, improving speed and molecular properties on computational benchmarks.

title: Structure-based drug design by denoising voxel grids

abstract: A confidence sequence (CS) is a sequence of confidence sets that contains a target parameter of an underlying stochastic process at any time step with high probability. This paper proposes a new approach to constructing CSs for means of bounded multivariate stochastic processes using a general gambling framework, extending the recently established coin toss framework for bounded random processes. The proposed gambling framework provides a general recipe for constructing CSs for categorical and probability-vector-valued observations, as well as for general bounded multidimensional observations through a simple reduction. This paper specifically explores the use of the mixture portfolio, akin to Cover’s universal portfolio, in the proposed framework and investigates the properties of the resulting CSs. Simulations demonstrate the tightness of these confidence sequences compared to existing methods. When applied to the sampling without-replacement setting for finite categorical data, it is shown that the resulting CS based on a universal gambling strategy is provably tighter than that of the posterior-prior ratio martingale proposed by Waudby-Smith and Ramdas.

paragraphs: A confidence sequence provides uncertainty sets that remain valid across time, allowing an analyst to inspect accumulating data without committing to a single stopping point. This paper extends gambling-based constructions from scalar bounded observations to bounded random vectors. The target is the mean of a multivariate stochastic process.

The framework gives constructions for categorical observations and probability vectors, plus a reduction for general bounded multidimensional data. The authors examine mixture-portfolio strategies analogous to Cover’s universal portfolio. These betting strategies determine confidence sets through the statistical guarantees attached to their accumulated performance.

Simulations show tighter confidence sequences than existing methods. For sampling finite categorical data without replacement, the universal-gambling construction is provably tighter than a particular posterior-prior-ratio martingale method. The contribution combines a general multivariate recipe with stronger results in that specific sampling setting; the abstract does not establish that every portfolio choice dominates every alternative confidence sequence.
summary.tldr: A multivariate gambling framework builds time-valid confidence sequences, with tight empirical and without-replacement guarantees.

title: Gambling-Based Confidence Sequences for Bounded Random Vectors

abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of online tracking in linear control systems, where the objective is to follow a moving target. Unlike classical tracking control, the target is unknown, non-stationary, and its state is revealed sequentially, thus, fitting the framework of online non-stochastic control. We consider the case of quadratic costs and propose a new algorithm, called predictive linear online tracking (PLOT). The algorithm uses recursive least squares with exponential forgetting to learn a time-varying dynamic model of the target. The learned model is used in the optimal policy under the framework of receding horizon control. We show the dynamic regret of PLOT scales with $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{TV_T})$, where $V_T$ is the total variation of the target dynamics and $T$ is the time horizon. Unlike prior work, our theoretical results hold for non-stationary targets. We implement our online control algorithm on a real quadrotor, thus, showcasing one of the first successful applications of online control methods on real hardware.

paragraphs: Tracking a moving target becomes difficult when its future motion is unknown and its behavior changes over time. This paper studies that situation for linear control systems with quadratic costs. The target’s state is revealed sequentially, so the controller must learn about its motion while continuing to act.

PLOT learns a changing model of the target using recursive least squares with exponential forgetting. Forgetting reduces the influence of older information, allowing the learned dynamics to adapt. The controller then uses that model within receding horizon control, repeatedly planning ahead using its current prediction of the target.

The authors prove a dynamic regret bound of O(√(T V_T)), where T is the time horizon and V_T measures total variation in the target dynamics. The bound explicitly relates performance to how much the target’s dynamics change and applies to non-stationary targets. They also implement PLOT on a real quadrotor. The contribution combines an adaptive prediction model, a tracking controller, a theoretical guarantee for changing targets, and a demonstration on physical hardware.
summary.tldr: PLOT learns changing target dynamics online, uses them for predictive control, and provides a regret bound plus a quadrotor demonstration.

title: Predictive Linear Online Tracking for Unknown Targets

abstract: Echoing recent calls to counter reliability and robustness concerns in machine learning via multiverse analysis, we present PRESTO, a principled framework for mapping the multiverse of machine-learning models that rely on latent representations. Although such models enjoy widespread adoption, the variability in their embeddings remains poorly understood, resulting in unnecessary complexity and untrustworthy representations. Our framework uses persistent homology to characterize the latent spaces arising from different combinations of diverse machine-learning methods, (hyper)parameter configurations, and datasets, allowing us to measure their pairwise (dis)similarity and statistically reason about their distributions. As we demonstrate both theoretically and empirically, our pipeline preserves desirable properties of collections of latent representations, and it can be leveraged to perform sensitivity analysis, detect anomalous embeddings, or efficiently and effectively navigate hyperparameter search spaces.

paragraphs: Models that learn latent representations can produce different embeddings when methods, datasets, or hyperparameters change. PRESTO treats this collection of possible representations as an object of study. Its goal is to make variability across these choices measurable, helping researchers understand sensitivity rather than examining each embedding in isolation.

The framework uses persistent homology to characterize latent spaces. Those characterizations support pairwise similarity and dissimilarity measurements as well as statistical reasoning about distributions of representations. This creates a common basis for comparing embeddings produced by diverse combinations of modeling and data choices.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that the pipeline preserves desirable properties of collections of latent representations. They also demonstrate uses in sensitivity analysis, anomalous-embedding detection, and efficient hyperparameter search. These applications matter because differences between embeddings can reveal unstable choices or unusual outcomes, while similarities can help organize a search. PRESTO offers a framework for analyzing that wider landscape of learned representations.
summary.tldr: PRESTO uses persistent homology to compare latent representations and support sensitivity analysis, anomaly detection, and hyperparameter search.

title: Mapping the Multiverse of Latent Representations

abstract: While overparameterization in machine learning models offers great benefits in terms of optimization and generalization, it also leads to increased computational requirements as model sizes grow. In this work, we show that by leveraging the inherent low-dimensional structures of data and compressible dynamics within the model parameters, we can reap the benefits of overparameterization without the computational burdens. In practice, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach for deep low-rank matrix completion as well as fine-tuning language models. Our approach is grounded in theoretical findings for deep overparameterized low-rank matrix recovery, where we show that the learning dynamics of each weight matrix are confined to an invariant low-dimensional subspace. Consequently, we can construct and train compact, highly compressed factorizations possessing the same benefits as their overparameterized counterparts. In the context of deep matrix completion, our technique substantially improves training efficiency while retaining the advantages of overparameterization. For language model fine-tuning, we propose a method called "Deep LoRA", which improves the existing low-rank adaptation (LoRA) technique, leading to reduced overfitting and a simplified hyperparameter setup, while maintaining comparable efficiency. We validate the effectiveness of Deep LoRA on natural language tasks, particularly when fine-tuning with limited data.

paragraphs: Overparameterized models can be easier to optimize and generalize well, but their extra parameters increase computation. This paper investigates whether low-dimensional structure in data and training dynamics can preserve those advantages within a much smaller representation. Its theoretical starting point is deep, overparameterized low-rank matrix recovery.

For that setting, the authors show that each weight matrix's learning dynamics remain within an invariant low-dimensional subspace. This allows them to construct compact factorizations that retain the benefits of the larger parameterization. In deep matrix completion, the resulting method substantially improves training efficiency while preserving the advantages attributed to overparameterization.

The reported benefits are less overfitting and a simpler hyperparameter setup at comparable efficiency. Experiments on natural-language tasks support its usefulness, particularly with limited fine-tuning data. The matrix-recovery theory supplies the structural motivation, while the language-model experiments establish the reported practical benefits in adaptation.
summary.tldr: Compressing low-dimensional training dynamics preserves overparameterization benefits in matrix learning and motivates Deep LoRA for less overfitting in language-model adaptation.

title: Compressible Dynamics in Deep Overparameterized Low-Rank Learning & Adaptation

abstract: Text-to-video models have demonstrated substantial potential in robotic decision-making, enabling the imagination of realistic plans of future actions as well as accurate environment simulation. However, one major issue in such models is generalization – models are limited to synthesizing videos subject to language instructions similar to those seen at training time. This is heavily limiting in decision-making, where we seek a powerful world model to synthesize plans of unseen combinations of objects and actions in order to solve previously unseen tasks in new environments. To resolve this issue, we introduce RoboDreamer, an innovative approach for learning a compositional world model by factorizing the video generation. We leverage the natural compositionality of language to parse instructions into a set of lower-level primitives, which we condition a set of models on to generate videos. We illustrate how this factorization naturally enables compositional generalization, by allowing us to formulate a new natural language instruction as a combination of previously seen components. We further show how such a factorization enables us to add additional multimodal goals, allowing us to specify a video we wish to generate given both natural language instructions and a goal image. Our approach can successfully synthesize video plans on unseen goals in the RT-X, enables successful robot execution in simulation, and substantially outperforms monolithic baseline approaches to video generation.

paragraphs: RoboDreamer addresses generalization in video-based world models for robot planning. Such models can imagine future actions as videos, but may struggle when instructions differ from those seen during training. The paper focuses on generating plans for unfamiliar combinations of objects and actions using components already encountered during learning.

The method decomposes natural-language instructions into lower-level primitives and conditions a collection of models on those primitives. This factorizes video generation around language’s compositional structure. A new instruction can then be expressed as a combination of familiar components, providing a mechanism for compositional generalization. The factorization also accommodates a goal image alongside a language instruction.

The authors report successful video-plan generation for unseen goals in RT-X, successful robot execution in simulation, and substantial improvements over monolithic video-generation baselines. These findings connect the compositional design to both generated plans and simulated action execution. The contribution is a world-model architecture that uses instruction structure to support new combinations, including goals specified through both language and images.
summary.tldr: RoboDreamer decomposes instructions into reusable components to generate robot video plans for unseen combinations and goals.

title: RoboDreamer: Learning Compositional World Models for Robot Imagination

abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of estimation and learning under temporal distribution shift. Consider an observation sequence of length $n$, which is a noisy realization of a time-varying ground-truth sequence. Our focus is to develop methods to estimate the groundtruth at the final time-step while providing sharp point-wise estimation error rates. We show that, without prior knowledge on the level of temporal shift, a wavelet soft-thresholding estimator provides an optimal estimation error bound for the groundtruth. Our proposed estimation method generalizes existing researches (Mazetto and Upfal, 2023) by establishing a connection between the sequence’s non-stationarity level and the sparsity in the wavelet-transformed domain. Our theoretical findings are validated by numerical experiments. Additionally, we applied the estimator to derive sparsity-aware excess risk bounds for binary classification under distribution shift and to develop computationally efficient training objectives. As a final contribution, we draw parallels between our results and the classical signal processing problem of total-variation denoising (Mammen and van de Geer 1997; Tibshirani 2014 ), uncovering novel optimal algorithms for such task.

paragraphs: When the process producing observations changes over time, estimating its present state requires separating genuine change from noise. This paper considers a noisy sequence whose underlying truth varies and focuses on estimating that truth at the final time step. Its goal is a sharp guarantee for this particular estimate, rather than an error measure averaged over the whole sequence.

The proposed estimator uses wavelet soft-thresholding, which reduces small coefficients in a transformed representation of the sequence. The analysis connects temporal variation to sparsity in that representation: how the sequence changes is related to how many wavelet coefficients matter. The authors prove an optimal estimation error bound without requiring advance knowledge of the amount of temporal shift.

Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings. The authors also use the estimator to obtain sparsity-aware excess risk bounds for binary classification under changing distributions and to construct efficient training objectives. Finally, connections to total-variation denoising yield additional optimal algorithms, linking adaptive learning from changing data with a classical signal-processing problem.
summary.tldr: A wavelet estimator achieves an optimal error bound for the current state of a changing process without prior knowledge of its temporal shift.

title: Adaptive Estimation and Learning under Temporal Distribution Shift

abstract: Probabilistic verification problems of neural networks are concerned with formally analysing the output distribution of a neural network under a probability distribution of the inputs. Examples of probabilistic verification problems include verifying the demographic parity fairness notion or quantifying the safety of a neural network. We present a new algorithm for solving probabilistic verification problems of neural networks based on an algorithm for computing and iteratively refining lower and upper bounds on probabilities over the outputs of a neural network. By applying state-of-the-art bound propagation and branch and bound techniques from non-probabilistic neural network verification, our algorithm significantly outpaces existing probabilistic verification algorithms, reducing solving times for various benchmarks from the literature from tens of minutes to tens of seconds. Furthermore, our algorithm compares favourably even to dedicated algorithms for restricted probabilistic verification problems. We complement our empirical evaluation with a theoretical analysis, proving that our algorithm is sound and, under mildly restrictive conditions, also complete when using a suitable set of heuristics.

paragraphs: Probabilistic verification asks what can be formally established about a neural network's outputs when its inputs follow a probability distribution. This supports questions such as quantifying safety or checking demographic parity. The objective is to bound probabilities of output events, connecting network behavior to how inputs are distributed.

The proposed algorithm computes lower and upper probability bounds and refines them iteratively. It adapts bound propagation and branch-and-bound techniques from verification methods that do not explicitly reason about probabilities. The progressively tightened bounds provide a way to solve probabilistic verification problems using tools already effective for constraining neural-network outputs.

On several published benchmarks, the method reduces solving times from tens of minutes to tens of seconds. It also compares favorably with specialized algorithms for restricted versions of the problem. The theoretical analysis proves soundness and establishes completeness under mildly restrictive conditions with suitable heuristics. The distinction matters: reliable bounds are proved, while the completeness result depends on the stated conditions and heuristic choices.
summary.tldr: Branch and bound with bound propagation accelerates formal probability checks for neural networks while providing soundness and conditional completeness guarantees.

title: Solving Probabilistic Verification Problems of Neural Networks using Branch and Bound

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer a more energy-efficient alternative to Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) by mimicking biological neural principles, establishing them as a promising approach to mitigate the increasing energy demands of large-scale neural models. However, fully harnessing the capabilities of SNNs remains challenging due to their discrete signal processing and temporal dynamics. ANN-SNN conversion has emerged as a practical approach, enabling SNNs to achieve competitive performance on complex machine learning tasks. In this work, we identify a phenomenon in the ANN-SNN conversion framework, termed temporal misalignment, in which random spike rearrangement across SNN layers leads to performance improvements. Based on this observation, we introduce biologically plausible two-phase probabilistic (TPP) spiking neurons, further enhancing the conversion process. We demonstrate the advantages of our proposed method both theoretically and empirically through comprehensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, CIFAR10-DVS, and ImageNet across a variety of architectures, achieving state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks process discrete events over time and offer a promising route to more energy-efficient neural computation. Converting an artificial neural network into a spiking one is a practical way to obtain competitive performance, but the resulting temporal behavior creates challenges that do not arise in the same form in the original network.

The authors identify temporal misalignment through a revealing observation: randomly rearranging spikes across layers can improve the converted network's performance. This indicates that the arrangement of spikes in time matters for conversion quality. Motivated by that observation, they introduce biologically plausible two-phase probabilistic spiking neurons to improve the conversion process.

The paper supports the proposed method with both theoretical analysis and experiments across several architectures. Evaluations on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CIFAR10-DVS, and ImageNet achieve reported state-of-the-art results. The contribution links a specific temporal phenomenon to a neuron design that improves converted networks, advancing the practical use of spiking models through changes to their signal dynamics.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies temporal misalignment in converted spiking networks and introduces probabilistic neurons that improve conversion performance.

title: Temporal Misalignment in ANN-SNN Conversion and its Mitigation via Probabilistic Spiking Neurons

abstract: Federated Prompt Learning (FPL) adapts pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to federated learning through prompt tuning, leveraging their transferable representations and strong generalization capabilities. Traditional methods often require uniform prompt lengths for federated aggregation, limiting adaptability to clients with diverse prompt lengths and distribution biases. In this paper, we propose Federated Prompt Learning for Heterogeneous Client Adaptation (FedPHA), a novel framework that combines a fixed-length global prompt for efficient aggregation with local prompts of varying lengths to capture client-specific data characteristics. Additionally, FedPHA designs Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) based projection and bidirectional alignment to disentangle global conflicts arising from client heterogeneity, ensuring that personalized client tasks effectively utilize non-harmful global knowledge. This approach ensures that global knowledge improves model generalization while local knowledge preserves local optimization. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of FedPHA in achieving a balance between global and personalized knowledge in federated learning scenarios.

paragraphs: Federated prompt learning adapts pretrained vision-language models across clients by tuning prompts. A common constraint is that prompts must have the same length so they can be aggregated. The paper argues that this restricts adaptation when clients differ both in their preferred prompt lengths and in the distributions of their local data.

FedPHA separates the shared and personalized parts of the prompt. A fixed-length global prompt supports aggregation across clients, while local prompts can vary in length to capture client-specific characteristics. This arrangement allows a common mechanism for sharing knowledge without requiring every client’s personalized prompt to take the same form.

The framework also uses a projection based on singular value decomposition and bidirectional alignment to disentangle conflicts in global knowledge caused by client differences. These mechanisms are intended to let personalized tasks use beneficial shared knowledge while preserving local optimization. Experiments validate the approach’s ability to balance global and personalized information. The contribution combines flexibility in local prompts with explicit handling of conflicting information during knowledge sharing.
summary.tldr: FedPHA combines a shared fixed-length prompt with variable-length local prompts and alignment mechanisms to support heterogeneous federated clients.

title: FedPHA: Federated Prompt Learning for Heterogeneous Client Adaptation

abstract: As Language Model (LM) capabilities advance, evaluating and supervising them at scale is getting harder for humans. There is hope that other language models can automate both these tasks, which we refer to as AI Oversight. We study how model similarity affects both aspects of AI oversight by proposing Chance Adjusted Probabilistic Agreement (CAPA)–a metric for LM similarity based on overlap in model mistakes. Using CAPA, we first show that LLM-as-a-judge scores favor models similar to the judge, generalizing recent self-preference results. Then, we study training on LM annotations, and find complementary knowledge between the weak supervisor and strong student model plays a crucial role in gains from weak-to-strong generalization. As model capabilities increase, it becomes harder to find their mistakes, and we might defer more to AI oversight. However, we observe a concerning trend–model mistakes are becoming more similar with increasing capabilities, pointing to risks from correlated failures. Our work underscores the importance of reporting and correcting for model similarity, especially in the emerging paradigm of AI oversight.

paragraphs: Using language models to evaluate and supervise other models could ease the burden of human oversight. This paper studies a potential weakness in that arrangement: models may make similar mistakes. The authors introduce Chance Adjusted Probabilistic Agreement, or CAPA, to measure model similarity through overlap in their errors.

With this metric, they find that language-model judges favor models similar to themselves. The effect extends beyond a judge preferring its own outputs. They also examine learning from model-generated annotations, finding that complementary knowledge between a weaker supervisor and a stronger student plays a crucial role in weak-to-strong generalization gains. What the supervisor knows differently therefore matters alongside its overall capability.

The study observes that mistakes become more similar as model capabilities increase. At the same time, more capable models can be harder for humans to assess, encouraging greater reliance on automated oversight. This combination points to correlated-failure risks. The findings motivate reporting and correcting for model similarity when evaluating judges or choosing models to provide supervision.
summary.tldr: Shared mistakes can bias model-based judging and weaken supervision, making model similarity an important factor in AI oversight.

title: Great Models Think Alike and this Undermines AI Oversight

abstract: Robustness to outliers is important in machine learning. Many classical problems, including subspace embedding, clustering, and low-rank approximation, lack scalable, outlier-resilient algorithms. This paper considers machine learning problems of the form $\min_{x\in \mathbb{R}^d} F(x)$, where $F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n F_i(x)$, and their robust counterparts $\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d} F^{(m)}(x)$, where $F^{(m)}(x)$ denotes the sum of all but the $m$ largest $F_i(x)$ values. We develop a general framework for constructing $\epsilon$-coresets for such robust problems, where an $\epsilon$-coreset is a weighted subset of functions $\{F_1(x),…,F_n(x)\}$ that provides a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation to $F(x)$. Specifically, if the original problem $F$ has total sensitivity $T$ and admits a vanilla $\epsilon$-coreset of size $S$, our algorithm constructs an $\epsilon$-coreset of size $\tilde{O}(\frac{mT}{\epsilon})+S$ for the robust objective $F^{(m)}$. This coreset size can be shown to be near-tight for $\ell_2$ subspace embedding. Our coreset algorithm has scalable running time and leads to new or improved algorithms for the robust optimization problems. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our coresets outperform uniform sampling on real-world data sets.

paragraphs: Many optimization problems add together costs contributed by individual data points. A robust version can discard the largest m costs, reducing the influence of outliers. This paper develops a general way to compress such robust objectives into weighted subsets, called coresets, while preserving an approximation guarantee.

The construction starts from properties of the original, untrimmed problem. If its total sensitivity is T and it admits a standard coreset of size S, the robust coreset has size roughly mT divided by the approximation tolerance, plus S, with logarithmic factors suppressed. This explicitly relates the extra compression cost of robustness to the number of discarded contributions and the sensitivity of the original objective.

For Euclidean subspace embedding, the authors show that the coreset size is near-tight. They also report scalable running time and new or improved algorithms for robust optimization problems. On real datasets, the resulting coresets outperform uniform sampling. The framework makes robust compression depend on reusable properties of the underlying non-robust problem.
summary.tldr: A sensitivity-based framework constructs compact weighted approximations for objectives that discard outliers, with near-tight size guarantees for Euclidean subspace embedding.

title: Robust Sparsification via Sensitivity

abstract: Divergence-free symmetric tensors (DFSTs) are fundamental in continuum mechanics, encoding conservation laws such as mass and momentum conservation. We introduce Riemann Tensor Neural Networks (RTNNs), a novel neural architecture that inherently satisfies the DFST condition to machine precision, providing a strong inductive bias for enforcing these conservation laws. We prove that RTNNs can approximate any sufficiently smooth DFST with arbitrary precision and demonstrate their effectiveness as surrogates for conservative PDEs, achieving improved accuracy across benchmarks. This work is the first to use DFSTs as an inductive bias in neural PDE surrogates and to explicitly enforce the conservation of both mass and momentum within a physics-constrained neural architecture.

We prove that RTNNs can approximate any sufficiently smooth DFST with arbitrary precision and demonstrate their effectiveness as surrogates for conservative PDEs, achieving improved accuracy across benchmarks. This work is the first to use DFSTs as an inductive bias in neural PDE surrogates and to explicitly enforce the conservation of both mass and momentum within a physics-constrained neural architecture.

paragraphs: Conservation laws constrain how physical systems can evolve. In continuum mechanics, divergence-free symmetric tensors provide a mathematical representation of conservation properties such as mass and momentum conservation. Riemann Tensor Neural Networks, or RTNNs, build this tensor condition into the architecture, making physical structure a direct constraint on the functions the network can represent.

The architecture satisfies the divergence-free symmetric tensor condition to machine precision. The authors also prove that RTNNs can approximate any sufficiently smooth tensor satisfying that condition to arbitrary precision. The smoothness qualification matters: the approximation result applies to the stated class of tensors. Together, these results combine built-in physical consistency with expressive capacity within that class.

The authors evaluate RTNNs as learned surrogates for conservative partial differential equations and report improved accuracy across benchmarks. Their contribution explicitly enforces both mass and momentum conservation through a physics-constrained neural architecture. The findings support using conservation structure as an inductive bias: it shapes the model’s possible outputs while retaining the ability to approximate a broad class of physically compatible functions.
summary.tldr: RTNNs enforce divergence-free symmetric tensor structure to machine precision and improve conservative-PDE surrogate accuracy in the reported benchmarks.

title: Riemann Tensor Neural Networks: Learning Conservative Systems with Physics-Constrained Networks

abstract: The field of mechanistic interpretability in pre-trained transformer models has demonstrated substantial evidence supporting the ”linear representation hypothesis”, which is the idea that high level concepts are encoded as vectors in the space of activations of a model. Studies also show that model generation behavior can be steered toward a given concept by adding the concept’s vector to the corresponding activations. We show how to leverage these properties to build a form of logical implication into models, enabling transparent and interpretable adjustments that induce a chosen generation behavior in response to the presence of any given concept. Our method, Logical Implication Model Steering (LIMS), unlocks new hand-engineered reasoning capabilities by integrating neuro-symbolic logic into pre-trained transformer models.

Studies also show that model generation behavior can be steered toward a given concept by adding the concept’s vector to the corresponding activations. paragraphs: This paper builds on evidence for the linear representation hypothesis: high-level concepts can be represented by vectors in a Transformer’s internal activations. Prior steering work shows that adding a concept vector can shift generated text toward that concept. The authors use these ideas to construct interventions whose effects depend on a concept being present.

Logical Implication Model Steering, or LIMS, builds a form of logical implication into generation. A selected concept serves as the condition, and a chosen generation behavior serves as the response. This makes the intended relationship between trigger and intervention explicit, providing a transparent way to describe the adjustment being introduced.

The contribution combines symbolic logical structure with the internal representations of a pretrained neural model. The authors describe it as enabling new hand-engineered reasoning capabilities through interpretable adjustments. Its significance lies in making steering conditional: the intervention is organized around when a concept should cause a particular behavior. The abstract presents this as a form of logical implication within generation, without claiming a general guarantee of logical correctness.
summary.tldr: LIMS uses concept representations to conditionally steer Transformer generation through interpretable logical-implication interventions.

title: The Logical Implication Steering Method for Conditional Interventions on Transformer Generation

abstract: Post-training quantization is a key technique for reducing the memory and inference latency of large language models by quantizing weights and activations without requiring retraining. However, existing methods either (1) fail to account for the varying importance of hidden features to the end loss or, when incorporating end loss, (2) neglect the critical interactions between model weights. To address these limitations, we propose GuidedQuant, a novel quantization approach that integrates gradient information from the end loss into the quantization objective while preserving cross-weight dependencies within output channels. GuidedQuant consistently boosts the performance of state-of-the-art quantization methods across weight-only scalar, weight-only vector, and weight-and-activation quantization. Additionally, we introduce a novel non-uniform scalar quantization algorithm, which is guaranteed to monotonically decrease the quantization objective value, and outperforms existing methods in this category. We release the code at https://github.com/snu-mllab/GuidedQuant.

To address these limitations, we propose GuidedQuant, a novel quantization approach that integrates gradient information from the end loss into the quantization objective while preserving cross-weight dependencies within output channels. GuidedQuant consistently boosts the performance of state-of-the-art quantization methods across weight-only scalar, weight-only vector, and weight-and-activation quantization. paragraphs: Quantizing a language model reduces the precision of its weights or activations to lower memory requirements and inference latency. The paper argues that good quantization decisions need two kinds of information: how much hidden features matter to the final loss, and how changes to different weights interact with one another.

GuidedQuant brings gradients from the final loss into its quantization objective while retaining dependencies between weights within output channels. This connects local numerical approximations to their importance for the model’s end objective. Preserving weight interactions also avoids treating every weight change as if its effect could be assessed independently.

The authors report consistent improvements to state-of-the-art methods across weight-only scalar quantization, weight-only vector quantization, and joint weight-and-activation quantization. They additionally introduce a non-uniform scalar quantization algorithm that is guaranteed to monotonically decrease its quantization objective and outperforms existing methods in that category. That guarantee concerns the specified optimization objective; the broader performance improvements are supported by the reported experiments across quantization settings.
summary.tldr: GuidedQuant improves LLM quantization by combining final-loss gradients with dependencies between weights.

title: GuidedQuant: Large Language Model Quantization via Exploiting End Loss Guidance

abstract: Reward shaping has been demonstrated to be an effective technique for accelerating the learning process of reinforcement learning (RL) agents. While successful in empirical applications, the design of a good shaping function is less well understood in principle and thus often relies on domain expertise and manual design. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel automated approach for designing reward functions from offline data, possibly contaminated with the unobserved confounding bias.We propose to use causal state value upper bounds calculated from offline datasets as a conservative optimistic estimation of the optimal state value, which is then used as state potentials in Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS). When applying our shaping function to a model-free learner based on UCB principles, we show that it enjoys a better gap-dependent regret bound than the learner without shaping. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first gap-dependent regret bound for PBRS in model-free learning with online exploration. Simulations support the theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Reward shaping helps reinforcement-learning agents learn faster by supplementing the feedback they receive. Choosing useful shaping signals often depends on manual design and domain knowledge. This paper develops an automated alternative that draws on previously collected data, including data that may be biased by unobserved factors affecting the recorded outcomes.

The method calculates causal upper bounds on state values from the offline dataset. These bounds provide optimistic estimates of how valuable states could be while accounting for possible confounding. The estimates become state potentials in potential-based reward shaping, providing the learner with an additional signal derived from the offline evidence.

The theoretical result applies when this shaping function is used with a model-free learner based on upper-confidence-bound principles. In that setting, the authors establish a better gap-dependent regret bound than for the learner without shaping. This concerns accumulated learning performance during online exploration. Simulations support the analysis, suggesting that appropriately constructed bounds can turn imperfect historical data into useful guidance for subsequent learning.
summary.tldr: Causal value bounds from potentially confounded offline data provide automated reward shaping with improved regret guarantees for a specified learner.

title: Automatic Reward Shaping from Confounded Offline Data

abstract: We present a novel self-supervised feature learning method using Vision Transformers (ViT) as the backbone, specifically designed for object detection and instance segmentation. Our approach addresses the challenge of extracting features that capture both class and positional information, which are crucial for these tasks. The method introduces two key components: (1) a positional encoding tied to the cropping process in contrastive learning, which utilizes a novel vector field representation for positional embeddings; and (2) masking and prediction, similar to conventional Masked Image Modeling (MIM), applied in parallel to both content and positional embeddings of image patches. These components enable the effective learning of intertwined content and positional features. We evaluate our method against state-of-the-art approaches, pre-training on ImageNet-1K and fine-tuning on downstream tasks. Our method outperforms the state-of-the-art SSL methods on the COCO object detection benchmark, achieving significant improvements with fewer pre-training epochs. These results suggest that better integration of positional information into self-supervised learning can improve performance on the dense prediction tasks.
originalAbstract: We present a novel self-supervised feature learning method using Vision Transformers (ViT) as the backbone, specifically designed for object detection and instance segmentation. Our approach addresses the challenge of extracting features that capture both class and positional information, which are crucial for these tasks. The method introduces two key components: (1) a positional encoding tied to the cropping process in contrastive learning, which utilizes a novel vector field representation for positional embeddings; and (2) masking and prediction, similar to conventional Masked Image Modeling (MIM), applied in parallel to both content and positional embeddings of image patches. These components enable the effective learning of intertwined content and positional features. We evaluate our method against state-of-the-art approaches, pre-training on ImageNet-1K and fine-tuning on downstream tasks. Our method outperforms the state-of-the-art SSL methods on the COCO object detection benchmark, achieving significant improvements with fewer pre-training epochs. These results suggest that better integration of positional information into self-supervised learning can improve performance on the dense prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Object detection and instance segmentation need representations that capture both what an object is and where it is located. This paper develops self-supervised learning for a Vision Transformer with those joint requirements in mind. Its focus is on integrating positional information into feature learning rather than treating location as an incidental addition.

The method introduces positional encoding tied to the cropping process used in contrastive learning, with positions represented through a vector field. It also masks and predicts both content embeddings and positional embeddings of image patches in parallel. These two components encourage the model to learn intertwined representations of visual content and spatial position.

The authors pretrain on ImageNet-1K and then fine-tune for downstream tasks. On COCO object detection, their approach surpasses leading self-supervised methods while using fewer pretraining epochs. This supports the idea that richer positional learning can improve representations for dense prediction. The result connects the pretraining objective to the downstream need to recognize objects and localize them, rather than learning class-related content alone.
summary.tldr: Joint self-supervised learning of content and position improves object detection while requiring fewer pretraining epochs in the reported comparison.

title: Self-Supervised Learning of Intertwined Content and Positional Features for Object Detection

abstract: We continue to study the learning-theoretic foundations of generation by extending the results from Kleinberg and Mullainathan [2024] and Li et al. [2024] to account for noisy example streams. In the noiseless setting of Kleinberg and Mullainathan [2024] and Li et al. [2024], an adversary picks a hypothesis from a binary hypothesis class and provides a generator with a sequence of its positive examples. The goal of the generator is to eventually output new, unseen positive examples. In the noisy setting, an adversary still picks a hypothesis and a sequence of its positive examples. But, before presenting the stream to the generator, the adversary inserts a finite number of negative examples. Unaware of which examples are noisy, the goal of the generator is to still eventually output new, unseen positive examples. In this paper, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions for when a binary hypothesis class can be noisily generatable. We provide such conditions with respect to various constraints on the number of distinct examples that need to be seen before perfect generation of positive examples. Interestingly, for finite and countable classes we show that generatability is largely unaffected by the presence of a finite number of noisy examples.

paragraphs: This paper studies a theoretical version of learning to generate new valid examples. An adversary chooses a rule from a binary hypothesis class and supplies examples that satisfy it. The generator’s eventual goal is to produce new positive examples it has not already seen. The paper extends this setup to streams containing misleading examples.

The noise model is specific: the adversary inserts a finite number of negative examples into a stream of positive ones, and the generator does not know which entries are wrong. The authors give necessary and sufficient conditions for a hypothesis class to permit successful generation despite that corruption. They consider different constraints on how many distinct examples must be observed before generation becomes perfectly positive.

For finite and countable hypothesis classes, the authors find that generatability is largely unchanged by a finite number of noisy examples. This establishes a form of robustness for the theoretical generation problem. Its scope depends on eventual success and finite corruption; the result concerns whether reliable novel generation is possible under those conditions.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes when generators can eventually produce unseen positive examples despite finitely many hidden negative examples in their input stream.

title: Generation from Noisy Examples

abstract: Sparse tensor programs are essential in deep learning and graph analytics, driving the need for optimized processing. To meet this demand, specialized hardware accelerators are being developed. Optimizing these programs for accelerators is challenging for two reasons: program performance is highly sensitive to variations in sparse inputs, and early-stage accelerators rely on expensive simulators. Therefore, ML-based cost models used for optimizing such programs on general-purpose hardware are often ineffective for early-stage accelerators, as they require large datasets for proper training. To this end, we introduce COGNATE, a novel framework that leverages inexpensive data samples from general-purpose hardware (e.g., CPUs) to train cost models, followed by few-shot fine-tuning on emerging hardware. COGNATE exploits the homogeneity of input features across hardware platforms while effectively mitigating heterogeneity, enabling cost model training with just 5% of the data samples needed by accelerator-specific models to achieve comparable performance. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate that COGNATE outperforms existing techniques, achieving average speedups of 1.47$\times$ (up to 5.46$\times$) for SpMM and 1.39$\times$ (up to 4.22$\times$) for SDDMM.

Meanwhile, early accelerator development often depends on expensive simulators, making it costly to collect enough performance measurements to train a useful optimization cost model.

COGNATE first trains cost models using inexpensive samples from general-purpose hardware such as CPUs, then adapts them with a small amount of data from the emerging hardware. These results connect reduced training-data requirements with improvements in the execution speed of the optimized sparse programs.
summary.tldr: COGNATE transfers cost models from general-purpose hardware to emerging accelerators, reducing data needs and accelerating sparse tensor programs.

title: COGNATE: Acceleration of Sparse Tensor Programs on Emerging Hardware using Transfer Learning

abstract: Diffusion-based purification (DBP) methods aim to remove adversarial noise from the input sample by first injecting Gaussian noise through a forward diffusion process, and then recovering the clean example through a reverse generative process. In the above process, how much Gaussian noise is injected to the input sample is key to the success of DBP methods, which is controlled by a constant noise level $t*$ for all samples in existing methods. In this paper, we discover that an optimal $t*$ for each sample indeed could be different. Intuitively, the cleaner a sample is, the less the noise it should be injected, and vice versa. Motivated by this finding, we propose a new framework, called Sample-specific Score-aware Noise Injection (SSNI). Specifically, SSNI uses a pre-trained score network to estimate how much a data point deviates from the clean data distribution (i.e., score norms). Then, based on the magnitude of score norms, SSNI applies a reweighting function to adaptively adjust $t*$ for each sample, achieving sample-specific noise injections. Empirically, incorporating our framework with existing DBP methods results in a notable improvement in both accuracy and robustness on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1K, highlighting the necessity to allocate distinct noise levels to different samples in DBP methods. Our code is available at: https://github.com/tmlr-group/SSNI.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based adversarial purification first adds Gaussian noise to an input and then uses a reverse generative process to recover a clean example. The amount of added noise is crucial. This paper finds that the best amount can vary between samples, challenging the use of one fixed noise level for every input.

The proposed Sample-specific Score-aware Noise Injection framework, or SSNI, uses a pretrained score network to estimate how far an input deviates from the clean-data distribution. It uses score norms as this signal, then applies a reweighting function to choose the noise level for each sample. The motivation is that cleaner inputs should generally need less added noise than more corrupted ones.

When incorporated into existing purification methods, SSNI improves both accuracy and robustness on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1K. The contribution changes how purification effort is allocated across samples while working with existing diffusion-based methods. The empirical findings support adapting the noise level to the input instead of treating all samples as requiring the same intervention.
summary.tldr: SSNI adapts diffusion-purification noise to each input using score norms, improving reported accuracy and robustness.

title: Sample-specific Noise Injection for Diffusion-based Adversarial Purification

abstract: Deep latent variable models learn condensed representations of data that, hopefully, reflect the inner workings of the studied phenomena. Unfortunately, these latent representations are not statistically identifiable, meaning they cannot be uniquely determined. Domain experts, therefore, need to tread carefully when interpreting these. Current solutions limit the lack of identifiability through additional constraints on the latent variable model, e.g. by requiring labeled training data, or by restricting the expressivity of the model. We change the goal: instead of identifying the latent variables, we identify relationships between them such as meaningful distances, angles, and volumes. We prove this is feasible under very mild model conditions and without additional labeled data. We empirically demonstrate that our theory results in more reliable latent distances, offering a principled path forward in extracting trustworthy conclusions from deep latent variable models.

paragraphs: Deep latent variable models compress observations into representations that researchers may want to interpret as underlying properties of a phenomenon. A problem arises when those representations are not statistically identifiable: the observed data do not uniquely determine the latent variables. Consequently, an interpretation tied to a particular representation may lack a unique statistical basis.

This paper changes the object of identification to relationships within the representation. It asks whether meaningful distances, angles, and volumes can be determined even when the latent variables themselves cannot. The authors prove that this is possible under very mild model conditions and without requiring additional labeled data.

Empirical results show that the theory produces more reliable latent distances. This offers a way to extract interpretable information from models whose individual latent coordinates remain ambiguous. The contribution is a principled basis for studying geometric relationships, broadening what researchers can meaningfully conclude without first imposing the extra labels or expressivity restrictions used by other approaches.
summary.tldr: Meaningful latent distances, angles, and volumes can be identifiable under mild conditions even when latent variables are not.

title: Identifying Metric Structures of Deep Latent Variable Models

abstract: To fully leverage the capabilities of diffusion models, we are often interested in optimizing downstream reward functions during inference. While numerous algorithms for reward-guided generation have been recently proposed due to their significance, current approaches predominantly focus on single-shot generation, transitioning from fully noised to denoised states. We propose a novel framework for inference-time reward optimization with diffusion models. Our approach employs an iterative refinement process consisting of two steps in each iteration: noising and reward-guided denoising. This sequential refinement allows for the gradual correction of errors introduced during reward optimization. Finally, we provide a theoretical guarantee for our framework. Finally, we demonstrate its superior empirical performance in protein and DNA design.

While numerous algorithms for reward-guided generation have been recently proposed due to their significance, current approaches predominantly focus on single-shot generation, transitioning from fully noised to denoised states. We propose a novel framework for inference-time reward optimization with diffusion models. Our approach employs an iterative refinement process consisting of two steps in each iteration: noising and reward-guided denoising. paragraphs: A diffusion model’s output may need to satisfy a downstream objective measured by a reward function. This paper studies how to optimize that reward during inference. Many existing reward-guided methods generate a sample in one progression from a fully noisy state to a denoised result, concentrating optimization into that single generation process.

The proposed framework repeatedly refines a candidate. Each iteration first adds noise and then performs reward-guided denoising. Repeating these two steps allows errors introduced during reward optimization to be corrected gradually. This makes refinement an ongoing process in which the generated result can be revisited through further noising and denoising.

The authors provide a theoretical guarantee for the framework and report superior empirical performance in protein and DNA design. These applications demonstrate the approach in settings where generation is evaluated through downstream design objectives. The contribution is an inference-time optimization framework that uses repeated refinement to improve reward-directed generation, with support from both theory and the reported biological design experiments.
summary.tldr: Repeated noising and reward-guided denoising let diffusion models refine candidates during inference, with theoretical support and reported gains in protein and DNA design.

title: Reward-Guided Iterative Refinement in Diffusion Models at Test-Time with Applications to Protein and DNA Design

abstract: Estimating causal effects is crucial in domains like healthcare, economics, and education. Despite advances in machine learning (ML) for estimating conditional average treatment effects (CATE), the practical adoption of these methods remains limited, due to the complexities of implementing, tuning, and validating them. To address these challenges, we formalize the search for an optimal ML pipeline for CATE estimation as a counterfactual Combined Algorithm Selection and Hyperparameter (CASH) optimization. We introduce AutoCATE, the first end-to-end, automated solution for CATE estimation. Unlike prior approaches that address only parts of this problem, AutoCATE integrates evaluation, estimation, and ensembling in a unified framework. AutoCATE enables comprehensive comparisons of different protocols, yielding novel insights into CATE estimation and a final configuration that outperforms commonly used strategies. To facilitate broad adoption and further research, we release AutoCATE as an open-source software package.

paragraphs: AutoCATE addresses the practical work involved in estimating how treatment effects vary with observed characteristics. Although machine learning offers methods for conditional average treatment effect estimation, choosing, tuning, and validating those methods can make adoption difficult. The paper treats those connected decisions as a single automated pipeline selection problem.

The authors formulate this search as counterfactual Combined Algorithm Selection and Hyperparameter optimization. In plain language, the system searches over both the estimation approach and its settings within a framework designed for treatment effect estimation. AutoCATE brings evaluation, estimation, and ensembling together, so automation covers the full process described in the paper.

The unified framework also makes it possible to compare different protocols systematically. The authors report that these comparisons yield insights into treatment effect estimation and a final configuration that performs better than commonly used strategies. They release an open-source package to support use and further research. The contribution is an integrated way to organize and automate methodological choices that otherwise require substantial implementation effort.
summary.tldr: AutoCATE automates evaluation, estimator selection, tuning, and ensembling for conditional treatment effect estimation in one framework.

title: AutoCATE: End-to-End, Automated Treatment Effect Estimation

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in text and multimodal processing, yet they fundamentally lack physical awareness–understanding of real-world physical phenomena. In this work, we present ACORN, a framework that teaches LLMs physical awareness through sound, focusing on fundamental physical phenomena like the Doppler effect, multipath effect, and spatial relationships. To overcome data scarcity, ACORN introduce a physics-based simulator combining real-world sound sources with controlled physical channels to generate diverse training data. Using this simulator, we build AQA-PHY, a comprehensive Audio Question-Answer dataset, and propose an audio encoder that processes both magnitude and phase information. By connecting our audio encoder to state-of-the-art LLMs, we demonstrate reasonable results in both simulated and real-world tasks, such as line-of-sight detection, Doppler effect estimation, and Direction-of-Arrival estimation, paving the way for enabling LLMs to understand physical world.

paragraphs: Sound carries information about physical conditions, including motion, propagation paths, and spatial relationships. ACORN aims to teach language models to interpret such information, focusing on phenomena including the Doppler effect and multipath effects. The paper treats audio as a source of evidence about the physical world, extending beyond recognition of spoken content.

To address scarce training data, the authors create a physics-based simulator that combines real sound sources with controlled physical channels. They use it to construct AQA-PHY, an audio question-answering dataset. The framework also introduces an audio encoder that processes both magnitude and phase information, then connects that encoder to existing language models.

The authors report reasonable results on simulated and real-world tasks involving line-of-sight detection, Doppler-effect estimation, and direction-of-arrival estimation. These findings provide evidence that the framework can learn useful physical cues from sound in the studied settings. The contribution combines controlled data generation with an audio representation designed to retain physical information, offering a route toward broader physical awareness without claiming that the problem is solved.
summary.tldr: ACORN combines simulated physical acoustics and magnitude-and-phase audio encoding to teach language models to infer physical properties from sound.

title: Teaching Physical Awareness to LLMs through Sounds

abstract: Semi-supervised Federated Learning (SSFL) is a promising approach that allows clients to collaboratively train a global model in the absence of their local data labels. The key step of SSFL is the re-labeling where each client adopts two types of available models, namely global and local models, to re-label the local data. While various technologies such as using the global model or the average of two models have been proposed to conduct the re-labeling step, little literature delves deeply into the performance dominance and limitations of the two models. In this paper, we first theoretically and empirically demonstrate that the local model achieves higher re-labeling accuracy over local data while the global model can progressively improve the re-labeling performance by introducing the extra data knowledge of other clients. Based on these findings, we propose BSemiFL which re-labels the local data through the collaboration between the local and global model in a Bayesian approach. Specifically, to re-label any given local sample, BSemiFL first uses Bayesian inference to assess the closeness of the local/global model to the sample. Then, it applies a weighted combination of their pseudo labels, using the closeness as the weights. Theoretical analysis shows that the labeling error of our method is smaller than that of simply using the global model, the local model, or their simple average. Experimental results show that BSemiFL improves the performance by up to $9.8%$ as compared to state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: BSemiFL addresses how clients should assign training labels to their unlabeled data when learning a shared model together. Each client has access to a local model and a global model informed by other clients. Choosing which model to trust matters because these models bring different kinds of knowledge to the same sample.

The paper’s theoretical and empirical analysis finds that local models label their own data more accurately, while the global model can progressively improve labeling by contributing knowledge from other clients. BSemiFL turns this complementary relationship into a sample-specific decision. Bayesian inference estimates how closely each model relates to a particular sample, and those estimates determine the weights used to combine their proposed labels.

The theoretical analysis establishes lower labeling error than using either model alone or averaging them equally. Experiments report performance improvements of up to 9.8% over state-of-the-art methods. The contribution is a principled way to balance local familiarity with shared knowledge during the labeling step that supports subsequent collaborative training.
summary.tldr: BSemiFL uses Bayesian, sample-specific weighting of local and global predictions to improve labels for semi-supervised federated learning.

title: BSemiFL: Semi-supervised Federated Learning via a Bayesian Approach

abstract: In combinatorial semi-bandits, a learner repeatedly selects from a combinatorial decision set of arms, receives the realized sum of rewards, and observes the rewards of the individual selected arms as feedback. In this paper, we extend this framework to include graph feedback, where the learner observes the rewards of all neighboring arms of the selected arms in a feedback graph $G$. We establish that the optimal regret over a time horizon $T$ scales as $\widetilde{\Theta}(S\sqrt{T}+\sqrt{\alpha ST})$, where $S$ is the size of the combinatorial decisions and $\alpha$ is the independence number of $G$. This result interpolates between the known regrets $\widetilde\Theta(S\sqrt{T})$ under full information (i.e., $G$ is complete) and $\widetilde\Theta(\sqrt{KST})$ under the semi-bandit feedback (i.e., $G$ has only self-loops), where $K$ is the total number of arms. A key technical ingredient is to realize a convexified action using a random decision vector with negative correlations. We also show that online stochastic mirror descent (OSMD) that only realizes convexified actions in expectation is suboptimal. In addition, we describe the problem of combinatorial semi-bandits with general capacity and apply our results to derive an improved regret upper bound, which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: The paper studies repeated decisions in which a learner chooses several options, called arms, at once. Ordinary semi-bandit feedback reveals the rewards of the selected arms. Here, a graph adds information: selecting an arm also reveals rewards for its neighbors. The question is how this extra visibility changes the difficulty of learning.

The authors establish an optimal regret rate of S√T + √(αST), up to logarithmic factors. Regret measures the learner’s accumulated shortfall relative to the best fixed decision. Here, S is the number of selected arms, T is the time horizon, and α is the graph’s independence number. The result connects the known full-information and ordinary semi-bandit rates.

A crucial ingredient is how a fractional decision becomes an actual random selection: the selected components must have suitable negative correlations. The authors show that merely matching the fractional action in expectation within online stochastic mirror descent is suboptimal. They also derive an improved regret upper bound for a general-capacity version of the problem.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes optimal regret for combinatorial semi-bandits with graph feedback and shows why correlations in randomized decisions matter.

title: Adversarial Combinatorial Semi-bandits with Graph Feedback

abstract: Large language models (LLMs)  excel in many reasoning tasks but continue to face significant challenges, such as lack of robustness in reasoning, struggling with cross-task generalization, and inefficiencies in scaling up reasoning capabilities. Current training paradigms, including next-token prediction and reinforcement learning from human feedback, often fall short in adaptability to diverse reasoning tasks. Existing approaches, such as prompt optimization and iterative output refinement, offer performance improvement, but can be inefficient and lack effective generalization. To overcome these limitations, this position paper argues for a transformative shift in how LLMs approach reasoning. Drawing inspiration from cognitive science, particularly meta-reasoning theories such as Dual-Process Theory and Metacognitive Reasoning, we propose a Bayesian meta-reasoning framework for LLMs. Our approach integrates self-awareness, monitoring, evaluation, regulation, and meta-reflection, to enhance LLMs' ability to refine reasoning strategies and generalize across tasks. We revisit existing LLM reasoning methods, identify key challenges, and suggest  directions for future research.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that language models need better ways to manage their own reasoning. Although they perform well on many tasks, the authors identify persistent difficulties with robustness, transferring reasoning across tasks, and efficiently expanding reasoning capabilities. Improving prompts or repeatedly revising answers can help, but these approaches can be inefficient and generalize poorly.

The proposed direction is a Bayesian framework for meta-reasoning: reasoning about how to reason. Drawing on cognitive science, including Dual-Process Theory and Metacognitive Reasoning, the framework brings together self-awareness, monitoring, evaluation, regulation, and reflection. These components are intended to help a model examine and adjust its reasoning strategies.

The central motivation is adaptability across different reasoning demands. A model would have mechanisms for assessing its approach and refining that approach as part of the reasoning process. The paper revisits existing methods, identifies challenges, and outlines future research directions; it presents the framework as a proposed path toward stronger reasoning and cross-task generalization.
summary.tldr: The authors propose Bayesian meta-reasoning to help language models monitor, evaluate, and adapt their reasoning strategies across tasks.

title: Position: LLMs Need a Bayesian Meta-Reasoning Framework for More Robust and Generalizable Reasoning

abstract: Consistency training encourages a model to produce similar outputs across related inputs or sampling procedures. Such methods are simple, scalable, and largely label-free, but their effects on model alignment remain poorly understood. Could the self-bootstrapping nature of these methods amplify undesired behavior in models? We test seven consistency training methods on 108 model organisms: open-source models (7B–70B) fine-tuned to exhibit various forms of controlled misaligned behavior. We find that outcomes vary significantly: consistency training generally suppresses reward hacking and emergent misalignment but amplifies sycophancy. We present evidence that distribution shifts induced by the consistency labeling process, rather than variation in the selection operators, may be the primary driver of systematic alignment effects. Finally, we present a unifying theoretical framework to derive conditions under which consistency training will amplify or suppress misalignment. In total, our study establishes that consistency training is not alignment-neutral, and that its use in critical systems should be carefully audited.

The findings motivate auditing consistency training in critical applications, with attention to which behaviors its labeling process reinforces.
summary.tldr: Consistency training has behavior-dependent alignment effects, generally reducing some misalignment while amplifying sycophancy in controlled experiments.

title: Consistency Training Can Entrench Misalignment

abstract: We work in the adaptive query model, where one is given a point set $P \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ and seeks to construct a data structure that can answer correctly and efficiently a sequence of adaptive queries. In this model, an adversary observes the answers returned by the data structure to previous queries $q_1, \ldots, q_{i-1}$ and, based on this information, chooses the next query point $q_i$. This setting captures strong forms of adaptivity that naturally arise in modern machine learning pipelines, and rules out many classical randomized techniques that assume oblivious queries. Our focus is the problem of furthest neighbor search in this adaptive setting, a fundamental problem in several learning tasks, including diversity maximization, outlier and anomaly detection, adversarial example generation, and more. We present the first adversarially robust data structure for $c$-approximate furthest neighbor queries that achieves query time $\tilde{O}( \min( d n^{1/c^2}, n^{2/c^2} + d))$. This matches the $n$ dependency in the query time of the seminal result by Indyk [SODA’03] for $c$-approximate furthest neighbor in the oblivious setting, and improves upon the $\tilde{O}(n + d)$ query time achieved via the adaptive distance estimation framework of Cherapanamjeri and Nelson [NeurIPS’20] for a wide range of natural parameters. To complement this result, we present an adversarial attack against oblivious approximate furthest neighbor algorithms. Specifically, we show that the data structure from the algorithm by Indyk fails to maintain its guarantees against adaptive queries.

paragraphs: Furthest-neighbor search asks which stored point lies farthest from a query, with approximate search allowing a controlled departure from the exact answer. This paper studies a demanding setting: each new query can depend on answers to earlier queries. Such feedback can undermine randomized search methods whose guarantees assume queries are chosen without observing the system’s previous responses.

The authors construct an adversarially robust data structure for c-approximate furthest-neighbor queries. For n points in d dimensions, its query time is approximately the smaller of d times n raised to 1/c² and n raised to 2/c² plus d, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Its dependence on n matches the cited classical result for queries without adaptive feedback.

The new bound also improves on the cited adaptive distance-estimation approach across a wide range of natural parameter choices. Complementing the construction, the authors give an adaptive attack against the classical furthest-neighbor data structure. Together, these results show both why adaptivity requires attention and how efficient approximate search can accommodate it.
summary.tldr: A new approximate furthest-neighbor data structure preserves guarantees under adaptive queries while matching classical dependence on dataset size.

title: Adversarially Robust Approximate Furthest Neighbor

abstract: and reconstruct complex geometry at high resolution. Recent methods often convert raw meshes into signed distance fields (SDFs), but this preprocessing can be lossy, especially for open or non-watertight assets. Render-supervised VAEs such as TripoSF avoid this conversion by matching rendered depth and normal maps, yet render losses supervise only the visible geometry for each view, leaving many latent voxels weakly constrained while still incurring unnecessary decoding and attention costs. We introduce Focusing, a view-consistent sparse-voxel training scheme for efficient 3D VAEs. Given a training view, Focusing performs depth-driven voxel carving directly in the structured latent space: voxels inconsistent with the rendered depth are removed before decoding, allowing the decoder and attention layers to operate only on locally relevant geometry. This view-dependent sparsity reduces memory and computation while concentrating learning on surface regions that contribute to the render. To stabilize training across shapes and viewpoints, we further propose adaptive zooming, which adjusts camera intrinsics to keep the number of active voxels within a target range and strengths supervision for fine details. The VAE is trained with render-based depth, normal, mask, and perceptual losses, together with sparse-voxel total variation and a brief TSDF warm-up to improve convergence and suppress holes. Across standard reconstruction benchmarks, Focusing improves Chamfer Distance and F-score over strong baselines while substantially reducing video random access memory (VRAM) consumption, enabling $1024^3$-resolution VAE training with $512^3$ trunks using as little as 50 GB of VRAM. These results demonstrate that local, view-consistent sparsity is an effective path toward higher-resolution and more efficient 3D VAE training.

title: Focusing: View-Consistent Sparse Voxels for Efficient 3D VAE Training

abstract: The insatiable demand for web-scale training data has exposed LLMs to a subtle but consequential threat: the absorption of malicious scam content into model weights and its subsequent reproduction during inference. In November 2024, this risk materialized when a developer reportedly lost 2,500 USD after ChatGPT generated an otherwise routine cryptocurrency trading script containing a live phishing URL. To systematically investigate this problem, we introduce Scam2Prompt, an automated auditing framework that crawls known scam websites, infers their functional intent, and synthesizes innocuous developer-style prompts — the kind of legitimate coding requests a programmer might naturally submit — to evaluate whether LLMs reproduce the underlying scam endpoints. Importantly, our approach requires neither jailbreaking nor adversarial prompting; all 1,377 prompts in our benchmark, Innoc2Scam-bench, which is automatically constructed by Scam2Prompt, were human-validated as benign coding tasks. Evaluation of seven production LLMs released in 2025 on Innoc2Scam-bench shows that the vulnerability proves both persistent and severe: malicious code generation rates range from 12.9% to 47.3% across the evaluated models, and no tested model proves immune. State-of-the-art guardrails and RAG-based agents offer only limited protection, underscoring an urgent need for explicit URL validation in LLM-assisted software development pipelines.
