paragraphs: Scam2Prompt investigates whether language models reproduce malicious web endpoints in response to ordinary coding requests. The concern is that scam content absorbed during training can later appear in generated code. The paper frames this as a risk that can arise even when the person requesting assistance has a legitimate task.

The auditing pipeline crawls known scam websites, infers their functional purpose, and generates developer-style requests that could expose reproduction of those endpoints. Its benchmark contains 1,377 prompts, all human-validated as benign coding tasks. The audit therefore does not depend on jailbreaks or adversarial instructions to elicit the problematic outputs.

Across seven production models, reported malicious-code generation rates range from 12.9% to 47.3%, with every tested model affected. The authors also find limited protection from leading guardrails and retrieval-augmented agents. These results establish a recurring vulnerability within the benchmark and motivate explicit URL validation in software-development workflows that incorporate model-generated code.
summary.tldr: Scam2Prompt finds that benign coding requests can cause production language models to reproduce malicious scam endpoints.

title: Scam2Prompt: A Scalable Framework for Auditing Malicious Scam Endpoints in Production LLMs

abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has received increasing attention for solving complex decision-making tasks. Networked MARL approaches offer a decentralized solution for parameter sharing to accelerate training via value aggregation. However, existing federated aggregations rely on convex averaging that may fail to converge to global optima and cause learning rollback in the online learning setting. In this paper, we formally characterize the learning rollback phenomenon arising from aggregating value estimates with unequal uncertainty under heterogeneous online update depths. We propose a novel adaptive global consensus (AGC) mechanism for Q-value aggregation in decentralized MARL policy evaluation, which dynamically adjusts aggregation weights based on agents’ uncertainty. We establish theoretical guarantees on accelerated convergence and bounded learning variance with empirical validations, advancing the state-of-art MARL theory.

paragraphs: Decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning allows agents to share value estimates to accelerate learning. However, agents may have performed different numbers of online updates, leaving their estimates with unequal uncertainty. The paper studies how averaging those estimates can undo learning progress, a phenomenon it calls learning rollback.

The authors formally characterize rollback under heterogeneous update depths and propose adaptive global consensus for Q-value aggregation in policy evaluation. The mechanism changes aggregation weights according to agents’ uncertainty. This makes the combination responsive to differences in the estimates instead of treating a conventional convex average as an adequate default throughout learning.

The paper establishes theoretical guarantees for accelerated convergence and bounded learning variance, accompanied by empirical validation. These results support accounting for uncertainty when agents exchange value information during online learning. The stated scope is decentralized policy evaluation: the contribution concerns how shared Q-value estimates are combined and how that combination affects convergence and variability, rather than a general guarantee of globally optimal policies for every multi-agent task.
summary.tldr: Uncertainty-aware Q-value aggregation addresses learning rollback and provides convergence and variance guarantees for decentralized multi-agent policy evaluation.

title: Value Aggregation with Uncertainty in Online Decentralized MARL

abstract: Visual localization in complex indoor environments remains a critical challenge for robotics and AR applications. Sequential localization, where pose estimates are refined over time, is important for autonomous agents. However, traditional methods often require storing extensive image databases or point clouds, leading to significant overhead. This paper introduces a novel, lightweight approach to sequential visual localization using 3D scene graphs. Our method represents the environment with a compact scene graph, where nodes represent objects (with coarse meshes) and edges encode spatial relationships. For each image in the localization phase, we extract per-patch semantic features, predicting object identities. Localization is performed within a particle filter framework. Each particle, representing a camera pose, projects the coarse object meshes from the scene graph into the image, assigning object identities to patches based on visibility. The similarity of the per-patch features, in the input image, and object features from the scene graph determines the weight of a particle. Subsequent images are incorporated sequentially, refining the pose estimate. By leveraging a compact scene graph and efficient semantic matching, our method significantly reduces storage while maintaining performance on real-world datasets. The code is available at https://github.com/DmblnNicole/sg2loc.

paragraphs: Indoor visual localization estimates a camera’s pose from what it sees. Repeating that process across an image sequence can refine the estimate, but conventional environment representations may require large image collections or point clouds. SG2Loc instead uses a compact 3D scene graph, with objects represented by coarse meshes and edges describing spatial relationships.

For each incoming image, the system extracts semantic features from image patches to predict object identities. A particle filter maintains candidate camera poses. Each candidate projects the graph’s object meshes into the image and determines which object identities should be visible in each patch. Agreement between the observed patch features and the graph’s object features sets the candidate’s weight.

As additional images arrive, the filter incorporates their evidence and refines the pose estimate. Evaluations on real-world datasets show substantially reduced storage while maintaining performance. The contribution lies in making a compact object-based environment representation useful for sequential localization: coarse geometry supplies visibility predictions, semantic matching scores those predictions, and the image sequence progressively improves the estimate.
summary.tldr: SG2Loc localizes a camera over time by matching image semantics against a compact 3D object graph within a particle filter.

title: SG2Loc: Sequential Visual Localization on 3D Scene Graphs

abstract: In this paper, we study the fully dynamic k-center with outliers problem, where points are inserted and deleted over time and the goal is to maintain an approximate clustering while discarding up to z outliers. Existing algorithms typically rely on radius guessing to maintain cluster representations, leading to update and query times that depend explicitly on the aspect ratio $\Delta$. We propose a layered-sampling framework that avoids radius guessing by maintaining a hierarchy of sampled structures, which can separate most inliers from potential outliers and refine the remaining uncertain points. The resulting algorithm achieves $\tilde{O}(k^2/\epsilon^4)$ update and query time independent of $\Delta$, while guaranteeing a constant-factor approximation with $(1+\epsilon)z$ outliers discarded. Under mild assumptions, our result is complemented by a lower bound in metric space query model.

We propose a layered-sampling framework that avoids radius guessing by maintaining a hierarchy of sampled structures, which can separate most inliers from potential outliers and refine the remaining uncertain points. The resulting algorithm achieves $\tilde{O}(k^2/\epsilon^4)$ update and query time independent of $\Delta$, while guaranteeing a constant-factor approximation with $(1+\epsilon)z$ outliers discarded. paragraphs: Dynamic clustering must keep its solution useful as points arrive and disappear. This paper studies the k-center problem with outliers, where a limited number of points may be excluded. Existing approaches often guess candidate clustering radii, making their update and query costs depend explicitly on the dataset’s aspect ratio, denoted Δ.

The proposed method replaces radius guessing with layered sampling. It maintains a hierarchy of sampled structures that separates most ordinary points from possible outliers, then refines the treatment of points whose status remains uncertain. This organization removes explicit dependence on Δ from the stated update and query time.

The algorithm achieves a constant-factor approximation with update and query time of approximately O(k²/ε⁴), suppressing logarithmic factors. Its guarantee allows discarding up to (1+ε)z points, slightly exceeding the original outlier budget z. That allowance is part of the result. A complementary lower bound holds under mild assumptions in the metric-space query model, adding a theoretical account of the problem’s computational difficulty.
summary.tldr: Layered sampling maintains approximate dynamic k-center clustering without aspect-ratio-dependent time, while allowing a modestly enlarged outlier budget.

title: New Algorithms for Fully-Dynamic k-center with Outliers

abstract: This work investigates the "small-vs-large gap", where repeating on fewer samples can lead to compute saving during training compared to using a larger dataset. This is observed across algorithmic tasks, architectures and optimizers and cannot be explained using prior theory. We argue that the speedup comes from appropriate layer-wise growth enabled by sampling biases, which is more pronounced when the dataset size is smaller. We provide both theoretical analysis and empirical evidence from various interventions. Our results suggest that using a smaller dataset with more repetitions is not just a fallback strategy under data scarcity, but can be proactively leveraged as a favorable inductive biases for optimization, particularly in reasoning tasks.

Our results suggest that using a smaller dataset with more repetitions is not just a fallback strategy under data scarcity, but can be proactively leveraged as a favorable inductive biases for optimization, particularly in reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies a counterintuitive training effect: repeatedly using fewer examples can require less computation to learn than using a larger dataset. The authors observe this small-versus-large gap across algorithmic tasks, model architectures, and optimizers. Their question concerns the dynamics of learning, rather than simply how much distinct data is available.

They argue that sampling biases in smaller datasets can encourage appropriate growth across the model’s layers. Because these biases are more pronounced with fewer samples, repeated exposure can create a favorable direction for optimization. The paper develops a theoretical analysis and uses empirical interventions to support this proposed explanation for the training speedup.

The findings suggest that dataset repetition can be a deliberate optimization choice, particularly for reasoning tasks, instead of serving only as a response to scarce data. The claim is that smaller repeated datasets can help under the investigated conditions; it does not establish that reducing data always improves training. The broader contribution is an explanation of how the composition and reuse of training samples can influence learning speed.
summary.tldr: The paper links faster learning from repeated smaller datasets to sampling biases that encourage favorable layer-wise growth.

title: Less Data, Faster Training: repeating smaller datasets speeds up learning via sampling biases

abstract: Pairwise comparisons combined with aggregation methods like Elo have become central to evaluating generative models, yet concerns remain that they reward superficial stylistic cues or display judge biases. In a more positive turn, we show that model rankings from pairwise comparisons strongly agree with ground-truth-based accuracy rankings when such ground truth is available for comparison. By converting five well-known benchmarks into free-form generative evaluations, we find that Elo rankings achieve a Spearman correlation above 0.9 with accuracy rankings and substantially outperform direct evaluation when the judge is weak. Furthermore, style and judge bias have only minor effects on model rankings, despite most judgments occurring on pairs where both candidate answers are correct (or incorrect). On such pairs, we find that repetition after the final answer (echo) is a causal driver of judge preference.

paragraphs: Comparing two generated answers and aggregating preferences into rankings is a common way to evaluate models. A concern is that judges may prefer attractive writing or familiar styles over correct answers. This paper tests how closely such preference rankings agree with accuracy rankings in settings where ground-truth answers are available.

The authors convert five established benchmarks into free-form generation tasks and aggregate pairwise judgments using Elo. The resulting rankings have Spearman correlations above 0.9 with rankings based on correctness. Pairwise evaluation also substantially outperforms direct evaluation when the judge is weak. These results indicate that comparative judgments can recover useful accuracy ordering in the tested settings despite concerns about judge reliability.

Style and judge bias have only minor effects on the overall rankings, even though most comparisons involve answers that share the same correctness status. Within those pairs, repeating content after the final answer, termed echo, causally influences preference. Thus, a local stylistic bias can coexist with strong aggregate agreement between preference rankings and accuracy.
summary.tldr: Across five benchmarks, pairwise preference rankings closely track accuracy rankings despite a detectable preference for repetition after final answers.

title: Correct Looks Better: Pairwise Comparisons Reveal Accuracy Rankings

abstract: Probabilistic circuits (PCs) enable exact and tractable inference but employ data independent mixture weights that limit their ability to capture local geometry of the data manifold. We propose Voronoi tessellations (VT) as a natural way to incorporate geometric structure directly into the sum nodes of a PC. However, naïvely introducing such structure breaks tractability. We formalize this incompatibility and develop two complementary solutions: (1) an approximate inference framework that provides guaranteed lower and upper bounds for inference, and (2) a structural condition for VT under which exact tractable inference is recovered. Finally, we introduce a differentiable relaxation for VT that enables gradient-based learning and empirically validate the resulting approach on standard density estimation tasks.

We propose Voronoi tessellations (VT) as a natural way to incorporate geometric structure directly into the sum nodes of a PC. However, naïvely introducing such structure breaks tractability. We formalize this incompatibility and develop two complementary solutions: (1) an approximate inference framework that provides guaranteed lower and upper bounds for inference, and (2) a structural condition for VT under which exact tractable inference is recovered. paragraphs: Probabilistic circuits are attractive because they permit exact inference with tractable computation. However, their mixture weights do not depend on the data, limiting how well they reflect local geometric structure. This paper investigates whether Voronoi tessellations can introduce that structure directly into the sum nodes where circuit components are combined.

The central difficulty is that a straightforward geometric modification destroys tractability. The authors formalize this incompatibility and develop two responses. One permits approximate inference while guaranteeing lower and upper bounds on the answer. The other identifies a structural condition on the Voronoi tessellation under which exact, tractable inference becomes possible again. The alternatives provide different ways to retain useful computational guarantees.

To make the geometric construction learnable, the paper introduces a differentiable relaxation that supports gradient-based optimization. The resulting approach is evaluated on standard density-estimation tasks. The contribution connects geometric expressiveness with controlled inference: bounds remain available in the approximate setting, while exact computation is recovered under the stated structural condition.
summary.tldr: Voronoi-based probabilistic circuits incorporate local geometry through bounded approximate inference or exact inference under a structural condition.

title: Geometry-Aware Probabilistic Circuits via Voronoi Tessellations

abstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) improves generalization by minimizing the worst-case loss within a fixed parameter-space radius neighborhood. SAM and its variants mainly rely on a first-order linearized surrogate, while flat minima are inherently a second-order (curvature) notion. We revisit this mismatch and propose Loss-Equated SAM (LE-SAM), which inverts the traditional SAM mechanism that replaces the fixed perturbation radius with a fixed loss-space budget, effectively removing gradient-norm–dominated learning signals and shifting optimization toward curvature-dominated terms. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and tasks demonstrate the strong generalization ability of LE-SAM that consistently outperforms SAM and even its variants, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
originalAbstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) improves generalization by minimizing the worst-case loss within a fixed parameter-space radius neighborhood. SAM and its variants mainly rely on a first-order linearized surrogate, while flat minima are inherently a second-order (curvature) notion. We revisit this mismatch and propose Loss-Equated SAM (LE-SAM), which inverts the traditional SAM mechanism that replaces the fixed perturbation radius with a fixed loss-space budget, effectively removing gradient-norm–dominated learning signals and shifting optimization toward curvature-dominated terms. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and tasks demonstrate the strong generalization ability of LE-SAM that consistently outperforms SAM and even its variants, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Sharpness-Aware Minimization trains a model by considering the worst loss near its current parameters. The usual method defines that neighborhood with a fixed radius in parameter space. This paper points out a mismatch: SAM commonly relies on a first-order approximation, while the flatness it seeks is fundamentally about second-order curvature.

Loss-Equated SAM changes what stays fixed during the perturbation step. Instead of imposing a constant distance in parameter space, it uses a fixed budget in loss space. According to the authors, this removes learning signals dominated by gradient magnitude and shifts optimization toward curvature-dominated terms. That change directly targets the mismatch between the approximation used to construct perturbations and the geometry motivating the method.

Across diverse benchmarks and tasks, the authors report that LE-SAM consistently generalizes better than SAM and its variants, reaching state-of-the-art performance in their experiments. The stated results support loss-based perturbation control as an effective route to sharper attention to curvature during training.
summary.tldr: LE-SAM replaces a fixed parameter-space perturbation radius with a fixed loss budget to emphasize curvature and improve reported generalization.

title: Fix the Loss, Not the Radius: Rethinking the Adversarial Perturbation of Sharpness-Aware Minimization

abstract: Deep learning optimization relies heavily on the assumption of smooth loss landscapes, a condition systematically violated by modern architectures due to non-smooth components like ReLU activations and quantization operators. In such non-smooth regimes, adaptive optimizers such as Adam suffer from gradient chattering—violent oscillations caused by conflicting signals within the Clarke subdifferential—leading to poor convergence and suboptimal generalization. To address this, we introduce Singularity-aware Adam (S-Adam), a novel optimizer that stabilizes training by dynamically modulating step sizes based on local geometric instability. Our key contribution is the Local Geometric Instability (LGI) metric, a computationally efficient estimator of the Clarke subdifferential diameter derived from the variance of randomized directional derivatives. S-Adam incorporates an adaptive damping mechanism $\exp(-\lambda \rho_t)$ that decelerates updates in high-instability regions while preserving fast convergence in smooth basins. We provide a rigorous convergence analysis using differential inclusions, proving that S-Adam converges almost surely to $(\delta, \epsilon)$-Clarke stationary points at the optimal $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ rate. Empirical evaluations on Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) and high-noise small-batch learning demonstrate that S-Adam consistently outperforms AdamW and Prox-SGD, achieving accuracy gains of up to +4.54% on CIFAR-100 and +4.27% on TinyImageNet while effectively mitigating gradient oscillations.

The paper connects these conflicts to gradient chattering: large oscillations that interfere with optimization. Singularity-aware Adam, or S-Adam, adjusts update sizes according to the instability of the local geometry.

summary.tldr: S-Adam probes local non-smooth geometry and damps unstable updates, reducing oscillations and improving reported training accuracy.

title: Singularity-aware Optimization via Randomized Geometric Probing: Towards Stable Non-smooth Optimization

abstract: Accelerating diffusion models via feature caching has progressed from static feature reuse to polynomial extrapolation, yet current cache-then-forecast strategies still rely on hand-crafted approximation families (e.g., Taylor or Hermite bases) that can misalign with the non-stationary, layer-specific dynamics of generative features. This paper introduces EigenCache, a training-free framework that re-frames diffusion acceleration as covariance-adaptive feature forecasting and uncertainty-aware temporal design. EigenCache models cached feature trajectories as time-indexed stochastic processes and estimates layer-wise temporal kernels from a small calibration set. Under the resulting scalar temporal-kernel approximation, the Gaussian-process posterior mean, i.e., Kriging, is risk-optimal within the scalar-weighted linear predictor class; under joint Gaussianity, it further coincides with the MMSE estimator. This formulation generalizes fixed-basis forecasting from a covariance-adaptive perspective while providing a closed-form posterior-variance proxy for prediction uncertainty. Leveraging this proxy, EigenCache selects computation anchors by maximizing a log-determinant information-gain objective over denoising timesteps, a monotone submodular objective with a near-optimal greedy solution. Across image, video, transformer, U-Net, and LoRA-adapted diffusion models, EigenCache achieves a strong speed–fidelity Pareto frontier and provides a principled mechanism for robust compute allocation.

paragraphs: Diffusion-model caching saves computation by reusing or forecasting intermediate features. Fixed forecasting formulas can fit poorly when feature dynamics differ across layers and change over time. EigenCache addresses this with a training-free approach that learns temporal covariance patterns from a small calibration set and uses them to forecast cached features.

The method represents feature trajectories as time-indexed stochastic processes and estimates a temporal kernel for each layer. Under its scalar temporal-kernel approximation, the Gaussian-process posterior mean minimizes risk among scalar-weighted linear predictors. With the additional assumption of joint Gaussianity, it is also the minimum mean-squared-error estimator. These qualifications define the scope of its optimality claim.

The same formulation supplies a posterior-variance proxy for uncertainty. EigenCache uses it to choose denoising timesteps for fresh computation through a log-determinant information objective with a near-optimal greedy solution. Across image and video models, multiple architectures, and LoRA adaptations, experiments show a strong balance between speed and fidelity. Forecasting and computation placement are thus guided by a shared model of temporal uncertainty.
summary.tldr: EigenCache uses learned temporal covariance and uncertainty estimates to forecast diffusion features and choose when fresh computation is most useful.

title: EigenCache: Rethinking Diffusion Acceleration as Covariance-Optimal Forecasting and Submodular Information Allocation

abstract: Weak-to-strong generalization (W2SG) is the phenomenon in which a powerful student model, trained on labels produced by a weaker teacher, ultimately outperforms the teacher on the target task. In this work, we theoretically investigate how W2SG can arise via a generalized bias–variance decomposition under Bregman divergence. We show that the expected population risk gap between the student and the teacher is characterized by the expected misfit between the two models. Unlike earlier misfit-based analyses, our theory removes several restrictive assumptions, e.g., it does not require the student hypothesis class to be convex. Our results indicate that W2SG is more likely when the student effectively approximates the teacher’s posterior mean. Specializing to squared loss, we provide a sufficient condition (illustrated through a concrete example) under which the student converges to its posterior mean teacher; in particular, increasing the student model size can ensure this convergence. For cross-entropy loss, our analysis further suggests that lowering the entropy of the student’s predictive distribution can promote W2SG. We also find that the reverse cross-entropy, unlike the standard forward cross-entropy, is less sensitive to the teacher’s predictive uncertainty. Finally, we verify these theoretical insights empirically and demonstrate that incorporating reverse cross-entropy consistently improves student performance.

paragraphs: A strong student can sometimes outperform the weaker teacher whose labels it learns from. This paper studies that phenomenon using a generalized bias–variance decomposition based on Bregman divergence. The analysis characterizes the expected population-risk gap through the expected mismatch between teacher and student, without requiring several earlier assumptions, including convexity of the student's hypothesis class.

The results indicate that improvement is more likely when the student approximates the teacher's posterior mean effectively. For squared loss, the authors give a sufficient condition for convergence to this mean teacher and illustrate it with an example. Within that result, increasing student size can ensure convergence; the claim is conditional rather than a general guarantee that larger students always outperform their teachers.

For cross-entropy, the analysis suggests that reducing student predictive entropy can promote weak-to-strong generalization. It also finds reverse cross-entropy less sensitive to teacher uncertainty than forward cross-entropy. Empirical tests support the theoretical insights, with reverse cross-entropy consistently improving student performance in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: A Bregman bias–variance analysis identifies conditions that favor students outperforming weaker teachers and motivates reverse cross-entropy training.

title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization via Bregman Bias–Variance Decomposition

abstract: We study high-dimensional convex empirical risk minimization (ERM) under general non-Gaussian data designs. By heuristically extending the Convex Gaussian Min–Max Theorem (CGMT) to non-Gaussian settings, we derive an asymptotic min–max characterization of key statistics, enabling approximation of the mean $\mu_{\hat{\theta}}$ and covariance $C_{\hat{\theta}}$ of the ERM estimator $\hat{\theta}$. Specifically, under a concentration assumption on the data matrix and standard regularity conditions on the loss and regularizer, we show that for a test covariate $x$ independent of the training data, the projection $\hat{\theta}^\top x$ approximately follows the convolution of the (generally non-Gaussian) distribution of $\mu_{\hat{\theta}}^\top x$ with an independent centered Gaussian variable of variance $\mathrm{tr}\!\big(C_{\hat{\theta}}\,\mathbb{E}[xx^\top]\big)$. This result clarifies the scope and limits of Gaussian universality for ERMs. Numerical simulations across diverse losses and models are provided to validate our theoretical predictions and qualitative insights.

paragraphs: This paper investigates when Gaussian approximations describe the behavior of models fitted by high-dimensional convex empirical risk minimization. Its focus is data that are not Gaussian. The central question is how much of the fitted model's predictive behavior can still be represented by Gaussian variation, and which effects of the original data distribution remain visible.

The authors heuristically extend the Convex Gaussian Min–Max Theorem to obtain an asymptotic characterization of estimator statistics, including approximate means and covariances. Under a data-matrix concentration assumption and regularity conditions on the loss and regularizer, they characterize the fitted model's projection onto an independent test input. Approximately, this projection combines the mean estimator's projection with an independent, centered Gaussian contribution.

The mean-projection term can remain non-Gaussian, while the Gaussian contribution has variance determined by estimator covariance and the test input's second moment. This decomposition explains how Gaussian-like fluctuations can coexist with persistent non-Gaussian behavior. Simulations across different losses and models support the predictions and qualitative conclusions. The result is an approximate, assumption-dependent account of universality and its breakdown, grounded in a heuristic theoretical extension.
summary.tldr: A heuristic analysis characterizes predictions as an approximately Gaussian fluctuation plus a potentially non-Gaussian mean contribution under stated assumptions.

title: Characterization of Gaussian Universality Breakdown in High-Dimensional Empirical Risk Minimization

abstract: While sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have generated significant excitement, a series of negative results have added to skepticism about their usefulness. Here, we establish a conceptual distinction that reconciles competing narratives surrounding SAEs. We argue that even if SAEs may be less effective for acting on known concepts, SAEs are especially powerful tools for discovering unknown concepts. This distinction separates existing negative results from positive results, and suggests several classes of SAE applications. Specifically, we outline use cases for SAEs in (i) ML interpretability, explainability, fairness, auditing, and safety, and (ii) social and health sciences.

paragraphs: This position paper addresses conflicting assessments of sparse autoencoders. Enthusiasm about their usefulness has been challenged by negative results, but the authors argue that the disagreement partly reflects different goals. They distinguish using a sparse autoencoder to act on a concept already known to the researcher from using it to discover a concept that was previously unrecognized.

That distinction changes how evidence should be interpreted. A method could be less effective at the first task while remaining valuable for the second. The authors argue that sparse autoencoders are especially powerful for discovering unknown concepts, and use this separation to reconcile positive findings with negative ones. The claim allows weaknesses in some applications without treating them as decisive evidence against every use.

The paper then outlines applications organized around discovery. These include interpretability, explanation, fairness, auditing, and safety within machine learning, as well as work in social and health sciences. Its contribution is a conceptual framework and application agenda: evaluate the tool against the purpose it serves, and give exploratory discovery a distinct place in judging its usefulness.
summary.tldr: Sparse autoencoders may be especially useful for discovering unknown concepts even when they are less effective at acting on known ones.

abstract: The paper is concerned with two-class active learning. While the common approach for collecting data in active learning is to select samples close to the classification boundary, better performance can be achieved by taking into account the prior data distribution. The main contribution of the paper is a formal framework that incorporates clustering into active learning. The algorithm first constructs a classifier on the set of the cluster representatives, and then propagates the classificationdecision to the other samples via a local noise model. The proposed model allows to select the most representative samples as well as to avoid repeatedly labeling samples in the same cluster. During the active learning process, the clustering is adjusted using the coarse-to-fine strategy in order to balance between the advantage oflarge clusters and the accuracy of the data representation. The results of experiments in image databases show a better performance ofour algorithm compared to the current methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies active learning for two classes, where a learner chooses which examples should receive labels. Selecting examples near a classification boundary is a common strategy, but it does not fully use information about how the data are distributed. The proposed framework brings clustering into that choice so that the learner can request labels for representative examples.

The algorithm first builds a classifier using representatives of the clusters. It then extends those decisions to other examples through a local noise model. This provides a way to use a representative's classification beyond that single example while accounting for local uncertainty. It also helps avoid spending repeated labeling effort on samples from the same cluster.

The clusters change during learning through a coarse-to-fine process. Larger clusters provide broader coverage, while finer clusters can represent the data more accurately. The method balances those benefits rather than fixing the grouping throughout learning. Experiments on image databases report better performance than the compared methods, supporting the usefulness of incorporating data distribution into sample selection.
summary.tldr: Adaptive clustering helps an active learner choose representative examples and avoid redundant labeling, with improved results on image databases.

title: Active learning using pre-clustering

abstract: This paper presents an algorithm to estimate simultaneously both mean and variance of a non parametric regression problem. The key point is that we are able to estimate variance locally unlike standard Gaussian Process regression or SVMs. This means that our estimator adapts to the local noise. The problem is cast in the setting of maximum a posteriori estimation in exponential families. Unlike previous work, we obtain a convex optimization problem which can be solved via Newton’s method.
originalAbstract: This paper presents an algorithm to estimate simultaneously both mean and variance of a non parametric regression problem. The key point is that we are able to estimate variance locally unlike standard Gaussian Process regression or SVMs. This means that our estimator adapts to the local noise. The problem is cast in the setting of maximum a posteriori estimation in exponential families. Unlike previous work, we obtain a convex optimization problem which can be solved via Newton’s method.

paragraphs: Regression involves estimating how an output changes with its inputs, but observations can also differ in how noisy they are. This paper presents an algorithm that estimates both the mean response and the variance in a nonparametric regression problem. Its central feature is estimating variance locally, allowing the estimated noise level to vary across the input space.

Local variance estimation matters because a prediction of the average response does not describe how widely observations fluctuate around that response. By estimating both quantities together, the method adapts to local noise. The authors identify this capability as a difference from standard Gaussian process regression and support vector machines.

The estimation problem is formulated using maximum a posteriori estimation within exponential families. This combines the estimation of mean and variance in a single mathematical framework. The authors obtain a convex optimization problem, contrasting their formulation with previous work, and state that it can be solved with Newton’s method. The contribution thus concerns both what the model estimates and how the joint estimation problem can be computed.
summary.tldr: The paper jointly estimates regression means and locally varying noise through a convex optimization formulation.

abstract: Many learning algorithms rely on the curvature (in particular, strong convexity) of regularized objective functions to provide good theoretical performance guarantees. In practice, the choice of regularization penalty that gives the best testing set performance may result in objective functions with little or even no curvature. In these cases, algorithms designed specifically for regularized objectives often either fail completely or require some modification that involves a substantial compromise in performance. We present new online and batch algorithms for training a variety of supervised learning models (such as SVMs, logistic regression, structured prediction models, and CRFs) under conditions where the optimal choice of regularization parameter results in functions with low curvature. We employ a technique called proximal regularization, in which we solve the original learning problem via a sequence of modified optimization tasks whose objectives are chosen to have greater curvature than the original problem. Theoretically, our algorithms achieve low regret bounds in the online setting and fast convergence in the batch setting. Experimentally, our algorithms improve upon state-of-the-art techniques, including Pegasos and bundle methods, on medium and large-scale SVM and structured learning tasks.

paragraphs: Many optimization guarantees depend on an objective having enough curvature, especially strong convexity. Yet the regularization choice that gives the best test performance may leave a learning objective nearly flat or without that curvature. This creates tension between the statistical choice of objective and the requirements of an efficient training algorithm.

The paper introduces online and batch algorithms based on proximal regularization. They solve the original problem through a sequence of modified optimization tasks whose objectives have greater curvature. This supplies useful optimization structure along the way while retaining the original learning problem as the goal. The approach applies to models including SVMs, logistic regression, structured predictors, and conditional random fields.

The theoretical results provide low regret in online learning and fast convergence in batch learning. Experiments on medium- and large-scale SVM and structured learning tasks report improvements over methods including Pegasos and bundle methods. These results support proximal regularization as a way to train effectively when the preferred regularization setting does not itself provide much curvature.
summary.tldr: Proximal regularization enables efficient online and batch training when the preferred learning objective has little or no curvature.

title: Proximal regularization for online and batch learning

abstract: The most commonly used learning algorithm for restricted Boltzmann machines is contrastive divergence which starts a Markov chain at a data point and runs the chain for only a few iterations to get a cheap, low variance estimate of the sufficient statistics under the model. Tieleman (2008) showed that better learning can be achieved by estimating the model's statistics using a small set of persistent "fantasy particles" that are not reinitialized to data points after each weight update. With sufficiently small weight updates, the fantasy particles represent the equilibrium distribution accurately but to explain why the method works with much larger weight updates it is necessary to consider the interaction between the weight updates and the Markov chain. We show that the weight updates force the Markov chain to mix fast, and using this insight we develop an even faster mixing chain that uses an auxiliary set of "fast weights" to implement a temporary overlay on the energy landscape. The fast weights learn rapidly but also decay rapidly and do not contribute to the normal energy landscape that defines the model.

Tieleman (2008) showed that better learning can be achieved by estimating the model's statistics using a small set of persistent "fantasy particles" that are not reinitialized to data points after each weight update. With sufficiently small weight updates, the fantasy particles represent the equilibrium distribution accurately but to explain why the method works with much larger weight updates it is necessary to consider the interaction between the weight updates and the Markov chain. We show that the weight updates force the Markov chain to mix fast, and using this insight we develop an even faster mixing chain that uses an auxiliary set of "fast weights" to implement a temporary overlay on the energy landscape. The fast weights learn rapidly but also decay rapidly and do not contribute to the normal energy landscape that defines the model.

paragraphs: Training restricted Boltzmann machines requires estimates of statistics under the model. Contrastive divergence obtains inexpensive estimates by starting short Markov chains at data points. Persistent contrastive divergence instead retains a small collection of simulated particles across weight updates. With sufficiently small updates, these particles accurately represent the equilibrium distribution.

This paper investigates why persistence can also work with much larger weight updates. The explanation requires considering learning and sampling together: the authors show that weight changes force the Markov chain to mix quickly. The evolving model therefore affects how the sampler moves, making the interaction between parameter updates and sampling central to the method's behavior.

Using that insight, the authors introduce auxiliary fast weights that learn rapidly and decay rapidly. They temporarily modify the energy landscape used by the chain, producing even faster mixing. These auxiliary weights do not form part of the normal energy landscape defining the model. Their role is to improve sampling through a temporary influence distinct from the model's learned parameters.
summary.tldr: Rapidly changing auxiliary weights improve persistent contrastive divergence by temporarily altering the sampling landscape to accelerate mixing.

title: Using fast weights to improve persistent contrastive divergence

abstract: While it is now well-known in the standard binary classi cation setup, that, under suitable margin assumptions and complexity conditions on the regression function, fast or even super-fast rates (i.e. rates faster than n^(-1/2) or even faster than n^-1) can be achieved by plug-in classi ers, no result of this nature has been proved yet in the context of bipartite ranking, though akin to that of classi cation. It is the main purpose of the present paper to investigate this issue. Viewing bipartite ranking as a nested continuous collection of cost-sensitive classi cation problems, we exhibit a global low noise condition under which certain plug-in ranking rules can be shown to achieve fast (but not super-fast) rates, establishing thus minimax upper bounds for the excess of ranking risk.

It is the main purpose of the present paper to investigate this issue. Viewing bipartite ranking as a nested continuous collection of cost-sensitive classi cation problems, we exhibit a global low noise condition under which certain plug-in ranking rules can be shown to achieve fast (but not super-fast) rates, establishing thus minimax upper bounds for the excess of ranking risk.

paragraphs: Bipartite ranking concerns ordering examples associated with two classes. This paper asks how quickly the excess ranking risk can decrease as training data increases. It focuses on plug-in ranking rules, following results showing that plug-in classifiers can achieve fast, and sometimes super-fast, rates under suitable assumptions.

The authors analyze ranking as a nested continuous family of cost-sensitive classification problems. This viewpoint connects the ranking task to classification problems with varying costs. They identify a global low-noise condition under which certain plug-in ranking rules achieve fast convergence rates, establishing minimax upper bounds on excess ranking risk.

The qualification on the rates is central: the paper establishes fast rates, but not super-fast ones. In the terminology used in the abstract, fast means faster than the inverse square root of sample size, while super-fast means faster than its inverse. The result therefore extends part of the classification picture to ranking under a stated low-noise condition without transferring the strongest classification rate claim.
summary.tldr: Under a global low-noise condition, certain plug-in ranking rules achieve fast, but not super-fast, excess-risk rates.

title: Minimax Learning Rates for Bipartite Ranking and Plug-in Rules
